2. CORE CONCEPTS & DEFINITIONS (all quotable verbatim)¶

2.2 The layered nature of governance¶

  • Governance has multiple dimensions and layers.
  • At the national level it entails the joint activity of the government + civil society + private sector, to ensure decisions and actions are transparent, inclusive, accountable and responsive to the needs of the people.
  • Memorise this as the "governance triangle": State — Market — Civil Society.

2.3 [ADDED] Government vs Governance (a 3-mark opener)¶

GovernmentGovernance

NatureFormal, hierarchical, authority-basedProcess-based, networked, negotiated
Legitimacy fromConstitutional officePerformance, consent, participation
Question askedWho rules?How are decisions made and enforced?

[ADDED] Governance ≠ Good Governance. Fukuyama's definition is value-neutral (capacity); UNDP/World Bank definitions are normative. conclusion resolves this — see §5.3.

2.4 TRANSPARENCY — the definitional & philosophical bank ¶

Master definition (liftable verbatim):Transparency in governance refers to the openness, clarity and accessibility of government processes, actions and decision-making to the public. It emphasises ensuring that citizens are informed about the activities and policies of their government, fostering accountability and trust. This principle is critical to good governance, as it helps reduce corruption, enhance civic engagement and improve public services.

Note the causal chain the definition hides — memorise it as a flow-line:

Openness → informed citizens → accountability + trust → ↓corruption, ↑civic engagement, ↑public services

ThinkerDomainArgument (liftable)The phrase to steal
Joseph Stiglitz (Nobel laureate, Economics) Information economics"Information is a public good" — access to information should be available to everyone. Transparency in governance is essential because it reduces the "information asymmetry" between the government and the public, ensuring citizens can hold governments accountableinformation asymmetry; information is a public good
Jeremy Bentham (classical utilitarian) Deterrence"The more strictly we are watched, the better we behave." Transparency discourages wrongdoing because individuals in power are aware that their actions are under public scrutinypublic scrutiny as deterrent
John Locke (17th-c. political philosopher)LegitimacyGovernments derive authority from the consent of the governed; for that consent to be meaningful, citizens must have access to information about the actions and motives of those in powerinformed consent → legitimacy
Amartya Sen (Nobel laureate, Economics) Welfare outcomesEmphasises the role of transparency in preventing famines and ensuring social welfare. Transparent governance contributes to better policy-making and implementation because it forces governments to be answerable to the peoplefamines and free press; answerability

Why this quartet wins marks: it gives you four different justifications for the same institution — economic (Stiglitz: market-failure/asymmetry), behavioural (Bentham: deterrence), political-philosophical (Locke: legitimacy of consent) and developmental (Sen: outcomes). Use one from each family instead of four transparency quotes that all say "trust".

[ADDED] Sen's famine argument, in full, for a 15-marker: Sen's Poverty and Famines (1981) and Development as Freedom (1999) argue no substantial famine has ever occurred in a functioning democracy with a free press and regular elections — because information flow forces early government response. This is the strongest empirical defence of transparency available to you. states the conclusion; this is the mechanism behind it.

▲ [ADDED] Attribution caution (consistent with §5.1): the Bentham line as worded is a popular condensation of his Panopticon argument, not a verifiable verbatim sentence. Safe as "as Bentham's panopticon logic is often summed up…". Stiglitz's "information is a public good" is genuine (Nobel lecture, 2001; On Liberty, the Right to Know, and Public Disclosure, 1999) and is the safest of the four to attribute directly.

Cross-reference: Transparency is aspect #1 of the seven in §5.1 and characteristic #3 of good governance in §10.1. §2.4 supplies the theory; §3.3 supplies the statute (RTI) that operationalises it.

2.5.1 The four definitions, in ascending order of usefulness¶

SourceDefinition (liftable)The word to steal
The source's own working definitionE-governance = "the use of Information and Communication Technology (ICT) to transform the way governments interact with citizens, businesses, and other government agencies." The objective is "to provide efficient, transparent, and accessible public services while enhancing citizen participation in governance."transform, not digitise; and note the three counterparties — they are the G2C/G2B/G2G map of §4.11.1 stated as a definition
Subhash Bhatnagar ("a leading expert on e-governance in developing countries")"The application of information technology to the processes of government functioning to bring about 'SMART' governance, i.e., Simple, Moral, Accountable, Responsive, and Transparent governance."SMART — Simple · Moral · Accountable · Responsive · Transparent. The single most liftable acronym in the module
Dr Nandan Nilekani (the architect of India's Aadhaar system)"E-governance is not just about technology, but about fundamentally changing the way government interacts with citizens, improving transparency, accountability, and efficiency in public service delivery.""not just about technology" — this is the thesis sentence of the 2024, 2020 and 2018 PYQs, in the words of the man who built the platform
The United Nations E-Government Survey"E-Government (or E-Governance) is the use of ICT and its application by the government for the provision of information and public services to the people. It aims at improving the quality of governance through improved participation, efficiency, and transparency."participation · efficiency · transparency — the three-part test to close on

Open any e-governance answer with Bhatnagar and close it with Nilekani. Bhatnagar gives you a standard (SMART) against which any project can be graded; Nilekani gives you the caution that the standard is not met by procurement. Between them they frame every PYQ in §17's e-governance table.

▲ One caution the source does not give and you should.The source treats e-government* and e-governance as interchangeable — the UN definition it quotes literally brackets them together. [ADDED] The distinction is examinable and costs one line: e-government is the delivery of services by electronic means; e-governance is the **use of ICT to change how decisions are made and how the state is held to account. The Interactive Service Model (§5.7.2) is precisely where e-government becomes e-governance — which is why the 2024 PYQ is about that model and no other.

2.5.2 The measurement instrument ¶

  • UN e-Government Development Index (EGDI) — "measures the willingness and capacity of countries to use ICTs for delivering public services."
  • India ranked 97 out of 193 countries in the 2024 survey, which the source itself reads as "reflecting the scope for improvement."
  • ▲ [ADDED] The EGDI is a composite of three sub-indices — the Online Service Index (OSI), the Telecommunication Infrastructure Index (TII) and the Human Capital Index (HCI). Cite the three components, because they are the answer to the 2021 PYQ in one line: India's constraint is not the service layer but the infrastructure and human capital layers — which is exactly what §13.10's rural and gender data shows. ▲ Verify the current rank and the sub-index scores before the exam; the source gives the rank and nothing beneath it.
  • The examiner's point, and it is the most usable sentence in §2.5:India runs one of the largest digital public-infrastructure estates in the world and sits in the bottom half of the index that measures it — because the EGDI grades reach and capability, not scale. §13.10.1's 821 million users and §13.10.4's 5.88 lakh service centres are not a refutation of the rank; they are the reason the rank is a paradox worth writing about.

2.6 THE CITIZEN'S CHARTER — the definitional bank ¶

2.6.1 The two definitions the source gives, and why it gives two¶

#Definition (verbatim from )The word to steal
1 "Citizen's Charter is a written, voluntary declaration by service providers that highlights the standards of service delivery that they must subscribe to, availability of choice for consumers, avenues for grievance redressal and other related information.""written, voluntary declaration" — the whole of the Charter's weakness is in the second adjective
2 "A Citizen's Charter is an official document issued by public service providers (government agencies, ministries, departments, or local authorities) that outlines the standard of services that the public can expect from the organization. Its purpose is to make public services more transparent, accountable, and responsive by explicitly setting service standards, timelines, grievance mechanisms, and citizen rights.""official document"; transparent · accountable · responsive; standards · timelines · grievance mechanisms · citizen rights

The two definitions are not the same claim, and the gap between them is the examinable point.Definition 1 calls the Charter voluntary; Definition 2 calls it official. Both are true and they are the reason the instrument under-performs: it is issued with the authority of the state and undertaken with the obligation of a promise. ▲ The source never reconciles them — but its own "Absence of Legal Backing" slide (§5.8.3) does the work: "The Charter lacks statutory backing, which limits its enforceability. Citizens have no legal recourse if the services promised under the Charter are not delivered."

Open any Charter answer with the collision, not with a definition:a Citizen's Charter is an official document containing a voluntary promise — which is why India has spent thirty years trying to convert it into a statute (§3.20).

2.6.2 The four elements every Charter must contain (assembled from Definition 1 + Definition 2 — a guaranteed one-marker)¶

  1. Standards of service delivery the provider "must subscribe to" — what is promised.
  2. Timelines — by when.
  3. Availability of choice for consumers — the element candidates always drop, and it is the one that carries the UK origin (§13.11.1).
  4. Avenues for grievance redressal — what happens when the promise fails.

(Definition 2 adds a fifth: citizen rights.)

Mnemonic: standards · timelines · choice · redressal. ▲ Note what is not in either definition: a designated officer, an appeal, a penalty or compensation. Those four appear only when a legislature supplies them — Madhya Pradesh 2010, Karnataka 2011, Maharashtra's RTS Act** (§3.20, §3.19.4) — which is the single most useful sentence in this module.

InstrumentSource of obligationWhat the citizen getsEnforceable?

2.7 AI IN GOVERNANCE — the definitional bank ¶

2.7.1 The source's definition, clause by clause¶

Verbatim:

"Artificial Intelligence (AI) in governance refers to the use of data-driven algorithms, machine learning, automation, and predictive analytics by the state to improve policy formulation, service delivery, regulation, and public administration."

ClauseWhat it is doingThe word to steal
"data-driven algorithms, machine learning, automation, and predictive analytics"The four techniques. Note that the source does not distinguish them, and you should not either — the examinable distinction is not technicalpredictive — the one technique that is genuinely new to governance; the other three are e-governance continued
"by the state"The scope limiter, and the most important two words in the definition. This is AI used by government, not AI regulated by governmentby the state
"to improve policy formulation, service delivery, regulation, and public administration"The four functions. Read them as a ladder of ambition: administration is housekeeping, service delivery is e-governance, regulation is enforcement, and policy formulation is the state's core deliberative actpolicy formulation — the limb that raises every democratic objection in §14

The examinable point the source never states, and it should open your answer.The definition covers AI as an instrument of the state and says nothing about AI as an object of the state's regulation. ▲ These are two different syllabus questions and candidates routinely fuse them. teaches only the first. Say so explicitly and you have separated yourself in one line:"AI in governance" is the state's use of algorithmic capability; "AI governance" is the state's regulation of it — India has a strategy for the first and, as this module records, no statute for the second (§3.21.1). ▲ And note the source's own conclusion slide slips between the two senses — it warns against "unchecked algorithmic governance", which is a regulatory claim resting on a definition that never mentioned regulation.

▲ [No text is missing from the definition.] The slide's third line renders as "the … state … to … improve" with wide gaps — that is justified-text spacing in the PDF export, not a redaction. The sentence is complete as quoted above; the compendium checked the page at source resolution.

2.7.2 The three-word test — what makes AI governance rather than computing [ADDED — the source gives no test]¶

  1. AUTOMATION — the machine performs a task a clerk performed. This is §5.9.1's stage 1 and raises no constitutional question.
  2. PREDICTION — the machine states what is likely, about a person or a place, before it happens. This is where predictive policing (§4.13.8) and dropout early-warning (§4.13.6) live, and where Art. 14 enters (§3.21.4).
  3. DECISION — the machine's output determines an entitlement, a liability or a suspicion. This is where Art. 21 due process enters, and it is the only one of the three that the source's "human-in-the-loop" reform (§15, reform 91) actually addresses.

Use the ladder to grade any example in one line:automation is efficiency, prediction is power, and decision is jurisdiction. Then apply it to the source's own scope map (§5.9.2) and the shape of the topic appears at once:chatbots and e-Courts digitisation are automation; crop-yield, outbreak and dropout models are prediction; ▲ fraud detection in DBT, facial-recognition matching and technology-based crop-insurance yield estimation are decision — and all three are deployed at national scale in this source (§4.13.3, §4.13.8).

2.7.3 AI in governance against the compendium's other technology layers [ADDED — the comparison the source never draws]¶

LayerWhat the citizen interacts withWhat the state gainsThe citizen's remedy
Computerisation (§5.9.1 stage 1)A recordStorage and retrievalRTI Act 2005 — the record is disclosable (§3.3)
E-Governance (§2.5, §4.11)A portalService delivery at distance▲ None by default; a State RTS Act where one exists (§3.19.4)
AI Governance (§2.7)▲ An output about them they may never seePrediction, targeting, detection▲ None at all — no disclosure duty, no clock, no appeal, no explanation

This table is the strongest argument in the module and it takes one sentence to state:each layer of Indian digital governance has given the citizen a new thing to receive and, until the last one, a way to contest it — AI is the first layer that produces a determination about a citizen with no corresponding right to see it, question it or appeal it. Note the specific loss: the RTI Act reaches a record*; ▲ it does not obviously reach a model, a training dataset or a *score [ADDED — untested; see]. That single observation converts §3.3's RTI material into live AI material, and it is the cheapest cross-module marks in this version.**

3.3 THE RIGHT TO INFORMATION ACT, 2005 — provision by provision ¶

3.3.1 "Public authority" — the definition that decides coverage ¶

"Public authority" means any authority or body or institution of self-government established or constituted —

  • (a) by or under the Constitution;
  • (b) by any other law made by Parliament;
  • (c) by any other law made by State Legislature;
  • (d) by notification issued or order made by the appropriate Government, and includes any —

- (i) body owned, controlled or substantially financed;

- (ii)non-Government organisation substantially financed.

Why this matters: limbs (d)(i) and (d)(ii) are the litigation frontier — "substantially financed" is what drags NGOs, private schools, colleges, co-operative societies and sports bodies (BCCI) into RTI. Every "should X be under RTI?" question turns on this clause.

[ADDED] This is Sec. 2(h). The Act's other key definitions — Sec. 2(f) "information", Sec. 2(j) "right to information" — are not in; see gaps.

3.3.2 Suo motu / proactive disclosure — Sec. 4 ¶

Verbatim: "It shall be a constant endeavour of every public authority to take steps to provide as much information suo motu to the public at regular intervals through various means of communications, including internet, so that the public have minimum resort to the use of this Act to obtain information."

The single most examinable line in the Act. The statutory intent is that RTI applications should be rare — a well-run state makes the Act largely unnecessary. Pair it with RaaG's finding that ~50% of applications exist only because Sec. 4 is not complied with (§13) and you have a complete argument in three sentences.

3.3.3 Request for obtaining information — Sec. 6¶

  • A person desiring information shall make a request in writing or through electronic means, in English or Hindi or in the official language of the area, accompanying such fee as may be prescribed, to — (a) the Central Public Information Officer (CPIO) or State Public Information Officer (SPIO) of the concerned public authority;
  • (b) the Central/State Assistant Public Information Officer (APIO), specifying the particulars of the information sought.
  • Proviso: where the request cannot be made in writing, the CPIO/SPIO shall render all reasonable assistance to the person making the request orally to reduce the same in writing. (The literacy safeguard — quote it in any "RTI and the marginalised" answer.)
  • An applicant shall NOT be required to give any reason for requesting the information, or any personal details except those necessary for contacting him.
  • Transfer of application: where the information is held by another public authority, or its subject matter is more closely connected with the functions of another public authority, the public authority shall transfer the application (or the appropriate part of it) to that other public authority and inform the applicant immediately about such transfer — transfer to be made as soon as practicable and in no case later than five days from receipt.

"No reasons required" is the philosophical heart of the Act — it converts information from a favour granted on justification into a right exercised without explanation. Contrast directly with the Official Secrets Act mindset (§3.4), where the citizen must justify access.

3.3.4 Disposal of request — Sec. 7 (the timelines examiners love)¶

SituationTime limitConsequence
Ordinary requestAs expeditiously as possible, and in any case within 30 days of receipt — either provide the information on payment of prescribed fee or reject it for any of the permitted reasons—
Information concerning the life or liberty of a person 48 hours of receiptThe Act's emergency channel
Failure to decide within the period—The CPIO/SPIO "shall be deemed to have refused the request" — deemed refusal, which is what opens the appeal
Transfer to another public authority (Sec. 6)Not later than 5 daysApplicant informed immediately

Deemed refusal is the concept to name. Without it, inaction would be un-appealable and the Act would die by silence.

[ADDED] Not in but standard: first appeal to a senior officer within 30 days (Sec. 19(1)), second appeal to the CIC/SIC within 90 days (Sec. 19(3)); the burden of proving denial was justified lies on the PIO (Sec. 19(5)); fee is waived for BPL applicants and where the authority misses the deadline (Sec. 7(5)/7(6)). Verify before quoting.

3.3.5 Exemption from disclosure of information — Sec. 8(1) (learn the sequence a–j)¶

ClauseExempted information
(a)Disclosure of which would prejudicially affect the sovereignty and integrity of India, the security, strategic, scientific or economic interests of the State, relation with foreign State, or lead to incitement of an offence
(b)Information expressly forbidden to be published by any court of law or tribunal, or the disclosure of which may constitute contempt of court
(c)Disclosure of which would cause a breach of privilege of Parliament or the State Legislature
(d)Commercial confidence, trade secrets or intellectual property, disclosure of which would harm the competitive position of a third party — unless the competent authority is satisfied that larger public interest warrants disclosure
(e)Information available to a person in his fiduciary relationship — unless larger public interest warrants disclosure
(f)Information received in confidence from a foreign Government
(g)Disclosure of which would endanger the life or physical safety of any person, or identify the source of information or assistance given in confidence for law enforcement or security purposes
(h)Information which would impede the process of investigation or apprehension or prosecution of offenders
(i)Cabinet papers, including records of deliberations of the Council of Ministers, Secretaries and other officers — Proviso: the decisions of the Council of Ministers, the reasons thereof, and the material on the basis of which the decisions were taken, SHALL be made public after the decision has been taken and the matter is complete or over
(j) Personal information the disclosure of which has no relationship to any public activity or interest, or which would cause unwarranted invasion of the privacy of the individual — unless the CPIO/SPIO or the appellate authority is satisfied that the larger public interest justifies disclosure

The Parliament-parity proviso (originally attached to Sec. 8(1)):"Provided that the information which cannot be denied to the Parliament or a State Legislature shall not be denied to any person."

This single line embodies the Act's equality principle — the citizen stands in the shoes of the legislator. ▲ Its scope has since been narrowed by the DPDP Act 2023 — see §3.5.

Structural point worth a mark: exemptions (d), (e) and (j) carry a public interest override; the rest do not. Knowing which clauses can be overridden is the difference between a generic and a precise answer.

3.3.6 Penalty and disciplinary action — Sec. 20 ¶

Penalty — Sec. 20(1)Disciplinary action — Sec. 20(2)
Trigger (identical list)CPIO/SPIO has, without any reasonable cause, refused to receive an application, or not furnished information within the time specified, or denied the request, or knowingly given incorrect, incomplete or misleading information, or destroyed information which was the subject of the request, or obstructed in any manner in furnishing the informationSame list, but qualified by "without any reasonable cause and persistently"
Imposed byCentral/State Information Commission, at the time of deciding any complaint or appealSame
Quantum₹250 per day till application is received or information furnished — total not to exceed ₹25,000Recommend disciplinary action against the CPIO/SPIO under the service rules applicable to him
SafeguardsCPIO/SPIO must be given a reasonable opportunity of being heard before any penalty; the burden of proving that he acted reasonably and diligently is ON the CPIO/SPIO—

The reversed burden of proof is the pro-disclosure design feature — the citizen need not prove bad faith; the officer must prove diligence. Note the escalation logic: one lapse → penalty; persistent lapses → disciplinary action.

3.3.7 Overriding effect — Sec. 22 ¶

The RTI Act overrides any other law inconsistent with it, including the Official Secrets Act, 1923. (Applied in §3.4.)

3.3.8 Exemption of organisations — Sec. 24(2) & the Second Schedule¶

The Centre may, by notification, add intelligence and security organisations to the Second Schedule, placing them outside RTI. CERT-In was added at serial number 27 in 2023 — see §3.4.4.

3.4 THE OFFICIAL SECRETS ACT, 1923 vs RTI ¶

3.4.1 The core relationship¶

The relationship between the RTI Act, 2005 and the Official Secrets Act (OSA), 1923 is defined by a tension between the principles of transparency and secrecy in governance. Both laws serve legitimate purposes but address fundamentally different objectives: RTI aims to foster openness and public participation in democratic processes, while OSA seeks to safeguard national security by preventing the disclosure of sensitive information.

3.4.2 Different philosophies — secrecy vs transparency ¶

RTI Act, 2005OSA, 1923
Origin & eraEnacted in a post-liberalisation, post-globalisation IndiaColonial-era law designed to protect the state's security apparatus
Rooted inDemocratic accountability and the public's right to knowPreventing espionage, unauthorised disclosure of state documents, and activities threatening the integrity of the British Empire in India
Emerged fromDemands for greater transparency, reducing corruption, enabling citizens to hold public authorities accountableThe assumption that certain information must remain secret to preserve national security and diplomatic interests
Core premiseInformation is a public good, and access to it is essential for an informed citizenrySecrecy is the default; disclosure is the deviation

3.4.3 Balancing national security and the right to know¶

  • The RTI Act gives citizens the right to access information held by public authorities, but this right is not absolute. Under Sec. 8, categories are exempt if disclosure could harm the sovereignty and integrity of India, security, foreign relations, or lead to incitement of offences.
  • This is where the OSA becomes relevant: information classified as "secret" under OSA — especially concerning defence, intelligence and security — may fall under these exemptions.
  • However, there is NO explicit provision in the OSA that defines "official secrets" or the scope of protected information, leading to a broad and often arbitrary interpretation by authorities.

3.4.4 Does RTI supersede OSA? ¶

  • The RTI Act, via Sec. 22, states it will override any other law (including OSA) in cases of inconsistency.
  • In theory, RTI takes precedence over OSA, except when the public interest in maintaining confidentiality clearly outweighs the public interest in disclosure.
  • Meaning: secrecy is the exception, not the rule — government information should generally be disclosed unless national security is demonstrably at risk.Key OSA provisions:
  • "Prohibited place" — the operative but undefined concept.
  • Penalty for spying — 3 years and 14 years. [ADDED] The 14-year maximum attaches to offences touching defence/security installations; 3 years to lesser categories. does not map which is which — verify against the bare Act before quoting a specific figure.
  • Unauthorised communication (the s.5-type offence): any person having in his possession or control any secret official code or password, or any sketch, plan, model, article, note, document or information which relates to or is used in a prohibited place, or which is likely to assist an enemy, or which relates to a matter the disclosure of which is likely to affect the sovereignty and integrity of India, the security of the State or friendly relations with foreign States, or which has been entrusted in confidence to him by a person holding office under Government, or to which he has had access owing to his position — commits an offence if he:

- (a)wilfully communicates the code/password/sketch/plan/model/article/note/document or information to any person other than a person to whom he is authorised to communicate it, or a Court of Justice, or a person to whom it is in the interests of the State his duty to communicate it;

- (b)uses the information for the benefit of any foreign power or in any manner prejudicial to the safety of the State;

- (c)retains the sketch/plan/model/article/note/document when he has no right to retain it, or contrary to his duty, or wilfully fails to comply with directions regarding its return or disposal;

- (d)fails to take reasonable care of, or so conducts himself as to endanger the safety of, the sketch, plan etc.

  • Unauthorised use of uniforms; falsification of reports, forgery, personation and false documents: if any person, for the purpose of gaining admission or of assisting any other person to gain admission to a prohibited place, or for any other purpose prejudicial to the safety of the State — (a)uses or wears, without lawful authority, any naval, military, air force, police or other official uniform, or any uniform so nearly resembling the same as to be calculated to deceive, or falsely represents himself to be a person entitled to wear it.
  • Offences by companies: if the person committing an offence under the Act is a company, every person who at the time of the offence was in charge of, and was responsible to, the company for the conduct of its business, as well as the company, shall be deemed guilty and liable to be proceeded against and punished accordingly.

3.4.5 Areas of overlap and tension ¶

  • Classified documents: a key area of conflict. The OSA does not specify what constitutes classified information, allowing authorities broad discretion to label documents secret. This discretion has led to over-classification of information, often with the aim of avoiding public scrutiny.
  • Public interest test: the RTI Act contains a public interest override — even if information falls within an exempt category, it can still be disclosed if there is a larger public interest at stake (e.g. corruption or human rights violations). OSA has no such provision, creating a rigid framework that can stifle public access to crucial information.Live illustrations:Rafale · investigative journalism · corruption in defence purchases.

[ADDED] In the Rafale review (2019) the Supreme Court rejected the Government's objection that the petitioners relied on documents "stolen" from the Ministry of Defence, holding the documents admissible and noting the RTI Act's overriding effect — the single best case to cite for §3.4.4. Verify the citation before using it as a formal case reference.

3.4.6 Case law and reform recommendations¶

SourceYearPosition
Manohar Parrikar v. Goa State Information Commission 2014The court upheld the principle that public interest must be balanced with concerns of national security, reinforcing that OSA should not be misused to suppress information unless its release genuinely threatens state interests
Law Commission of India, 43rd Report 1971Argued for codifying the definition of "official secrets", ensuring the OSA does not obstruct public access to information that serves democratic accountability, particularly where public welfare or governance issues are at stake
Second Administrative Reforms Commission Report of June 2006Inter alia recommended that the OSA, 1923 should be REPEALED and substituted by a chapter in the National Security Act containing provisions relating to official secrets

Answer structure for "RTI vs OSA": philosophies (§3.4.2) → Sec. 8 + Sec. 22 legal position (§3.4.3–4) → over-classification & absence of a public interest test in OSA (§3.4.5) → Parrikar + Law Commission 43rd + 2nd ARC repeal recommendation (§3.4.6) → conclude with "secrecy is the exception, not the rule."

3.4.7 RTI & CERT-In — the 2023 exemption ¶

What happened: The Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) was exempted from the purview of the RTI Act in 2023 by including it in the Second Schedule of the RTI Act, which lists intelligence and security organisations exempt from disclosing information under RTI. CERT-In is the national agency responsible for handling cybersecurity incidents in India and plays a crucial role in preventing, responding to and mitigating cyber threats. The Centre used its powers under sub-section (2) of Section 24 of the RTI Act, including CERT-In at serial number 27 of the Second Schedule.

Positives:

  1. Protection of national security — CERT-In deals with sensitive cybersecurity issues such as hacking attempts, cyber espionage, critical infrastructure security and national defence cyber threats. Disclosure of specific details could harm national security by exposing vulnerabilities hostile actors could exploit. Exemption ensures sensitive data on cyber defences, threat intelligence and coordination with international security agencies remains protected.
  2. Enhancing cybersecurity operations — CERT-In collaborates with private companies, international agencies and government bodies; exemption fosters trust and cooperation, as firms may be more willing to share sensitive data knowing it will not be publicly disclosed. A more confidential environment allows CERT-In to respond swiftly without details being prematurely disclosed, which could compromise ongoing investigations or response efforts.
  3. Protection of personal data and confidential information — CERT-In works with businesses and individuals whose private data might be involved in cyber incidents; exemption prevents sensitive personal or business-related information from becoming publicly accessible, protecting data privacy.
  4. Preventing cyber panic — ensures potentially alarming information about ongoing threats, vulnerabilities or attacks does not lead to unnecessary public fear or panic. Disclosure of unverified or incomplete information could cause public mistrust and confusion, especially where incidents are still under investigation.

Negatives:

  1. Reduced transparency and accountability — limits public oversight of CERT-In's operations. Given the increasing importance of cybersecurity in governance, there are concerns that CERT-In's actions, spending or collaborations might not be scrutinised effectively. This can create trust deficits, especially where questions arise about how CERT-In handles breaches of government databases, investigations into cybercrimes, or collaborations with private companies.
  2. Possibility of misuse — without RTI scrutiny, CERT-In's powers could be misused to withhold information the public has a legitimate right to know — e.g. significant breaches affecting citizens, companies or even electoral processes. This could lead to lack of disclosure where public interest, rather than national security, is at stake — major cyberattacks affecting personal data, election integrity or public infrastructure.
  3. Limited information on major cyber incidents — citizens and researchers may face barriers to understanding the scale and nature of cyber threats impacting India. Since CERT-In is not obliged to share information under RTI, it could prevent transparency in incidents with broader public or economic consequences, such as data breaches involving large-scale public databases (e.g. Aadhaar) or critical infrastructure like the power grid. This also affects public awareness and reduces factual data available to researchers, journalists and advocacy groups.

This is a ready-made 10-marker ("Critically examine the exemption of CERT-In from the RTI Act"): 4 arguments each way, plus the structural critique that Sec. 24(2) allows exemption by executive notification without parliamentary scrutiny [ADDED].

3.5 THE DIGITAL PERSONAL DATA PROTECTION (DPDP) ACT, 2023 & RTI ¶

✓ Corroboration note. repeats this entire section slide-for-slide and word-for-word — the divider, the four fault-line headings, the Sec. 8(1) reinterpretation and Sec. 35. Nothing was added, nothing was changed. Treat the wording below as and therefore safe to quote.

3.5.1 What the DPDP Act changed in RTI ¶

  • The law changed the text and context of RTI by reinterpreting the provisions of Section 8(1). Those provisions stated that "information which cannot be denied to the Parliament or a State Legislature shall not be denied to any person."
  • Now it is only applicable to Section 8(1)(j) and not to the whole of Section 8(1).

Say this precisely in the exam: the Parliament-parity proviso, which once anchored all of Sec. 8(1), has been shrunk to a single clause. Combined with the deletion of the public-interest and public-activity qualifiers in 8(1)(j) [ADDED], personal information becomes near-absolutely exempt — which is why activists call it the single biggest dilution of RTI since 2005.

3.5.2 The four fault-lines¶

▲ Both decks give these four as heading-only slides with no body text. reproduces the same four titles, again blank. [ADDED] What this now tells you: the blankness is deliberate lecture design — these are oral-delivery slides, not a rendering fault or a truncated file. So the lecturer's own words are not recoverable from any PDF; check your class notes or the recording. The content below is my [ADDED] reconstruction — verify before quoting.

#Fault-line[ADDED] content
1Broad definitions of personal dataDPDP defines "personal data" as any data about an individual who is identifiable by or in relation to such data — wide enough to cover names of beneficiaries, muster rolls, ration lists, officials' postings and service records. Almost any record naming a person becomes arguably exempt
2Increased denials based on personal data protectionPIOs acquire a safe, un-appealable ground for refusal; expect a rise in blanket 8(1)(j) denials for welfare beneficiary lists, MGNREGA muster rolls and PDS records — precisely the data used for social audit
3Lack of public interest overrideThe amended 8(1)(j) removes the "unless larger public interest justifies disclosure" balancing test for personal data — the PIO no longer weighs, he simply refuses. Mirrors the OSA's rigidity critiqued in §3.4.5
4Impact on journalistic and investigative workThe DPDP Act contains no journalistic exemption (unlike the 2018 Srikrishna draft and the EU GDPR). Investigative reporting on assets, appointments, contracts and beneficiaries loses its documentary base — cf. CWG and Adarsh, both broken with RTI-obtained records (§13.2)

3.5.3 Section 35, DPDP Act 2023 — the immunity clause (: + )¶

Verbatim: "No suit, prosecution or other legal proceedings shall lie against the Central Government, the Board, its Chairperson and any Member, officer or employee thereof for anything which is done or intended to be done in good faith under the provisions of this Act or the rules made thereunder."

Read this alongside RTI Sec. 20's reversed burden of proof (§3.3.6) and the contrast writes itself: RTI makes the official prove diligence; DPDP presumes good faith and bars proceedings. That single comparison is a high-value analytical line on the transparency–privacy trade-off.

3.6 THE WHISTLE BLOWERS PROTECTION ACT, 2014 ¶

3.6.1 What whistleblowing is (liftable)¶

The audacious act of exposing any kind of information or activity within a private, public or government organisation that is deemed illegal, unethical, or simply not right. This encompasses a vast spectrum of misconduct, ranging from corruption and fraud to abuse of power and other forms of malfeasance. Whistleblowers, those unsung heroes, play an indispensable role in shedding light on these dark practices. Often at great personal risk — including their careers, safety and well-being — they stand up for justice, ensuring organisations are held to the highest ethical and legal standards. Their courage and determination make them vital watchdogs in our society.

3.6.2 Structure of the Act¶

#FeatureContent
1Coverage and scopeCovers public servants across various government bodies, including central and state governments, public sector undertakings (PSUs), statutory authorities and other entities receiving government funding. Allows any person, including whistleblowers, to make complaints against corruption, abuse of power, or criminal activities by public servants
2Mechanism for complaintsComplaints made to a Competent Authority, responsible for receiving and acting on the disclosures. Complaints must be in writing, and the whistleblower is expected to provide adequate evidence or information for the investigation
3Confidentiality of identity Great emphasis on maintaining the confidentiality of the identity of whistleblowers. The identity of the complainant cannot be disclosed to anyone except authorities directly involved in the investigation or the competent authority
4Protection against victimisation Protection from retribution such as harassment, demotion or dismissal from employment. Any whistleblower who feels victimised after filing a complaint can report it to the competent authority, which can order appropriate action to safeguard the whistleblower
5Penalties for false complaintsPenalises malicious or false complaints — knowingly making false allegations can attract imprisonment up to 2 years and fines, depending on the seriousness
6ProcedureOn receiving a complaint, the competent authority must conduct a preliminary inquiry to determine if the disclosure warrants a full investigation. If investigation is deemed necessary, the authority can recommend disciplinary or criminal action against the public servant involved

Exceptions to disclosure: certain disclosures are exempt from investigation — complaints relating to matters that affect the sovereignty, integrity and security of India, and foreign relations. The Act is not applicable to the Special Protection Group and the Army.

3.6.3 Issues with the Act ¶

IssueDetail
No anonymous complaints The Act does not recognise anonymous complaints. For a complaint to be acted upon, the whistleblower must disclose their identity; without this disclosure, the competent authority is not obliged to investigate. The central contradiction: the Act promises confidentiality but forecloses anonymity
Potential for biased investigationsLack of impartiality — the Competent Authority tasked with investigating is often a senior official within the same organisation or hierarchy as the person accused. This internal structure can compromise the neutrality of the investigation, potentially leading to biased outcomes
Weak implementation in organisationsWhistleblower protection policies are not effectively implemented in many industries; programmes and policies outlined in organisational manuals are often not actively promoted or explained to employees, leading to lack of awareness and underuse of the mechanisms
No incentives for whistleblowersThe Act provides no monetary or other rewards, even where disclosures lead to a successful investigation or action — a lack of incentive that may discourage individuals from coming forward. [ADDED] Contrast the US False Claims Act / SEC bounty model, where whistleblowers receive a share of recoveries
Limited applicationDoes not apply to the private sector or state government employees.

▲ [CONFLICT: internal to — reproduced identically in ] — The Coverage and Scope slide states the Act covers public servants across "central and state governments", while a later slide states it "does not apply to the private sector or state govt employees." These cannot both be right as written. [ADDED] Resolution: the Act as passed covers public servants of the Centre and, in respect of state matters, applies to States with the State Government as competent-authority designator; the practical position is that most States have not notified machinery, so state employees are effectively uncovered. Treat the later slide as describing practice, the earlier as describing text. Verify before writing either as a flat statement.

▲ [CONFLICT: & vs §3.2 of this compendium] — Both decks describe the Act's provisions in the present operative tense, and neither ever states that the Act is not in force. §3.2 records it as "amendment pending; not operational." [ADDED] The accurate position: the Act received Presidential assent on 9 May 2014 but has never been brought fully into force — rules were not notified, and the Whistle Blowers Protection (Amendment) Bill, 2015 (which sought to bar disclosures falling in RTI Sec. 8(1) categories) lapsed with the 16th Lok Sabha. So: a law on the books, not on the ground. This is itself the best possible conclusion line for a whistleblowing answer — and a fact omits entirely.

3.7 THE LOKPAL AND LOKAYUKTAS ACT, 2013 ¶

How to use §3.7 and §4.2 together: §3.7 is the statute — what the Lokpal may look at, what it may not, and what happens after. §4.2 is the institution — who sits on it, how they get there, and how they leave. An "Is the Lokpal effective?" answer needs both; a "powers and jurisdiction" answer needs only this one.

3.7.1 Why the Act exists — the four-fold rationale (liftable verbatim; this is the Statement of Objects in slide form)¶

  1. The Constitution of India has established a Democratic Republic to ensure justice for all.
  2. India has ratified the United Nations Convention Against Corruption (UNCAC).
  3. The Government's commitment to clean and responsive governance has to be reflected in effective bodies to contain and punish acts of corruption.
  4. Necessary to enact a law, for more effective implementation of the said Convention and to provide for prompt and fair investigation and prosecution in cases of corruption.

Why this slide is worth memorising: it gives you the only "why an ombudsman?" argument you need, and it is tri-anchored — constitutional (justice for all), international (UNCAC), and administrative (prompt and fair investigation). Open any Lokpal answer with point 2 + point 4: "India ratified the UN Convention Against Corruption, and the Lokpal Act 2013 was enacted for its more effective implementation." That single sentence converts a domestic-politics answer into an international-obligations answer, which examiners reward.

[ADDED] The missing history the slide omits — India signed UNCAC in 2005 and ratified it in May 2011; the Act was passed after the Anna Hazare / India Against Corruption movement (2011) and the rival Jan Lokpal Bill, received assent on 1 January 2014 and came into force on 16 January 2014. The idea itself is older: the First ARC (1966–70) proposed Lokpal and Lokayukta (§11.2), and eight Lokpal Bills failed between 1968 and 2011. Verify the bill-count figure before quoting it.

3.7.2 Jurisdiction ¶

  • Jurisdiction of the Lokpal to include the Prime Minister, Ministers, members of Parliament, Groups A, B, C and D officers and officials of Central Government.
  • Societies, trusts and associations receiving foreign donation: the Act's reach extends to any body "in receipt of donation from any foreign source under the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act, 2010 in excess of ten lakh rupees in a year or such higher amount as the Central Government may, by notification, specify."

The two things to notice.

(i) It reaches the top. Unlike the CVC — which covers the bureaucracy but "except the political authorities" (§4.4) — the Lokpal reaches the PM, Ministers and MPs. That is the whole point of the institution, and the entire reason it took 45 years to legislate.

(ii) It reaches outside government. The FCRA ₹10-lakh clause pulls foreign-funded NGOs and trusts into an anti-corruption ombudsman's jurisdiction. Pair this with RTI Sec. 2(h)(d)(ii) — "non-Government organisation substantially financed" (§3.3.1). Both statutes use funding as the trigger for accountability, not legal form. That is a genuinely sophisticated observation and it works in any "should NGOs be publicly accountable?" question.

▲ [ADDED] Nuance on Groups C and D: the Lokpal's jurisdiction covers all four groups, but the procedure differs — complaints against Group C and D officials are referred to the CVC, which proceeds under the CVC Act and reports back; for Groups A and B the CVC conducts a preliminary inquiry and reports to the Lokpal, which then decides. own CVC slide (§4.3.4) says the Commission inquires into Lokpal referrals "in respect of Gr. A, B, C & D officials" — true, but it hides this difference in consequence. Verify the exact split before writing it as a bare rule.

3.7.3 The exclusions — what the Lokpal cannot touch ¶

(a) Exceptions for the Prime Minister (liftable)

  • Excluded subject-matter:international relations, external and internal security, public order, atomic energy and space.
  • Procedural lock:inquiry only when a full bench of the Lokpal consisting of its Chairperson and all Members considers the initiation of inquiry and at least two-thirds of its Members approves of such inquiry.

The examinable tension in one line: the PM is inside the jurisdiction (§3.7.2) but fenced by subject-matter and supermajority. Argue it both ways — for: an ombudsman able to destabilise a sitting PM on a frivolous complaint would be a constitutional hazard; against: the five excluded heads are exactly the fields in which the largest procurement scandals arise (defence, atomic energy, space), so the carve-out may exempt the most consequential corruption. Note the symmetry with WBPA's exceptions (sovereignty, integrity, security, foreign relations — §3.6.2) and RTI Sec. 8(1)(a) (§3.3.5): the same national-security fence appears in all three transparency statutes. Spotting that pattern across three Acts is a differentiating point.

[ADDED] The Act also requires such an inquiry to be held in camera, and if the Lokpal decides the complaint should be dismissed, the records shall not be published or made available to anyone. Verify before quoting.

(b) Parliamentary privilege — the Article 105(2) bar (verbatim)

"The Lokpal shall not inquire into any matter involved in, or arising from, or connected with, any such allegation of corruption against any member of either House of Parliament in respect of anything said or a vote given by him in Parliament or any committee thereof covered under the provisions contained in clause (2) of article 105 of the Constitution."

This is the cash-for-votes hole, and it is the single best cross-link in the module.Article 105(2) immunises an MP for anything said or any vote given in Parliament. Read literally — as the Supreme Court did in P.V. Narasimha Rao v. State (1998) [ADDED] — a bribe taken in order to vote became unreachable. The 2024 development: a seven-judge bench in Sita Soren v. Union of India (March 2024) overruled Narasimha Rao, holding that bribery is not protected by parliamentary privilege because the crime is complete on acceptance, irrespective of how the member later votes. [ADDED] Verify the case name and date before citing — but if it holds, the Lokpal Act's bar has been substantially narrowed by the judiciary, and saying so is a high-value, current-affairs-aware line.

3.7.4 Powers over the investigating machinery ¶

Verbatim: "The powers of superintendence over, and to give direction to the Delhi Special Police Establishment in respect of the matters referred by the Lokpal for preliminary inquiry or investigation to the Delhi Special Police Establishment under this Act."

Read the qualifier — it is the whole critique. Superintendence exists only "in respect of the matters referred by the Lokpal." The CBI remains, in every other respect, under the Central Government, with the CVC exercising general superintendence for PCA offences (§4.3.4). So the Lokpal directs a force it does not own, does not staff and does not fund. This is precisely the "Lack of Independence" critique itself records (§14, issue 22): the Lokpal still relies heavily on the CBI for investigations, which raises concerns about the autonomy of its investigations since the CBI itself has been subject to political interference. Link to Vineet Narain (1997) and the "caged parrot" observation [ADDED].

3.7.5 Special Courts ¶

  • The Central Government shall constitute such number of Special Courts, as recommended by the Lokpal, to hear and decide the cases arising out of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988 or under this Act.
  • The Special Courts constituted shall ensure completion of each trial within a period of one year from the date of filing of the case in the Court.

Two marks hide here.(i) The courts are constituted by the Central Government, only "as recommended by" the Lokpal — again, recommendation, not command. (ii) The one-year trial norm is the Act's answer to the standard objection that anti-corruption law dies in delay. Pair it with the RTI Sec. 7 thirty-day rule and the WBPA preliminary inquiry to show that all three statutes attach time-limits to accountability — and that in each case the time-limit is the first provision to be honoured in the breach.

3.7.6 Declaration of assets — and the 2016 Amendment ¶

  • Every public servant shall make a declaration of his assets and liabilities.
  • A public servant shall furnish to the competent authority the information relating to —

- (a) the assets of which he, his spouse and his dependent children are, jointly or severally, owners or beneficiaries;

- (b) his liabilities and that of his spouse and his dependent children.

  • 2016 Amendment: the mode of disclosure moved from 'website' to the 'manner prescribed by the Central Government'.

The 2016 Amendment is a small phrase with a large effect — and it is the same move as the 2019 RTI Amendment. In 2016, public disclosure on a website became disclosure in whatever manner the executive prescribes; in 2019, Information Commissioners' tenure and salary moved from the statute to central rules (§4.1.4). Name the pattern: "transfer of accountability terms from statute to executive rule-making." Two statutes, two amendments, one technique. Deploy this in any question on the erosion of oversight institutions — it is far stronger than complaining about either amendment alone.

[ADDED] The 2016 amendment also extended the filing deadline repeatedly and relaxed the requirement that spouses' and dependents' assets be publicly disclosed, following objections from NGOs and civil servants. Verify before quoting the detail.

3.7.7 Limitation — the seven-year bar ¶

Verbatim: "The Lokpal shall not inquire or investigate into any complaint, if the complaint is made after the expiry of a period of seven years from the date on which the offence mentioned in such complaint is alleged to have been committed."

Why this matters more than it looks. Grand corruption — defence procurement, PPP concessions, resource allocation — typically surfaces long after the decision, often only when a contract matures or a whistleblower retires. A seven-year clock running from commission, not from discovery, therefore excludes precisely the category of case the Lokpal was created for. Contrast the RTI Act, which has no limitation on the age of the record sought, and note that the Kushmal pond scam (§13.2) and the CWG/Adarsh exposés all turned on old records. Reform line → §15.

3.7.8 The LOKAYUKTA tier — and the Karnataka case study ¶

[ADDED] The Act's name is plural for a reason: it obliges every State to establish a Lokayukta, by law, within one year of the Act's commencement. The Centre legislated the state tier but left its design to the States — which is why Lokayuktas vary enormously in power. (Maharashtra was the first State to create a Lokayukta, in 1971 — verify.)

KARNATAKA LOKAYUKTA — the rise and dilution:

  • Justice N. Santosh Hegde (2006–2011).
  • Played a major role in investigating high-profile corruption cases, most notably the illegal mining scam involving politicians, including former Chief Minister B. S. Yediyurappa. This led to the resignation of the Chief Minister and increased public awareness of corruption issues.
  • The Karnataka Lokayukta was effective in initiating action against corrupt government officials, bringing accountability in public offices.
  • ▲ Over the years, its powers were diluted. The establishment of the Anti-Corruption Bureau (ACB) in Karnataka in 2016 took away many of its functions, leading to a significant reduction in its effectiveness.

This is the single most valuable case study in — use it as the proof of concept and the proof of fragility in one example. It establishes, empirically, that an ombudsman with a determined incumbent can topple a sitting Chief Minister. It then establishes that the same institution can be hollowed out in five years by creating a parallel body under executive control. The lesson to write: the binding constraint on an ombudsman is not its statutory powers but the political tolerance for their use — institutions are diluted not by repeal but by duplication. That sentence answers half the questions this topic generates.

[ADDED] The sequel worth knowing: the Karnataka High Court struck down the 2016 ACB notification in August 2022, restoring the Lokayukta's investigative powers. Verify before citing — but if correct, the case becomes even better: dilution by executive notification, reversal by judicial review.

3.8 SECTION 17A, PREVENTION OF CORRUPTION ACT, 1988 ¶

Heading (as in the Act): Enquiry or Inquiry or investigation of offences relatable to recommendations made or decision taken by public servant in discharge of official functions or duties.

"No police officer shall conduct any enquiry or inquiry or investigation into any offence alleged to have been committed by a public servant under this Act, where the alleged offence is relatable to any recommendation made or decision taken by such public servant in discharge of his official functions or duties, without the previous approval —

  • (a) in the case of a person who is or was employed, at the time when the offence was alleged to have been committed, in connection with the affairs of the Union, of that Government;
  • (b) in the case of a person who is or was employed, at the time when the offence was alleged to have been committed, in connection with the affairs of a State, of that Government;
  • (c) in the case of any other person, of the authority competent to remove him from his office, at the time when the offence was alleged to have been committed."

Argue this one both ways — it is designed for a "critically examine" question.

The defence: honest officers stopped taking decisions after a wave of prosecutions over bona fide commercial and policy judgments (the "policy paralysis" argument). 17A protects the decision, not the decider — it applies only where the alleged offence is "relatable to a recommendation made or decision taken… in discharge of official functions." It restores the older Sec. 6A DSPE Act protection that the Supreme Court had struck down in Subramanian Swamy v. CBI (2014) [ADDED] for creating an unconstitutional class of protected senior officers.

The critique: it makes the executive the gatekeeper of investigations into the executive, reintroducing by statute what the Court removed by judgment; and the approving authority is often the very government whose decision is under scrutiny. Combined with the Lokpal's seven-year bar (§3.7.7) and its dependence on the CBI (§3.7.4), it produces the outcome itself records: no significant convictions (§14, issue 23).

[ADDED] The safety valve to mention: approval is not required where a person is arrested on the spot on the charge of accepting or attempting to accept an undue advantage — i.e. trap cases proceed unhindered. And the 2018 amendment set a four-month outer limit for the approving authority to decide. Verify both before quoting.

The one-line link: Sec. 17A is to the anti-corruption architecture what Sec. 35 DPDP is to the data architecture (§3.5.3) and Sec. 8(1) is to RTI (§3.3.5) — a good-faith shield for the official, whose worth depends entirely on how honestly the shield is administered.

3.9 THE CENTRAL VIGILANCE COMMISSION ACT, 2003 — statutory basis ¶

The definition (liftable verbatim): The Central Vigilance Commission (CVC) is an apex governmental body in India that is responsible for promoting integrity, transparency and accountability in the country's public administration. It was established in 1964 as a result of the recommendations of the Santhanam Committee on Prevention of Corruption.Statutory anchor:Central Vigilance Commission Act, 2003.

The 1964 → 2003 gap is the exam point, and leaves it unexplained. [ADDED] The CVC existed for 39 years on an executive resolution alone — creatable, and therefore abolishable, by the government it was meant to police. Statutory status came only in 2003, in compliance with the Supreme Court's directions in Vineet Narain v. Union of India (1997) (§12.1), which also gave the CVC statutory supervision over the CBI. Write the sequence, not the date: executive body (1964) → judicial intervention (1997) → statutory body (2003). It demonstrates the judiciary as institution-builder, and it is the same arc as RTI's journey from Raj Narain (1975) to the Act of 2005.

Institutional detail — composition, appointment, tenure, removal, role and powers — is at §4.3. The turf-map against the Lokpal, CBI and UPSC is at §4.4.

3.10 THE DELHI SPECIAL POLICE ESTABLISHMENT ACT, 1946 — the CBI's legal basis ¶

How to use §3.10 and §4.5 together: §3.10 is the statute and the history — where the CBI came from, whose writ it runs under, and who superintends it. §4.5 is the institution — its placement, its Director, its constraints and its critique. The single most examinable fact in both is negative: there is no Central Bureau of Investigation Act.

3.10.1 The origin story — 1941 → 1946 → 1963 (liftable verbatim)¶

  • Special Police Establishment (S.P.E.) was created under a Deputy Inspector General of Police by the Government of India, in 1941, by an executive order.
  • The functions of the SPE were to investigate cases of bribery and corruption in transactions with which the War and Supply Department of the Government of India was concerned.
  • Towards the end of 1942, the activities of the SPE were extended to include cases of corruption in the Railways also, presumably because the Railways were strategically concerned with the movement and supply of war material.
  • Even after the end of the War, the need for a Central Government agency to investigate cases of bribery and corruption by Central Government employees was felt. The Delhi Special Police Establishment Act was therefore brought into force in 1946. This Act transferred the superintendence of the SPE to the Home Department and its functions were enlarged to cover all departments of the Govt. of India.
  • The DSPE acquired its popular current name, Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI), through a Home Ministry resolution dated 1.4.1963.Initially the offences that were notified by the Central Government related only to corruption by Central Govt. servants.
  • In due course, with the setting up of a large number of public sector undertakings, the employees of these undertakings were also brought under CBI purview. Similarly, with the nationalisation of the banks in 1969, the Public Sector Banks and their employees also came within the ambit of the CBI.

Read the sequence and the whole critique of the CBI writes itself: executive order (1941) → wartime statute (1946) → a resolution for the name (1963). The institution India relies on to investigate its most serious corruption was created for a war, given a statute to police one department's supply contracts, and renamed by administrative fiat. [ADDED] The Gauhati High Court held in 2013 (Navendra Kumar) that the CBI was not validly constituted; the Supreme Court stayed that judgment — verify before citing, but the fact that the question is even arguable is the point.

The one-line contrast that earns the mark: the Lokpal required a statute and 45 years of debate; the CBI, which does the actual investigating for it, has never had a statute of its own at all.

Note the expansion-by-accretion pattern — War & Supply (1941) → Railways (1942) → all departments (1946) → PSUs → public sector banks after the 1969 nationalisation → conventional crime (§3.10.4). The jurisdiction grew by notification and practice, never by a fresh mandate. That is the structural reason the Parliamentary Standing Committee now demands a new law defining its status, functions and powers (§3.10.5).

3.10.2 Jurisdiction and the consent architecture (the federalism section — this is where GS-II Polity meets GS-II Governance)¶

  • The jurisdiction of the SPE extended to all the Union Territories and could be extended also to the States with the consent of the State Government concerned. (This clause is the whole of the general-consent controversy, and it has been in the Act since 1946.)
  • State government's consent may be case-specific or general.
  • "Giving general consent would lead to the seamless investigation of corruption cases against central government employees in their states. This is consent by default, in the absence of which the CBI would have to apply to the state government in every case, and before taking even small actions."
  • ▲ CBI cannot take suo motu cognizance of a case in a state — whether in a matter of corruption involving government officials of the Centre and PSU staff, or an incident of violent crime.The avenue that survives withdrawal of consent:
  • If the case was not registered in that state.
  • Chhattisgarh case.

▲ [SLIDE IS BULLETS ONLY] gives the second bullet as the two words "Chhattisgarh case" with no explanation. [ADDED] It refers to the line of decisions permitting the CBI to register a case in Delhi (where it has jurisdiction) and then investigate acts committed in a non-consenting State, the Supreme Court having held in 2024 that a State's withdrawal of general consent does not bar the CBI from investigating an offence registered elsewhere. Verify the case name, court and year before citing it.

Why §3.10.2 is the most valuable half-page in. It converts the CBI from an administrative topic into a federalism topic, and federalism questions are asked every year. The structure of the argument:

For general consent: corruption by Central Government employees and PSU staff is a Union subject in substance; requiring a fresh application "before taking even small actions" makes investigation impossible in practice; withdrawal creates enforcement havens determined by which party governs a State.

Against: "Police" and "public order" are State subjects (Entries 1 and 2, List II) [ADDED]; the consent clause is not a courtesy but the constitutional price of a Union police force operating inside a State; and a State that has watched the agency deployed against its politicians is exercising a statutory right, not obstructing justice.

The line that resolves it without taking a side: the consent clause was drafted in 1946 for a police force investigating supply contracts; it is now the load-bearing joint of Centre–State relations in criminal investigation. The problem is not that States withdraw consent — it is that a 1946 clause is doing 2026 work. Reform → §15, #34.

[ADDED] Several States have withdrawn general consent since 2018 (commonly listed as West Bengal, Maharashtra, Kerala, Punjab, Rajasthan, Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Mizoram, Meghalaya, Telangana, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka — the list changes with governments). Do not memorise the list; write "several States, across parties" and cite the mechanism. names no State except Chhattisgarh.

3.10.3 Superintendence — the split (verbatim)¶

  • "The superintendence of the Delhi Special Police Establishment in so far as it relates to investigation of offences alleged to have been committed under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988 (49 of 1988), shall vest in the CVC."
  • "The superintendence of the said police establishment in all other matters shall vest in the Central Government."

Now put the three superintendence clauses in one place — this is the single best synthesis in the module, and only a candidate who has all four decks can write it:

Over whatSuperintendence vests inSource
PCA 1988 investigationsthe CVC§3.10.3, §4.3.4
Matters referred by the Lokpalthe Lokpal (superintendence and power to direct)§3.7.4
All other mattersthe Central Government§3.10.3

The argument: the CBI answers to three masters, none of whom owns it. The CVC superintends its corruption work but cannot appoint its Director (§4.3.4); the Lokpal directs only matters it has itself referred (§3.7.4); and the Central Government retains everything else — including cadre, postings, budget and the "all other matters" residue, which is where conventional crime, economic offences and every politically sensitive non-PCA case sits. Divided superintendence is not independence; it is three partial owners and one full employer.

Pair this with the caged parrot observation [ADDED] — the Supreme Court's description of the CBI in the coal-blocks hearings (2013) as "a caged parrot speaking in its master's voice". Verify the wording before quoting; does not contain it, but it is the most-cited line on this topic and §13.5.1 is the evidence for it.

3.10.4 What the CBI became — expanding role (verbatim)¶

  • Expanding Role: murder, kidnapping, terrorist crime, etc.
  • Supreme Court and the various High Courts of the country also started entrusting such cases for investigation to the CBI on petitions filed by aggrieved parties.
  • CBI is not only a premier anti-corruption investigative agency in India but it has also the experience of handling high profile conventional crimes, economic offences, banking frauds and crimes with international linkages.

Two examinable consequences of the expansion, and they pull in opposite directions.

(i) Judicial entrustment is a constitutional workaround. Because the CBI cannot take suo motu cognizance in a State (§3.10.2), the courts became the route by which it enters non-consenting territory — and a constitutional court's order does not require State consent [ADDED]. The same judiciary that is outside the Lokpal's reach (§12.4) is the gatekeeper of the CBI's reach.

(ii) Mission creep is a capacity problem. An agency built for departmental bribery now carries murder, kidnapping, terrorism, banking fraud and transnational crime — on 1,709 vacancies against a sanctioned 7,295 (§13.5.1). Every case the courts entrust is a case the anti-corruption mandate does not get. This is the strongest, least-partisan critique of the CBI available to you, and it needs no political claim at all.

3.10.5 The Parliamentary Standing Committee's indictment ¶

All liftable verbatim:

  • "The Committee feels that the Delhi Special Police Establishment Act has many limitations and therefore, recommends that there is a need to enact a new law and define the status, functions and powers of the CBI and also lay down safeguards to ensure objectivity and impartiality in its functioning."
  • "A total of 1,709 posts are vacant in the CBI against its sanctioned strength of 7,295 — impacts the effectiveness and efficiency of the agency."
  • "CBI should reduce its dependence on deputationists and strive to recruit permanent staff in the ranks of inspector of police and deputy superintendent of police."
  • ▲ "Annual report of CBI is also not accessible to the general public."
  • "CBI should maintain a case management system which would be a centralised database containing details of cases registered with it and the progress made in their disposal."

This slide is worth more than the rest of the CBI material combined, because it is a parliamentary source recommending structural reform — which means you can propose the reform without appearing partisan. Use it as the way-forward anchor for any CBI question (§15, #32–#35).

Note the four distinct diagnoses and keep them separate in the answer — examiners reward the taxonomy:

1. Legal — the DSPE Act has "many limitations"; the fix is a new law defining status, functions and powers, with safeguards for objectivity and impartiality.

2. Personnel — 1,709 of 7,295 posts vacant (≈23%), and dependence on deputationists. A deputationist's career depends on the parent cadre he returns to, not on the case he is investigating. Recruiting permanent inspectors and DySPs is therefore an independence reform disguised as a staffing reform — that sentence is the one to write.

3. Transparency — the annual report is not accessible to the general public. Cross-link hard to §3.3.2: the CBI is exempt from RTI under Sec. 24(2) and the Second Schedule [ADDED], the same mechanism that removed CERT-In in 2023 (§3.4.7). An agency whose annual report the public cannot read is being asked to be the instrument of public accountability.

4. Case management — no centralised database of cases registered and progress in disposal. Set this beside the Lokpal's 5,100 unregistered complaints (§13.4.1) and the pattern is unmistakable: India's accountability institutions fail first at the registry, not at the bench (§15, #23).

3.11 THE PREVENTION OF MONEY LAUNDERING ACT, 2002 (PMLA) ¶

✓ Corroboration note.Every slide of §3.11 — including the scan of the bare Act at §3.11.2 — reappears in unchanged. This matters more here than anywhere else in the compendium, because Sec. 45 is the only numbered statutory provision in the whole series, and it is now independently confirmed by two decks. ▲ What the second run did not do is correct anything: the heading-only PMLA divider and the heading-only “Amendment via Finance Act, 2018” slide reappear still empty, and the 0.75% / 93% contradiction (§13.5.2) is taught a second time without being noticed.

▲ [HEADING-ONLY SLIDE]"The Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002 (PMLA):" slide carries no body text. The Act's content reaches you only through the Sec. 45 scan, the case slides and the criticism slide — so §3.11.1 below is [ADDED] scaffolding, while §3.11.2 onwards is sourced.

3.11.1 What the Act does [ADDED] (minimum context needed to use the sourced material)¶

  • Money laundering = the process of projecting or claiming the proceeds of crime as untainted property. The Act is the domestic arm of an international obligation — the Vienna Convention, the FATF Forty Recommendations and the Palermo Convention — which is why Vijay Madanlal (§12.5.3) frames it as "part of a global response".
  • Structure: a scheduled offence (the "predicate offence") under another law generates proceeds of crime; the ED investigates the laundering of those proceeds as a separate offence; it may provisionally attach property, and arrest, with adjudication before an Adjudicating Authority and trial before a Special Court.
  • The feature that generates every criticism: the ED registers an ECIR (Enforcement Case Information Report), not an FIR, and the ECIR is not required to be supplied to the accused — verify before quoting; alludes to this only through the phrase "arrest without a First Information Report" (§3.11.4).

3.11.2 Section 45 — the twin conditions (verbatim from the Act, as scanned in — the only numbered provision anywhere in the four decks)¶

"Offences to be cognizable and non-bailable.45. (1) Notwithstanding anything contained in the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (2 of 1974) —

  • (a)every offence punishable under this Act shall be cognizable;
  • (b)no person accused of an offence punishable for a term of imprisonment of more than three years under Part A of the Schedule shall be released on bail or on his own bond unless —

- (i) the Public Prosecutor has been given an opportunity to oppose the application for such release; and

- (ii) where the Public Prosecutor opposes the application, the court is satisfied that there are reasonable grounds for believing that he is not guilty of such offence and that he is not likely to commit any offence while on bail:Provided that a person, who, is under the age of sixteen years, or is a woman or is sick or infirm, may be released on bail, if the Special Court so directs."

These are "the twin conditions", and you must be able to state why they invert criminal law. Ordinarily the prosecution must show why bail should be refused; under Sec. 45(b)(ii) the court must affirmatively satisfy itself that the accused is not guilty — at the bail stage, before trial. Two impossibilities are packed into one clause: a court must predict guilt on untested material, and the accused must prove a negative about the future ("not likely to commit any offence while on bail"). Bail law asks whether the accused will stand trial; Sec. 45 asks the court to pre-judge the trial itself.

The proviso is the most under-used fact here — under sixteen · a woman · sick · infirm may be released if the Special Court so directs. It is the hook for the K. Kavitha judgment (§12.5.5), and it is the reason a "women and bail" question can be answered from this module.

The words "Part A of the Schedule" matter: the twin conditions bite only where the scheduled offence carries more than three years. [ADDED] The Finance Act 2018 rewrote this phrase — see §12.5.2 — and never says what it changed, which is.

3.11.3 The same technique in other statutes (verbatim list)¶

  1. The Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940.
  2. The Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985.
  3. Unlawful Activities Prevention Act, 1967.

Why the lecturer put this slide immediately after Sec. 45 — and it is the key to the whole PMLA argument. The twin-condition device is not unique to the PMLA; it is the standard "special statute" bail architecture, already upheld for narcotics and terrorism. This is precisely the reasoning that saved Sec. 45 in Vijay Madanlal (§12.5.3): if the offence is grave enough, Parliament may make bail harder.

So the examinable question is not "are twin conditions constitutional?" — it is "is money laundering in the same class as terrorism and narcotics?" Argue it:

Yes: Vijay Madanlal itself — the offence poses a "serious threat to the sovereignty and integrity of the country", and the PMLA is part of a global response to money laundering and terror financing (§12.5.3).

No: the maximum punishment under the PMLA is seven years — lower than the offences the comparison relies on — and the predicate offences now include a very wide range of ordinary economic crimes (§3.11.4). A bail regime designed for terrorism, attached to a schedule of ordinary offences, is a proportionality problem — and Puttaswamy's proportionality test (§12.1) is the doctrine to name.

One line for the hall: the twin conditions are defensible in proportion to the gravity of the offence they guard — and the PMLA's schedule has grown much faster than its sentence.

3.11.4 The criticism of the PMLA ¶

  • Draconian Powers:"The ED's powers to arrest without a First Information Report (FIR), attach properties provisionally, and detain individuals have been criticized as draconian."
  • Low Conviction Rate:"Despite numerous investigations, the low conviction rate has raised concerns about the overuse of the Act to harass individuals, particularly political opponents or business figures (0.75%)."
  • Broad Definitions:"The broad definition of 'proceeds of crime' and wide range of offenses under other laws has expanded the scope of PMLA disproportionately."
  • Criticism of Arbitrary Use:"There have been allegations that the law is misused for political purposes, and the ED acts at the behest of ruling parties."
  • Burden of Proof:"The onus is on the accused to prove that the property or asset is not the proceeds of crime, which shifts the burden of proof contrary to the general legal principle of 'innocent until proven guilty'."

Order these three in your answer and they compound into one argument rather than five complaints:

1. Entry is easy — arrest without an FIR, every offence cognizable (Sec. 45(1)(a)).
