2. Exit is hard — the twin conditions (Sec. 45(1)(b)).

3. And in between, the presumption is reversed — the onus is on the accused.

Easy in, hard out, and the burden inverted while inside. The process is the punishment — which is exactly why the conviction rate (§13.5.2) is the decisive number and not a footnote.

▲ Note the "0.75%" and hold it — asserts it here and then, five slides later, records the Government's claim of a 93 per cent conviction rate. That contradiction is internal to this source and it is the most valuable thing in it — see the [CONFLICT] box at §13.5.2.

⚖️ Give the other side, or the answer is a polemic. [ADDED] The defence of these provisions: laundering is deliberately structured to defeat ordinary proof, the money moves faster than process, and attachment is provisional and subject to adjudication and appeal; FATF mutual-evaluation compliance requires effective confiscation powers. Concede the design, contest the administration — the powers are defensible; a 0.75% conviction rate on 5,297 registered cases is not evidence that they are being used as designed.

3.12 THE CONSTITUTIONAL SCHEME OF PUBLIC AUDIT — ARTICLES 148–151 AND 279 ¶

The institution is at §4.7; the statute that fills these Articles out is at §3.13; the case law is at §12.6; the audit findings are at §13.6.

3.12.1 Article 148 — the founding Article (verbatim, and the densest single slide in the source)¶

  • "There shall be a Comptroller and Auditor-General of India who shall be appointed by the President by warrant under his hand and seal and shall only be removed from office in like manner and on like grounds as a Judge of the Supreme Court."
  • "Oath in the Third Schedule."
  • "The salary and other conditions of service shall not be varied to his disadvantage after his appointment."
  • "The Comptroller and Auditor-General shall not be eligible for further office."
  • "Expenses of the office of the Comptroller and Auditor-General including all salaries, allowances and pensions payable to or in respect of persons serving in that office, shall be charged upon the Consolidated Fund of India."

Five protections in five lines — name them, because each one answers a different way of capturing an office.(i) Removal → only by the judge's route (address by both Houses on proved misbehaviour or incapacity, special majority [ADDED — Art. 124(4) machinery; the source says only "in like manner and on like grounds"]) — you cannot dismiss him. (ii) Salary and conditions frozen → you cannot starve him. (iii) Charged upon the Consolidated Fund → you cannot vote his office down. (iv) No further office → you cannot buy him with the next posting. (v) Oath → the obligation is to the Constitution, not to the ministry.

▲ Now note the one thing the Article does not protect — and it is the first thing an examiner will reward you for noticing.There is no selection committee, no eligibility qualification, no consultation requirement and no advertised criteria. The CAG is appointed by the President — i.e. on the advice of the Council of Ministers [ADDED — Art. 74]. The officer who audits the Union Government is chosen by the Union Government alone, and then made almost impossible to remove. Compare the CBI Director's PM + LoP + CJI (§4.5.4), the CVC's PM + Home Minister + LoP (§4.3.1), the CIC's three-member committee (§4.1.2) and the Lokpal's five-member committee (§4.2.4). The full comparison is at §4.4.5, and it is the single best "appointment to constitutional posts" argument in this compendium.

The post-office bar repays close reading. The text bars "further office" — [ADDED] under Art. 148(4) the bar is on office under the Government of India or under the Government of any State. ▲ By its terms it does not reach international appointments, private employment, academic or corporate boards, or a legislative seat. A bar drafted for the age of the government job is being read in an age of the post-retirement board seat — write that, and pair it with the Lokpal's much wider statutory bar (§4.2.7), which expressly extends to elections and diplomatic assignments. The younger statute learned what the older Article did not.

▲ A caution on scope. renders Art. 148 in four compressed bullets and omits clause (5) — that the conditions of service of persons serving in the Indian Audit and Accounts Department, and the administrative powers of the CAG, are prescribed by the President after consultation with the CAG [ADDED]. Write the five protections; do not claim you have quoted the whole Article.

3.12.2 Articles 149, 150 and 279 — three heading-only slides ▲ ¶

ArticleThe source gives[ADDED] — what it actually provides (verify before quoting)
Art. 149 ▲ **▲ "Duties and Powers of the Comptroller and Auditor-General" — title only, no body textThe CAG performs such duties and exercises such powers in relation to the accounts of the Union and of the States as may be prescribed by or under any law made by Parliament — this is the hinge Article: it is why the DPC Act, 1971 exists (§3.13), and why the CAG's powers are statutory even though his office is constitutional
Art. 150▲ "Form of Accounts of The Union and of The States" — title onlyThe accounts of the Union and of the States are kept in such form as the President may, on the advice of the CAG, prescribe — the auditor shapes the form of the very accounts he later audits
Art. 279▲ "Calculation of 'net proceeds'" — title only"Net proceeds" of any tax = the proceeds reduced by the cost of collection, and shall be ascertained and certified by the CAG, whose certificate shall be final — the CAG's federal financial role: the figure on which tax devolution to the States is calculated is certified by him and is not open to challenge

Art. 149 is the most important thing leaves blank, and you should treat the omission as itself examinable.The Constitution creates the office and then leaves its duties and powers to Parliament. An office protected by the Constitution, exercising powers granted by statute, over an executive that commands the majority which makes that statute. That single sentence explains the 1976 change (§4.7.4), it explains why the multi-member debate is a statutory-and-constitutional question (§4.7.7), and it is the reason the jurisdictional debate over performance audit (§4.7.6) can be argued at all — the mandate is not written in the Constitution, so its boundary is contestable.

Art. 279 is a free mark and almost nobody writes it. It gives you a GS-II federalism point and a GS-III public-finance point in one clause: the CAG certifies the net proceeds on which the Finance Commission's devolution formula operates, and his certificate is final. The auditor of the Union is also the arbiter of what the States are owed. Pair it with the "two questions" at §4.7.7 — the CAG is the CAG for the States as well as the Centre, which is exactly why the source asks whether the States must be consulted before the office is amended.

3.12.3 Article 151 — audit reports (verbatim — the accountability chain in two sentences)¶

  • "The reports of the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India relating to the accounts of the Union shall be submitted to the President, who shall cause them to be laid before each House of Parliament."
  • "The reports of the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India relating to the accounts of a State shall be submitted to the Governor of the State, who shall cause them to be laid before the Legislature of the State."

Read the verbs, because the whole theory of audit accountability is in them. The CAG submits; the President or Governor causes to be laid; the legislature then examines. The CAG has no power to act on his own findings whatsoever. He cannot prosecute, cannot surcharge, cannot recover, cannot direct. His entire executive force is the obligation of somebody else to place his report on a table. That is the single most important line to write about the CAG, and it is what makes §4.7.5 (the PAC/COPU chain) not a footnote but the mechanism.

The federal symmetry is worth one clause.One officer, two constitutional masters — he reports to the President for the Union and to each Governor for that State. India has a single audit institution for a federal polity, which is unusual and is the premise of the second of the source's two closing questions (§4.7.7).

▲ The gap the Article exposes. [ADDED] Laying a report before a House does not compel it to be discussed, and the CAG's reports are examined only when the PAC or COPU take them up. gives you the chain but no figure for how much of it functions — see. An accountability institution whose output must be adopted by someone else to have effect is only as strong as that someone else's appetite.

3.13 THE COMPTROLLER AND AUDITOR-GENERAL'S (DUTIES, POWERS AND CONDITIONS OF SERVICE) ACT, 1971 ¶

The statute Art. 149 contemplates. Cite it as "the CAG (DPC) Act, 1971".

3.13.1 Conditions of service (verbatim)¶

  • "CAG's Salary equal to the salary of the Judge of the Supreme Court."
  • "Term of Office: 6 years or 65 years of age; whichever is earlier."
  • "Resignation." ▲ (one-word bullet) — [ADDED] he may resign at any time by writing under his hand addressed to the President.
  • "1976 Amendment." ▲ (one-word bullet — expanded on a later slide; full treatment at §4.7.4)

Line the tenures up and a pattern appears that is worth a sentence in any answer on institutional design.CAG — 6 years or 65 · CVC — 4 years or 65 (§4.3.2) · Lokpal — 5 years or 70 (§4.2.5) · CIC — as the Central Government prescribes, max 65 (§4.1.4) · CBI/ED Directors — a two-year floor, annually extendable (§4.5.4, §4.6.4). The protection of a term falls exactly as you move from the Constitution to statute to executive discretion — and the power to interfere with an individual case rises in the same order.

▲ Note what the salary parity does and does not do.Parity with a Supreme Court judge is a status guarantee, and combined with Art. 148's freeze it cannot be reduced. But the CAG's establishment — the Indian Audit and Accounts Department — has no equivalent protection; its terms are set by the President after consultation (§3.12.1). The office is insulated; the department that does the work is not. Compare the CBI's 1,709 vacancies (§13.5.1) — the same asymmetry, one tier down.

3.13.2 The duty — what the CAG must audit (verbatim)¶

  1. "To audit all expenditure from the Consolidated Fund of India and of each State and of each Union territory having a Legislative Assembly and to ascertain whether the moneys shown in the accounts as having been disbursed were legally available for and applicable to the service or purpose to which they have been applied or charged and whether the expenditure conforms to the authority which governs it."
  2. "To audit all transactions of the Union and of the States relating to Contingency Funds and Public Accounts."

Take the first duty apart — there are three distinct audits inside one sentence, and naming them is what separates a describing answer from an analysing one.

(i) Legality — were the moneys "legally available"? (ii) Application — were they "applicable to the service or purpose to which they have been applied"? (iii) Authority — does the expenditure "conform to the authority which governs it"? This is regularity audit — and note that even at its narrowest it is not arithmetic: it asks whether money went where the legislature said it should.

This is also the textual hinge of the jurisdictional debate at §4.7.6.Nothing in this duty mentions efficiency, economy or effectiveness — the vocabulary of performance audit appears nowhere in the sourced text. That is precisely why the critics' objection is not frivolous, and why the answer to it has to be built on Art. 149's open-ended delegation and on Arvind Gupta* (2013) (§12.6.1) rather than on this clause.* Concede the textual point and win the argument elsewhere — that is the mature version of this answer.

▲ Note the reach the second duty quietly gives.Contingency Fund and Public Account transactions are not voted by the legislature in the way Consolidated Fund expenditure is. The CAG audits the money Parliament never voted on — which is where the audit is doing the most work and receiving the least attention.

3.13.3 Audit of bodies substantially financed from Union or State revenues (verbatim — the two-limb test)¶

  • "Where the grant or loan to a body or authority from the Consolidated Fund of India or of any State in a financial year is not less than rupees twenty-five lakhs and the amount of such grant or loan is not less than seventy-five percent of the total expenditure of that body or authority."

Learn it as a two-limb, conjunctive test — examiners test the "and".Limb 1: an absolute floor — ₹25 lakh.Limb 2: a proportion — 75% of that body's total expenditure. Both must be satisfied, so a body receiving ₹500 crore that is 40% of its budget falls outside, while one receiving ₹30 lakh that is 90% of its budget falls inside. The test is about dependence, not about size — and that is the principle to state.

This clause is the doorway out of government. It is how the CAG reaches societies, autonomous bodies, universities, NGOs and federations that are not government at all — and it is the natural statutory basis for the IOA report at §13.6.1 ▲ [ADDED — places the two slides in sequence but never states the basis on which the IOA was audited; do not assert it as sourced].

▲ The critique, and it is a good one. [ADDED] A 75% threshold means the largest recipients of public money are often the least auditable, because big institutions diversify their income. Public accountability follows the proportion of the grant, not the size of it — and PPP structures, where public risk is large but public expenditure through the entity is small, sit almost entirely outside this test. That is a first-class reform paragraph → §15, #45.

▲ A caution on section numbers.numbers only one provision of this Act — Sec. 23, and only inside the Kelkar case slide (§12.6.2). Follow the standing rule of this compendium: cite CAG provisions by name — "the substantially-financed provision of the DPC Act" — not by number. The one number you may write with confidence is Sec. 23, and the one from the other decks is Sec. 45, PMLA.

3.14 THE PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS ACT, 1993 (PHRA) ¶

Read this section against §3.7 (Lokpal). Both are statutory watchdogs created by a single Act that builds a three-tier structure. The Lokpal Act builds Lokpal → Lokayuktas → Special Courts; the PHRA builds NHRC → SHRCs → Human Rights Courts. The template is the same and the failure mode is the same — the tier below the apex is where the design collapses (§3.7.8 for the Lokayuktas; for the SHRCs).

3.14.1 What the Act creates, and where it comes from (verbatim)¶

  • Established: 1993.
  • Statutory Body — Protection of Human Rights Act (PHRA), 1993. (i.e. not constitutional — contrast the CAG at §4.7 and the UPSC at §4.9)
  • "It is in conformity with the Paris Principles, adopted at the first international workshop on national institutions for the promotion and protection of human rights held in Paris in 1991, and endorsed by the General Assembly of the United Nations in 1993."
  • "The NHRC is an embodiment of India's concern for the promotion and protection of human rights."

This is the only institution in the entire compendium whose founding statute is expressly benchmarked against an international standard — and that single fact drives everything in §4.8.7 and §13.7.2. A body that claims conformity with an external standard can be told by that standard's custodian that it no longer conforms. No other body in this compendium is externally rateable; the NHRC is, and has been downgraded twice.

▲ [CONFLICT — internal to ] on the date of the Paris Principles. This slide dates them 1991 (adopted at the Paris workshop), endorsed by the UNGA in 1993; the GANHRI slide (§4.8.7) says "the Paris Principles adopted in 1993." Both are defensible descriptions of the same sequence and the compendium resolves it rather than picking a side: drafted and adopted at the Paris workshop, October 1991; endorsed by the UN General Assembly, 1993 [ADDED — the intervening step, the UN Commission on Human Rights resolution of 1992, appears in neither slide; UNGA resolution 48/134 of 20 December 1993 is the standard citation — verify before writing the number]. Write "adopted 1991, endorsed by the UNGA 1993" and you are consistent with both slides.

3.14.2 The three-tier structure the Act provides for (verbatim — a guaranteed one-marker)¶

"The Act provides for:"

  1. National Human Rights Commission (NHRC)
  2. State Human Rights Commissions (SHRC)
  3. Human Rights Courts

▲ Note what the source does with tiers 2 and 3: nothing.SHRCs are named here and then appear only once more — in the tenure slide (§4.8.2), where the 2019 amendment applies to them equally — and Human Rights Courts are named here and never mentioned again. [ADDED] Minimum you need: Human Rights Courts are designated by the State Government with the concurrence of the Chief Justice of the High Court, one for each district, to try offences arising out of human rights violations — and the standard critique is that they are ordinary Sessions Courts re-labelled, with no separate cadre, no special procedure and no defined class of "human rights offences", so the tier is largely notional. ▲ Verify before writing; the source gives you none of it.

3.14.3 The two provisions the source does number (verbatim — and note the rarity)¶

ProvisionWhat it doesWhy it is in the criticism section, not the structure section
Section 11"Section 11 of the Act makes it dependent on the government for its manpower requirements."The Commission's staff are the government's to give
Section 32"According to Section 32 of the Act, the central government shall pay to the Commission by way of grants such sums of money as it may consider fit."The Commission's money is the government's to judge

These are the third and fourth numbered statutory provisions in six decks — after Sec. 45 PMLA and Sec. 23 DPC Act. Cite Sections 11 and 32 of the PHRA with confidence; continue to cite everything else in the Act by name of provision.

And note where they appear — the source numbers the two provisions that establish dependence, and numbers nothing that establishes power. That is the whole argument of §4.8.6 in one observation, and it is worth making explicitly in an answer.

The contrast to state in one line: the CAG's expenses are charged upon the Consolidated Fund (§3.12.1) and the Lokpal's are too (§4.2.7) — charged expenditure is non-votable. The NHRC's are grants "as [the government] may consider fit." Same architecture of independence in the appointment and removal provisions; opposite architecture in the money provision — and the money provision is the one that decides.

3.14.4 The 2019 amendment — what it changed (verbatim; institutional detail at §4.8.2)¶

  • "The original Act states that the chairperson and members of the NHRC and SHRC will hold office for five years or till the age of seventy years, whichever is earlier."
  • "The 2019 amendment reduces the term of office to three years or till the age of seventy years, whichever is earlier."
  • "The original Act allowed for the reappointment of members of the NHRC and SHRCs for a period of five years. The 2019 amendment removes the five-year limit for reappointment."

Learn the two halves as a pair, because the pair is the argument.Term cut 5 → 3 years and the cap on reappointment removed. Shorter terms plus unlimited renewal transfers power from the statute to whoever renews — the office-holder now faces a reappointment decision every three years, made by the executive-majority committee at §4.8.1. ▲ Contrast the CVC, CIC and Lokpal, where the standing critique is the executive-majority committee but the answer is no reappointment at all (§4.1.4, §4.2.5, §4.3.2). The NHRC is the one body in this compendium where reappointment is both permitted and uncapped — and reappointment, not appointment, is the stronger lever, because it operates on a serving office-holder deciding live cases.

▲ [ADDED] Two further 2019 changes the source does not state but its own composition slide silently reflects (§4.8.1): the Chairperson's eligibility was widened from "a former Chief Justice of the Supreme Court" to include "a Judge of the Supreme Court", and the ex-officio membership was expanded (the National Commission for Backward Classes, the NCPCR and the Chief Commissioner for Persons with Disabilities were added). The source's composition slide is the post-2019 position — say so if you reproduce it.Verify before asserting the amendment did it.

3.15 THE CONSTITUTIONAL SCHEME OF THE SERVICES — ARTICLES 310, 311 AND 312 ¶

This closes the compendium's oldest structural hole. Since, §3.1's constitutional Articles have been entirely [ADDED] scaffolding, and the standing note was that "no deck in this series has yet cited an Article of the Constitution directly." broke that for the CAG (Art. 148–151, 279); now does it for the services — Art. 310, 311, 312 and 315–320 are reproduced verbatim. §3.1's row "Efficiency in public employment — Articles 309–311, 315–323" is now sourced, not supplied — except Art. 309 and Art. 313, 321–323, which remain [ADDED].

3.15.1 Article 310 — the doctrine of pleasure (verbatim)¶

  • "Every person who is a member of a defence service or of a civil service of the Union or of an all-India service or holds any post connected with defence or any civil post under the Union, holds office during the pleasure of the President,"
  • "and every person who is a member of a civil service of a State or holds any civil post under a State holds office during the pleasure of the Governor of the State."

The phrase to lift is "holds office during the pleasure." [ADDED] It is the English doctrine of pleasure, imported and then cut down by Art. 311 — which is why the two Articles must always be written together. In India the doctrine is constitutional, not prerogative, so it operates subject to express constitutional limits; in England it was absolute.

The examiner's point: Art. 310 makes tenure precarious and Art. 311 makes dismissal procedurally hard. Security of tenure for the Indian civil servant is therefore procedural, not substantive — he cannot be removed without an inquiry, but he holds no right to the post. Set that against §14 issue 57: the protection the services actually lack is not against dismissal, which is nearly impossible, but against transfer, which is unregulated.

3.15.2 Article 311 — the two safeguards, and the three exceptions (verbatim)¶

The safeguards:

  • (1)"No person who is a member of a civil service of the Union or an all India service or a civil service of a State or holds a civil post under the Union or a State shall be dismissed or removed by a authority subordinate to that by which he was appointed." (the source's scan reads "a authority" and "a Slate" — OCR/typographical slips in the source; the Article reads "any authority" and "a State")
  • (2) "No such person as aforesaid shall be dismissed or removed or reduced in rank except after an inquiry in which he has been informed of the charges against him and given a reasonable opportunity of being heard in respect of those charges;"
  • First proviso — "Provided that where it is proposed after such inquiry, to impose upon him any such penalty, such penalty may be imposed on the basis of the evidence adduced during such inquiry and it shall not be necessary to give such person any opportunity of making representation on the penalty proposed:"The three exceptions — "Provided further that this clause shall not apply –"
  • (a)"where a person is dismissed or removed or reduced in rank on the ground of conduct which has led to his conviction on a criminal charge; or"
  • (b)"where the authority empowered to dismiss or remove a person or to reduce him in rank is satisfied that for some reason, to be recorded by that authority in writing, it is not reasonably practicable to hold such inquiry; or"
  • (c)"where the President or the Governor, as the case may be, is satisfied that in the interest of the security of the State, it is not expedient to hold such inquiry."
  • The finality clause — "If, in respect of any such person as aforesaid, a question arises whether it is reasonably practicable to hold such inquiry as is referred to in clause (2), the decision thereon of the authority empowered to dismiss or remove such person or to reduce him in rank shall be final."

Learn the three penalties Art. 311(2) covers — dismissal, removal, reduction in rank — and note what is missing: transfer, suspension, denial of promotion and compulsory retirement are not in the list. The Article protects against the punishments that end a career and says nothing about the ones that manage a career — which is precisely why TSR Subramaniam (§12.8) had to be litigated and why reform #51 (fixed tenure legislation) exists.

▲ The finality clause is the pressure point. Clause (b) lets the authority dispense with the inquiry on its own recorded satisfaction, and the closing words make its decision "final." [ADDED — the settled position, and worth one line] "Final" has been read as excluding an appeal, not judicial review: the satisfaction must be based on relevant material and is examinable for mala fides or perversity.Verify before writing; the source gives the clause and no gloss.

3.15.3 Article 312 — the All India Services (verbatim — the federalism Article)¶

  • "If the Council of States has declared by resolution supported by not less than two-thirds of the members present and voting that it is necessary or expedient in the national interest so to do, Parliament may by law provide for the creation of one or more all-India services (including an all-India judicial service) common to the Union and the States."
  • "The services known at the commencement of this Constitution as the Indian Administrative Service and the Indian Police Service shall be deemed to be services created by Parliament under this article."
  • "The all-India judicial service shall not include any post inferior to that of a district judge."

Three examinable points sit in these four lines, and most candidates get only the first.

(1) The gatekeeper is the Rajya Sabha, not the Lok Sabha — a special majority of members present and voting, on the ground of "national interest." The Council of States must consent to a service that will command the States — the Constitution's own acknowledgment that the AIS is a derogation from federalism, and the direct answer to KT Shah and T.T. Krishnamachari at §4.10.1.

(2) The IAS and IPS are deemed to be created under this Article — they were not created by an Art. 312 resolution, because they pre-date it. ▲ The IFoS (Indian Forest Service, 1966) is the only service actually created by the Art. 312 route [ADDED — verify], which is why the AIS remains three services and not thirty.

(3) The all-India judicial service is in the text of the Constitution and has never been created — the floor being set at district judge. A ready-made 10-marker: an enabling provision unused for seven decades, with the same objections (State autonomy, language, High Court control over the subordinate judiciary under Art. 233–235) [ADDED] that KT Shah made against the IAS.

▲ A heading the source never delivers. Slide 37 is titled "Central Services v All India Services" and is followed immediately by Art. 310 — the comparison it promises is never made anywhere in the source. [ADDED — supply it yourself; it is a two-line distinction and a likely one-marker] Central Services (IRS, IAAS, IFS etc.) are recruited, controlled and paid by the Union alone and serve only the Union. All India Services (IAS, IPS, IFoS) are recruited centrally but allotted to State cadres, serve both governments, and are subject to a dual control — the State employs them, the Union controls their cadre, discipline and deputation. That dual control is the AIS in one sentence, and it is the whole of the federalism argument at §4.10.2.

3.16 THE CONSTITUTIONAL SCHEME OF THE PUBLIC SERVICE COMMISSIONS — ARTICLES 315–320 ¶

3.16.1 Article 315 — Public Service Commissions for the Union and for the States (verbatim)¶

  1. "Public Service Commission for the Union and a Public Service Commission for each State."
  2. "Two or more States may agree that there shall be one Public Service Commission for that group of States, and if a resolution to that effect is passed by the House or, where there are two Houses, by each House of the Legislature of each of those States, Parliament may by law provide for the appointment of a Joint State Public Service Commission to serve the needs of those States."
  3. "The Public Service Commission for the Union, if requested so to do by the Governor of a State, may, with the approval of the President, agree to serve all or any of the needs of the State."

Three bodies, not one — UPSC, SPSC and JSPSC — and note who initiates each: the States' legislatures for a Joint Commission (Parliament then legislates), and the Governor for UPSC assistance (with the President's approval). Both routes are State-initiated, which is the constitutional courtesy the AIS design lacks.

3.16.2 Article 316 — appointment and term of office (verbatim)¶

  • "The Chairman and other members of a Public Service Commission shall be appointed, in the case of the Union Commission or a Joint Commission, by the President, and in the case of a State Commission, by the Governor of the State:"
  • "Provided that as nearly as may be one-half of the members of every Public Service Commission shall be persons who have held office for at least ten years either under the Government of India or under the Government of a State."
  • "A member of a Public Service Commission shall hold office for a term of six years from the date on which he enters upon his office or until he attains, in the case of the Union Commission, the age of sixty-five years, and in the case of a State Commission or a Joint Commission, the age of sixty-two years, whichever is earlier."
  • "A member of a Public Service Commission may resign from his office." (▲ the source omits the addressee; the Article requires resignation in writing to the President / Governor [ADDED])
  • "A person who holds office as a member of a Public Service Commission shall, on the expiration of his term of office, be ineligible for reappointment to that office."

The one-half proviso is the most under-used fact in this whole section. It is the only composition mandate in the compendium expressed as a proportion of prior government service — and it cuts both ways in an answer: it guarantees administrative experience, and it guarantees that half the body that recruits the bureaucracy is drawn from the bureaucracy. Pair it with the GANHRI pluralism criterion (§4.8.7): a body composed largely of former insiders is exactly what the Paris Principles call a pluralism deficit — and the NHRC was downgraded for it.

"Six years or 65" for the UPSC vs "six years or 62" for a State or Joint Commission — the only age asymmetry between Union and State offices anywhere in this compendium, and an easy Prelims trap. And note "ineligible for reappointment" — a flat bar, in the same words the CVC and CIC provisions use, and the opposite of the NHRC's post-2019 position (§3.14.4).

3.16.3 Article 317 — removal (verbatim — the strongest removal protection outside Art. 148)¶

  • "Chairman or any other member of a Public Service Commission shall only be removed from his office by order of the President on the ground of misbehaviour after the Supreme Court, on reference being made to it by the President, has, on inquiry held, reported that the Chairman or such other member, as the case may be, ought on any such ground to be removed."The direct grounds — "The President may by order remove from office the Chairman or any other member of a Public Service Commission if the Chairman or such other member, as the case may be,—"
  1. "is adjudged an insolvent; or"
  2. "engages during his term of office in any paid employment outside the duties of his office; or"
  3. "is, in the opinion of the President, unfit to continue in office by reason of infirmity of mind or body."Deemed misbehaviour — "If the Chairman or any other member of a Public Service Commission is or becomes in any way concerned or interested in any contract or agreement made by or on behalf of the Government of India or the Government of a State or participates in any way in the profit thereof or in any benefit or emolument arising therefrom otherwise than as a member and in common with the other members of an incorporated company, he shall be deemed to be guilty of misbehaviour."

This is the sixth appearance of the two-track removal template — CIC (§4.1.5), Lokpal (§4.2.6), CVC (§4.3.3), CAG (§4.7.1), NHRC (§4.8.2) and now the UPSC — and the UPSC's version is the strictest: note the word "only." Track 1: misbehaviour, but only after a Supreme Court reference and report. Track 2: three direct grounds, no reference needed. The deemed-misbehaviour clause is the detail that distinguishes it — a conflict of interest is not merely a ground, it is deemed to be the constitutional wrong itself, with the carve-out for holding shares in an incorporated company along with everyone else.

▲ [ADDED] The source omits Art. 317(2) — the President may suspend the Chairman or a member pending the Supreme Court's report. Worth one line; it is the mechanism that makes the reference workable. Verify before writing.

3.16.4 Article 318 — regulations, and the protective proviso (verbatim)¶

  • "In the case of the Union Commission or a Joint Commission, the President and, in the case of a State Commission, the Governor of the State may by regulations—""determine the number of members of the Commission and their conditions of service; and""make provision with respect to the number of members of the staff of the Commission and their conditions of service:"
  • "Provided that the conditions of service of a member of a Public Service Commission shall not be varied to his disadvantage after his appointment."

The same protective proviso you already hold for the CAG (Art. 148, §3.12.1).Learn the phrase once — "shall not be varied to his disadvantage after his appointment" — and it serves the CAG, the UPSC and, by contrast, the argument against the 2019 RTI Amendment, which moved the CIC's tenure and salary out of the statute and into central rules**.

▲ But note the asymmetry the Article creates and the source does not comment on: the number of members is left to executive regulation. A body whose individual members cannot be touched, but whose size the executive fixes by regulation, is protected at the level of the person and unprotected at the level of the institution — the identical technique flagged at the Lokpal's budget (§13.4.2) and the CAG's 1976 cadre separation (§4.7.4).

3.16.5 Article 319 — the post-office bar (verbatim — "On ceasing to hold office-")¶

WhoEligible forBarred from
Chairman, UPSCNothing"ineligible for further employment either under the Government of India or under the Government of a State"
Chairman, SPSCChairman or any other member of the UPSC, or Chairman of any other SPSC"any other employment either under the Government of India or under the Government of a State"

The logic is a one-way escalator: you may move up or across within the Public Service Commission system, and nowhere else — and the UPSC Chairman, at the top, may go nowhere at all. Compare the CAG, who is simply "not eligible for further office" (Art. 148, §3.12.1), and the Lokpal's post-office bar (§4.2.7). The design principle to state: the value of a post-office bar is that it removes the future favour* as an instrument of influence — which is exactly the objection to lateral entry at §4.10.4(ii), where the entrant arrives from, and returns to, the sector he regulates.*

3.16.6 Article 320 — functions of Public Service Commissions (verbatim — the consultation list)¶

  • (a)"on all matters relating to methods of recruitment to civil services and for civil posts;"
  • (b)"on the principles to be followed in making appointments to civil services and posts and in making promotions and transfers from one service to another and on the suitability of candidates for such appointments, promotions or transfers;"
  • (c)"on all disciplinary matters affecting a person serving under the Government of India or the Government of a State in a civil capacity, including memorials or petitions relating to such matters;"
  • (d)"on any claim by or in respect of a person who is serving or has served under the Government of India or the Government of a State or under the Crown in India or under the Government of an Indian State, in a civil capacity, that any costs incurred by him in defending legal proceedings instituted against him in respect of acts done or purporting to be done in the execution of his duty should be paid out of the Consolidated Fund of India, or, as the case may be, out of the Consolidated Fund of the State;"
  • (e)"on any claim for the award of a pension in respect of injuries sustained by a person while serving under the Government of India or the Government of a State or under the Crown in India or under the Government of an Indian State, in a civil capacity, and any question as to the amount of any such award,"

▲ The source starts the Article at clause (a) and therefore omits the two things that make the list intelligible [ADDED — supply both; this is the most load-bearing omission in the civil-services half]: Art. 320(1) — the duty to conduct examinations for appointments — and the opening words of Art. 320(3), which require that the Commission "shall be consulted" on the matters listed. And the point examiners actually test: the Commission's advice on these matters is not binding on the government, and the exclusions are made by regulations under Art. 320(3) proviso and reported to Parliament under Art. 323.Verify before writing; none of it is in the source.

State the consequence and you have the paragraph: the UPSC holds the strongest removal protection in the constitutional scheme after the CAG (§3.16.3), the strongest post-office bar anywhere (§3.16.5) — and its core output is advice nobody must accept. Protection is calibrated to the office, not to the power: the UPSC and the CAG are the two best-protected bodies in this compendium and the two whose findings bind least. That is "authority without consequence" (§14 issue 43) reappearing in a second institution, and stating it as a pattern is what a top answer does.

3.16.7 The financial guarantee (verbatim)¶

  • "The expenses of the Union or a State Public Service Commission, including any salaries, allowances and pensions payable to or in respect of the members or staff of the Commission, shall be charged on the Consolidated Fund of India or, as the case may be, the Consolidated Fund of the State."

"Charged on the Consolidated Fund" = non-votable — the legislature may discuss it but cannot vote it down. You now hold four bodies with this guarantee — the CAG, the Lokpal, the UPSC and, by contrast, the one without it: the NHRC, whose money is a grant "as [the government] may consider fit" (§3.14.3). Build the whole comparative answer on that single distinction. Charged expenditure is the practical definition of institutional independence in the Indian scheme, and the human rights body is the one that does not have it.

3.16.8 Article 321 — the Article this compendium has been missing (newly sourced from UPSC Citizen's Charter slide; the mandate is verbatim, the text of the Article is [ADDED])¶

A genuine surprise from a Citizen's Charter deck.reproduces the UPSC's own Citizen's Charter, which states the Commission's mandate as arising "under Article 320 and 321 of the Constitution of India" — ▲ and §3.16 has covered Art. 315–320 without ever citing Art. 321, because no deck had.

  • What the source states, verbatim:"The mandate of Union Public Service Commission, under Article 320 and 321 of the Constitution of India, includes: 1. Recruitment by conduct of competitive examinations; 2. Recruitment by Selection through Interviews…"
  • What Art. 321 provides [ADDED — verify wording before quoting]: Parliament (for the Union) or a State legislature (for a State) may by law provide for the exercise of additional functions by a Public Service Commission — including in respect of the services of local authorities, other corporate bodies or public institutions.
  • Why it matters, and it is a clean two-mark value-addition:Art. 320 fixes the UPSC's constitutional functions; Art. 321 is the elastic clause that lets a legislature add to them. It is the exact structural twin of Art. 149 for the CAG (§3.12.2) — a constitutional office whose core is entrenched and whose reach Parliament may extend by ordinary law.

Use it in any "constitutional bodies" answer:the Constitution entrenches these offices and then hands Parliament the dial — Art. 149 for the auditor, Art. 321 for the recruiter. ▲ The source cites the Article and never explains it; the explanation above is [ADDED].

3.17 THE PREAMBLE AND THE FOUR IDENTITY-WORDS — SOVEREIGN, SOCIALIST, SECULAR, DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC ¶

Why this section exists. Six decks quoted operative Articles. opens its comparative module with the Preamble reproduced as an image, and then spends forty slides arguing about two words inside it — socialist and secular. The Preamble is therefore not decoration here; it is the premise of the entire comparison (§5.4–§5.6).

3.17.1 The text, as the source reproduces it (verbatim — learn the sequence, not the sentence)¶

"WE, THE PEOPLE OF INDIA, having solemnly resolved to constitute India into a SOVEREIGN SOCIALIST SECULAR DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC and to secure to all its citizens: JUSTICE, social, economic and political; LIBERTY of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship; EQUALITY of status and of opportunity; and to promote among them all FRATERNITY assuring the dignity of the individual and the unity and integrity of the Nation; IN OUR CONSTITUENT ASSEMBLY this twenty-sixth day of November, 1949, do HEREBY ADOPT, ENACT AND GIVE TO OURSELVES THIS CONSTITUTION."

The four-part structure to write, because it is what a 2-mark opener is testing:source of authority (We, the People) → nature of the state (sovereign, socialist, secular, democratic republic) → objectives (justice, liberty, equality, fraternity) → date of adoption (26 November 1949).

3.17.2 What the source says the words do (verbatim)¶

  • "The Indian Constitution declares the country as a sovereign, socialist, secular, democratic republic. This form of socialism is meant to be inclusive and non-totalitarian."
  • "Indian socialism is rooted in democratic principles. It blends state intervention with the protection of individual rights and a market economy. Indian socialism stems from its colonial past and leaders like Jawaharlal Nehru and B.R. Ambedkar, who sought to uplift the socio-economically marginalized through state intervention while maintaining democracy."
  • "India practices positive secularism, which means the state actively engages with all religions to ensure equality while maintaining a distance from endorsing any one religion. The Indian model promotes sarva dharma sambhava (equal respect for all religions), making it unique compared to Western models of strict separation."

The three adjectives are doing three different jobs and an answer that says so is already above average.Sovereign is a claim against other states; democratic republic is a claim about how power is acquired; socialist and secular are claims about what the state may do with power once it has it. That is why only the last two are litigated — and both are litigated in §12.9.

3.17.3 ▲ What the source omits, and you must not — the 42nd Amendment [ADDED — the single most important gap in ]¶

FactWhy it decides the answer
"Socialist", "Secular" and "Integrity" were not in the Preamble as adopted on 26 November 1949 — they were inserted by the Constitution (Forty-second Amendment) Act, 1976The source argues that India is constitutionally socialist and secular by pointing at a text that only says so since 1976. An answer that quotes the Preamble without the amendment invites the obvious follow-up
The Constitution was adopted 26 Nov 1949 and came into force 26 Jan 1950The Preamble's own date is an adoption date, not a commencement date

Union of India*, November 2024; **verify the case name and date before writing it**]The live current-affairs line for a 2026 answer, and the source predates or ignores it

3.17.4 ▲ The religion Articles the source never cites [ADDED; verify wording before quoting]¶

argues secularism for twenty-five slides without naming a single Article of the Indian Constitution. These are the ones an examiner expects:

ProvisionWhat it gives you
Art. 25Freedom of conscience and the right freely to profess, practise and propagate religion — subject to public order, morality and health; Art. 25(2)(a) lets the state regulate secular activity associated with religious practice, and Art. 25(2)(b) lets it provide for social welfare and reform and throw open Hindu religious institutions to all classes — this is the textual home of "principled distance": the Constitution itself authorises intervention in religion for equality
Art. 26Freedom of a religious denomination to manage its own affairs in matters of religion — the provision the Essential Religious Practices doctrine construes (§12.9.5)
Art. 27No person may be compelled to pay taxes for the promotion of any particular religion — the closest Indian analogue to the Establishment Clause
Art. 28No religious instruction in wholly state-funded educational institutions — the direct comparator to Engel v. Vitale and Santa Fe (§12.10)
Art. 29–30Minority rights — conservation of culture; right to establish and administer educational institutions. India protects religion as a group right; the US and France protect it (or restrict it) as an individual liberty. That single contrast answers half of the 2024 PYQ
Art. 44 (DPSP)"The State shall endeavour to secure for the citizens a uniform civil code throughout the territory of India" — ▲ the source lists "UCC" as a one-word challenge and never cites the Article that creates the obligation
Art. 15, 16, 17Non-discrimination on grounds including religion; abolition of untouchability — the equality half of Indian secularism
Art. 368 + KesavanandaSecularism and socialism are part of the basic structure and beyond the amending power (§12.9.1)

The one-line synthesis, and it is the best available answer to "how is Indian secularism different?":The American and French constitutions tell the state what it may not do about religion; the Indian Constitution also tells it what it must do — open temples, abolish untouchability, fund minority schools, and endeavour towards a common civil code. A wall of separation cannot deliver social reform; principled distance is designed to.

3.18 THE FOREIGN CONSTITUTIONAL TEXTS SOURCED IN THIS COURSE ¶

3.18.1 The United States — the First Amendment (the source names the two clauses; the text is [ADDED])¶

  • "The First Amendment to the U.S. Constitution prohibits the establishment of religion (Establishment Clause) and protects the free exercise of religion (Free Exercise Clause)." (verbatim)
  • [ADDED — the words themselves, and they are short enough to lift] "Congress shall make no law respecting an establishment of religion, or prohibiting the free exercise thereof…"
  • "The United States follows the separationist model of secularism, where there is a clear division between church and state." (verbatim)

Two clauses, one tension, and every US case in §12.10 sits on it.Establishment restrains the state from religion; Free Exercise restrains the state for religion. Engel* and Santa Fe are Establishment cases and the state loses; Masterpiece Cakeshop is a Free Exercise case and the state loses. The American model is not "the state stays out" — it is "the citizen wins either way", which is a very different proposition and the one the 2024 PYQ is really about.*

3.18.2 France — laïcité and the law of 1905 (verbatim)¶

  • "France practices laïcité, which emphasizes a strict separation between religion and the state. The state is entirely neutral, and religion is seen as a private matter. This form of secularism dates back to the French Revolution and was formalized by the 1905 law that separated the Church and the state."
  • "The French Constitution guarantees freedom of religion, but there are strict rules regulating the public display of religious identity."
  • [ADDED — the provision the source alludes to but never quotes; verify] Article 1 of the French Constitution of 1958: France is an indivisible, secular (laïque), democratic and social Republic, which shall ensure the equality of all citizens before the law, without distinction of origin, race or religion, and shall respect all beliefs. Note what that sentence contains: "secular" and "social" in the same clause — exactly the pairing the Indian Preamble makes, arrived at from the opposite direction. That observation is worth a mark in the 2019 PYQ.

3.18.3 The United Kingdom — a constitution with no text ¶

  • A.V. Dicey, Introduction to the Study of the Law of the Constitution(1885) — "According to Dicey, parliamentary sovereignty consists of two parts: 1. Parliament can make or unmake any law. 2. No Parliament can pass laws that future Parliaments cannot change or repeal." (verbatim)
  • [ADDED — the context the source omits] The UK has no codified constitution and no entrenched bill of rights; there is therefore no constitutional text to compare — sovereignty is a common-law doctrine described by a nineteenth-century treatise-writer, which is itself the comparison. ▲ The UK also has an established church (the Church of England, with bishops sitting in the House of Lords), which makes it the one comparator in this module that is not secular at all — the source never mentions this, and it is the sharpest single fact available on the UK side.

3.19.4 THE ONE ENFORCEABLE LAYER — the State Right to Public Services Acts¶

Why this single screenshot carries a whole answer.It is the only e-governance instance in the compendium with all four accountability elements at once: a named service, a statutory clock, a named officer and a two-tier appeal. This is also the bridge to §15 reform #4 and to the Citizen's Charter line: an RTS Act is a Citizen's Charter with a designated officer and an appeal — which is precisely what a Charter lacks.

3.20 THE CITIZEN'S CHARTER AND THE LAW — the Bill that never passed and the two State Acts that did¶

3.20.1 The framing — read this before the sub-sections¶

▲ The Charter's defining legal fact is a negative one, and states it plainly (§5.8.3): "The Charter lacks statutory backing, which limits its enforceability. Citizens have no legal recourse if the services promised under the Charter are not delivered." Everything in this section is an attempt to cure that sentence — one attempt at the Centre, which failed, and two in the States, which worked.

3.20.2 THE RIGHT OF CITIZENS FOR TIME BOUND DELIVERY OF GOODS AND SERVICES AND REDRESSAL OF THEIR GRIEVANCES — the source's "Need a Law" slide (verbatim)¶

The source heads the slide "Need a Law" and gives the Bill's full title with (Citizens Charter) in parentheses — i.e. it treats the Bill as the Charter's statutory form.The three provisions the source reproduces, verbatim:

  1. "Every public authority should be mandated by law to publish a Citizens Charter." (the mandate — it converts the voluntary declaration of §2.6.1 into a duty)
  2. "The Charter shall detail the goods and services to be provided and their timelines for delivery." (the content — standards and clocks become statutory particulars)
  3. "A citizen should be legally empowered to file a complaint regarding any grievance related to:(a) citizens charter;(b) functioning of a public authority; or(c) violation of a law, policy or scheme." (the remedy — and note how wide (b) and (c) are)

Plus a two-line follow-on slide, verbatim and unelaborated: ▲ "Increased penalty in case of non-compliance." · "Companies as well as Citizens."

▲ Read the second line with care — the source gives it no sentence of explanation. The defensible reading, and the one to write: the Bill's grievance machinery was to be available to companies as well as citizens, i.e. the complainant class extended beyond natural persons. [ADDED — flagged as a reconstruction; do not quote it as the Bill's language]

The structural point that earns the mark, and the source does not make it:limb (c) — "violation of a law, policy or scheme" — is far wider than a Charter grievance.A Bill introduced to give the Citizen's Charter teeth would, on its own terms, have created a general statutory remedy against maladministration — which is why it was contested and why it lapsed [ADDED].

▲ Two things the source never says, and you must supply both [ADDED — verify before writing]: the Bill was introduced in the Lok Sabha in 2011 (commonly called the Citizens Charter Bill) and it LAPSED — it is not law. The source presents it in the prescriptive voice — "should be mandated" — with no date and no outcome. ▲ Never write about it as a live statute; write about it as the Centre's unfinished business, against which the two State Acts below are the contrast.

The resolution, and it is almost certainly not a mistake at all [ADDED — verify]: the Act was enacted in 2011 as the Karnataka Guarantee of Services to Citizens Act and was RENAMED the Karnataka Sakala Services Act by the Amendment Act of 2014.   • The Act requires a display board at the office, headed "Karnataka Sakala Services Act, 2011", carrying the Name of the Office and the Name of the Village/Taluk/District, and then a table of Scheduled Services with ten columns:

Why Form-A is worth more than the Act's summary, and this is the highest-value observation in the section.Compare its ten columns with the four elements of a Charter at §2.6.2. A Citizen's Charter promises a standard; Form-A names the officer who owes it, the officer who reviews him, the officer who reviews her, a clock against each of the three, and the rupee value of failure — and then compels the office to nail it to the wall. That is the entire difference between a charter and a guarantee, and it is a difference of five columns.

The acknowledgement requirement is the quiet masterstroke:the citizen cannot enforce a clock she cannot prove she started — which is why the first instruction on the board is to obtain the acknowledgement "compulsorily".

▲ One caution the source's own website screenshot invites: the portal advertises MIS and REPORT tabs — so the disposal data exists — and reproduces not one figure from either.

State the ladder in one sentence and you have the spine of every Charter answer: the Charter published a standard, the Guarantee Acts attached an officer and a penalty to it, and e-governance made the clock visible — and only the middle step created a right. 3.21 THE POLICY AND CONSTITUTIONAL SCAFFOLDING OF AI IN GOVERNANCE ▲ (; ▲ note the section title, and note it is the third of its kind: like §3.19 (e-governance) and §3.20 (the Citizen's Charter), there is no statute here at all)¶

3.21.1 The framing caution — read this before the sub-sections¶

▲ There is no AI statute in this source, and nothing in eleven decks that regulates an algorithm. The source concedes the absence itself: two of its six Way Forward points are "Ethical AI legislation" and an "Independent AI Regulatory Authority" (§15, reforms 92–93) — you do not ask for a law and a regulator that already exist.

The pattern to state, because it is now three modules deep and it is the compendium's sharpest structural observation.§3.19: e-governance rests on the NeGP 2006 and Digital India — policy, not law.§3.20: the Citizen's Charter rests on a lapsed Bill and two State Acts — policy centrally, law only in the States.§3.21: AI rests on a NITI Aayog strategy — policy, and not even a scheme. India's digital state has been built almost entirely through executive policy, and the citizen's enforceable rights against it exist only where a legislature has separately intervened. ▲ The one enforceable layer anywhere in this stack is still the State Right to Public Services Acts (§3.19.4, §3.20.3–§3.20.4) — and they guarantee a service, not an explanation.

▲ What this means for your answer: never write that AI in India is "unregulated" without naming what does apply — the DPDP Act 2023 (§3.5) governs the personal data that trains and feeds these systems, and it is the only statute in the compendium that touches this topic at all. ▲ The source never mentions the DPDP Act — so the connection is yours to make, and it is worth making: India regulates the input (personal data) and not the output (the algorithmic determination). ▲ And recall §3.5.3: the Act's own Section 35 lets the Union exempt any State instrumentality from its application — which means the statute closest to AI governance carries an exemption clause aimed precisely at the state actors §4.13 describes.

"Indian Policy Framework — 1. NITI Aayog – AI for All Strategy (2018)"

  • This is the entire policy framework as the source states it: one body, one document, one year. The substance is at §11.7, where the source's own evidence annexe expands it.
  • Learn the name precisely — the strategy is the National Strategy for Artificial Intelligence, and #AIforAll is its slogan and its stated goal (§11.7.1, sourced from slide 16).
  • ▲ Nothing else is named.No ministry, no mission, no rule, no advisory, no international instrument. If an answer needs more than one policy anchor, you do not have a second one from this course.

The observation worth a mark, and the source hands it to you without noticing:the governing document of India's AI policy is a strategy paper from a think-tank with no executive authority, published in 2018 — while §4.13's deployments run to late 2025* and cover policing, prisons, insurance settlement and school-level risk-scoring of 1+ crore children. The deployment has outrun the framework by seven years. ▲ That sentence is the single best opening for any "challenges of AI in governance" answer, and it is sourced entirely from this source's own two halves.*

▲ [CAUTION — attribution] The source displays this diagram under the heading "India's AI Governance Philosophy", immediately below the line "NITI Aayog – AI for All Strategy (2018)", and gives it no source of its own. The seven, as the diagram gives them:

#Sutra (verbatim from the diagram)What it decides
1 Trust is the FoundationThe diagram places this at the top — trust is presented as the precondition, not an outcome

Sutra 3 is the one to write about, because it is the only one that takes a side."Innovation over Restraint" is not a neutral principle — it is a stated preference for permissive regulation, and it sits in the same list as "Accountability" and "Fairness & Equity" without any rule for resolving the conflict between them. That is the whole Indian AI-policy debate in one diagram, and it is exactly the tension the source's own conclusion admits when it warns that "unchecked algorithmic governance… may weaken democratic oversight and civil liberties" (§5.9.5).

The sentence to carry:India's stated AI philosophy resolves in favour of innovation and its stated risks resolve in favour of restraint; until a statute chooses between them, the choice is made deployment by deployment by the deploying department itself — which is precisely what §4.13's eighteen systems show.

3.21.4 THE ETHICAL & CONSTITUTIONAL CHALLENGES — the three-Article slide (verbatim; the source's section 8)¶

"8. Ethical & Constitutional Challenges

Article 21 – Privacy and due process"

▲ That is the complete slide. Three lines, no text of any Article, no gloss, no case. It is nonetheless the most valuable slide in the lecture half, because it tells you the frame the course expects — and because of what it does to a standing gap in this compendium.

ArticleThe source's phraseWhat it must be argued as [ADDED — the argument is entirely yours]Where the evidence in this source is
Art. 14"Risk of discrimination"Equality before the law and equal protection of the laws. The AI claim: a model trained on historic administrative data reproduces historic administrative bias, and does so at scale and behind a technical justification. Arbitrariness is the classic Art. 14 vice, and an unexplainable determination is arbitrariness that cannot be examined▲ Predictive policing over CCTNS's 28-crore-record database and AFRS/Trinetra photo-matching (§4.13.8) — policing data records who was policed, not who offended
Art. 19"Free speech implications"Freedom of speech and expression, assembly and movement. The AI claim: pervasive automated identification chills lawful expression and assembly — the chilling effect argument▲ AI-enhanced CCTV and facial recognition in Delhi, Maharashtra and other cities; drone surveillance (§5.9.2 D, §4.13.8)
Art. 21"Privacy and due process"Life and personal liberty — and, since Puttaswamy, informational privacy (§12.11). The strongest limb: due process requires notice, reasons and a hearing before an adverse determination — and an algorithmic determination gives none of the three▲ JARVIS across 70 prisons and 700+ cameras; automated e-challans issued without a human in the loop; ~1.67 lakh children risk-flagged in Gujarat (§4.13.6, §4.13.8, §4.13.9)

Write the three Articles as one escalating argument, not three bullets, and you will outperform the slide by a distance:Art. 19 is about what the citizen stops doing when watched; Art. 14 is about who the system watches more closely; and Art. 21 is about the citizen's inability to answer back — the first is a chilling effect, the second a distributional defect, and the third a procedural void. Then close on the one that has a remedy: due process is the only limb of the three that a "human-in-the-loop" requirement actually cures (§15, reform 91) — which is why it is the reform to lead with.**
