4.1 CONSTITUTION OF THE CENTRAL INFORMATION COMMISSION ¶

4.1.1 Composition¶

The Central Information Commission shall consist of —

  • (a) the Chief Information Commissioner; and
  • (b) such number of Central Information Commissioners, not exceeding ten, as may be deemed necessary.

4.1.2 Appointment¶

  • The Chief Information Commissioner and Information Commissioners shall be appointed by the President on the recommendation of a committee consisting of —

- (i) the Prime Minister — Chairperson of the committee;

- (ii) the Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha; and

- (iii) a Union Cabinet Minister to be nominated by the Prime Minister.

The 2:1 executive majority is the standard critique — the PM plus his own nominee outvote the LoP. Use the same critique for the CVC, Lokpal and CBI Director committees (§4) to show pattern recognition.

4.1.3 Qualifications and disqualifications¶

  • Shall be persons of eminence in public life with wide knowledge and experience in law, science and technology, social service, management, journalism, mass media or administration and governance.
  • Shall NOT be a Member of Parliament or Member of the Legislature of any State or Union territory, nor hold any other office of profit, nor be connected with any political party, nor carry on any business or pursue any profession.

4.1.4 Tenure ¶

  • The Chief Information Commissioner shall hold office for such term as may be prescribed by the Central Government and shall not be eligible for reappointment; provided that no CIC shall hold office after attaining the age of sixty-five years.
  • Every Information Commissioner shall hold office for such term as may be prescribed by the Central Government or till he attains the age of sixty-five years, whichever is earlier, and shall not be eligible for reappointment as such Information Commissioner.
  • Proviso: every Information Commissioner shall, on vacating his office, be eligible for appointment as the Chief Information Commissioner.
  • Further proviso: where an Information Commissioner is appointed as Chief Information Commissioner, his term of office shall not be more than five years in aggregate as Information Commissioner and Chief Information Commissioner.

▲ [CAUTION — read the tenure text carefully] The phrase "such term as may be prescribed by the Central Government" is the post-2019-amendment wording: before the RTI (Amendment) Act, 2019, the Act itself fixed the term at five years. [ADDED] The RTI Rules, 2019 prescribe three years. So:

  • Pre-2019: 5 years or 65, fixed by statute.
  • Post-2019: term (and salary/allowances) fixed by the Central Government by rules — currently 3 years.
  • The "five years in aggregate" proviso in is a carry-over of the original scheme and sits awkwardly with a rule-prescribed 3-year term. Write the 2019 change as the substantive point (executive control over tenure = the CHRI "dilution" critique, §11.3) rather than committing to a bare number. This is exactly the "reduced the tenure and salary protections of Information Commissioners" concern itself records in the CHRI slide.

4.1.5 Removal ¶

  • The Chief Information Commissioner or any Information Commissioner shall be removed from office only by order of the President on the ground of proved misbehaviour or incapacity — after the Supreme Court, on a reference made to it by the President, has on inquiry reported that he ought on such ground be removed.
  • The President may by order remove the CIC or any IC on the grounds that he —

- (a) is adjudged an insolvent; or

- (b) has been convicted of an offence which, in the opinion of the President, involves moral turpitude; or

- (c)engages during his term of office in any paid employment outside the duties of his office; or

- (d) is, in the opinion of the President, unfit to continue in office by reason of infirmity of mind or body; or

- (e) has acquired such financial or other interest as is likely to affect prejudicially his functions as CIC or IC.

The two-track removal design — track 1 (proved misbehaviour or incapacity) requires a Supreme Court inquiry; track 2 (the five specific grounds) is a direct presidential order. The same template governs the CVC and Lokpal; learn it once, deploy it three times.

Security of tenure = independence. Link removal-protection to §11.3 (CHRI: weakened commissions) and §15 (reform: insulate appointments).

4.1.6 A structural gap in the Act ¶

The law provides for NO appeals against the decisions of the Commission. However, these decisions are being challenged in High Courts through writ petitions by many public authorities to deny information to citizens. In most of these cases, a stay is obtained ex-parte. (Developed further at §12.3 — dilution of RTI by the judiciary.)

4.2 THE LOKPAL — the institution ¶

Learn this against §4.1 (CIC), not separately. The architecture is the same in all three bodies — selection committee → qualifications → fixed tenure → two-track removal → post-office bar. What differs is who sits on the committee and how hard it is to remove the incumbent. §4.4 tabulates the differences; memorise the template once.

4.2.1 Composition ¶

The Lokpal shall consist of —

  • (a) a Chairperson, who is or has been a Chief Justice of India or is or has been a Judge of the Supreme Court or an eminent person; and
  • (b) such number of Members, not exceeding eight, out of whom fifty per cent shall be Judicial Members:
  • Provided that not less than fifty per cent of the Members of the Lokpal shall be from amongst the persons belonging to the Scheduled Castes, the Scheduled Tribes, Other Backward Classes, Minorities and women.

Two points examiners reward.(i) The 50% judicial requirement makes the Lokpal a quasi-judicial hybrid, not a purely administrative watchdog — contrast the CIC, which has no judicial-member requirement at all (§4.1.3). (ii) The 50% representation proviso is unusual in an oversight body — most Indian statutory commissions carry no such mandate. Read it as social-justice design imported into an integrity institution: the theory is that a body drawn from the same narrow elite it polices will not police it. [ADDED] The counter-argument worth conceding is that representation and independence are different variables, and the Act secures the first without guaranteeing the second.

4.2.2 Eligibility ¶

A person shall be eligible to be appointed —

  • (a) as a Judicial Member if he is or has been a Judge of the Supreme Court or is or has been a Chief Justice of a High Court;
  • (b) as a Member other than a Judicial Member, if he is a person of impeccable integrity and outstanding ability having special knowledge and expertise of not less than twenty-five years in the matters relating to anti-corruption policy, public administration, vigilance, finance including insurance and banking, law and management.

"Impeccable integrity and outstanding ability" + "not less than twenty-five years" is the phrase-pair to lift. Compare the CIC's softer "eminence in public life with wide knowledge and experience" (§4.1.3) — the Lokpal standard is higher and quantified, which is consistent with a body that can prosecute.

4.2.3 Disqualifications ¶

The Chairperson or a Member shall not be —

  • (i) a legislator or a member of a local body;
  • (ii) a person convicted of any offence involving moral turpitude;
  • (iii)less than 45 years of age;
  • (v) a person who has been removed or dismissed from the service of the Union or a State.
  • Nor may the office be combined with an office of profit, profession or business.

▲ [CAUTION — slide rendering] list runs (i), (ii), (iii), (v) — clause (iv) is missing, and clause (i) appears to merge two separate disqualifications. [ADDED] The standard statutory text separates them: (i) a member of Parliament or of the Legislature of any State or Union territory; (iv) a member of any Panchayat or Municipality. So the source has compressed (i) and (iv) into "legislator or a member of a local body" and left the numbering unrepaired. The substance is intact — write the four grounds, not the clause numbers.

The 45-year floor is the one to notice: the Lokpal is designed to be staffed by people at the end of a career, not the middle of one — which, combined with the post-office bar (§4.2.7), is a deliberate attempt to remove the incentive to please a future employer.

4.2.4 Appointment ¶

The Chairperson and Members shall be appointed by the President after obtaining the recommendations of a Selection Committee consisting of —

  • (a) the Prime Minister — Chairperson;
  • (b) the Speaker of the House of the People — Member;
  • (c) the Leader of Opposition in the House of the People — Member;
  • (d) the Chief Justice of India or a Judge of the Supreme Court nominated by him — Member;
  • (e)one eminent jurist, nominated by the President — Member.

Compare the three committees in one breath — this is the highest-yield comparison in §4.

  • CIC (3 members): PM + LoP + a Union Cabinet Minister nominated by the PM → 2:1 executive majority.
  • CVC (3 members): PM + Home Minister + LoP → 2:1 executive majority.
  • Lokpal (5 members): PM + Speaker + LoP + CJI/nominee + eminent jurist nominated by the President → the broadest committee of the three, and the only one with judicial representation.

The line to write: the Lokpal's selection committee is the most pluralistic in the Indian oversight architecture — yet the executive still nominates the eminent jurist and, in practice, controls the timetable. Broad composition guarantees legitimacy of choice; it does not guarantee that a choice is made at all. That sets up the appointment-delay critique (§13.4, §14 issue 21) perfectly.

4.2.5 Tenure ¶

  • The Chairperson and Members hold office for a term of five years or the age of seventy years, whichever is earlier.
  • Provided that he may — (a) by writing under his hand addressed to the President, resign his office; or (b) be removed from his office.
  • A Member shall be eligible to be appointed as a Chairperson, if his total tenure as Member and Chairperson does not exceed five years.

Contrast with the CIC and note who fixed the number. The Lokpal's 5 years / 70 sits in the statute; the CIC's term is now whatever the Central Government prescribes by rules (§4.1.4, post-2019). Security of tenure fixed by Parliament is independence; security of tenure fixed by the executive is permission. Also note the "five years in aggregate" cap on the Member→Chairperson route — the identical device appears in the RTI Act (§4.1.4), so it is a drafting convention worth naming.

4.2.6 Removal — the two-track template again¶

Track 1 — misbehaviour, via the Supreme Court:"The Chairperson or any Member shall be removed from his office by order of the President on grounds of misbehaviour after the Supreme Court, on a reference being made to it by the President on a petition signed by at least one hundred Members of Parliament, has, on an inquiry held in accordance with the procedure prescribed in that behalf, reported that the Chairperson or such Member, as the case may be, ought to be removed on such ground."Track 2 — direct presidential order. The President may, by order, remove the Chairperson or any Member if he —

  • (a) is adjudged an insolvent; or
  • (b)engages, during his term of office, in any paid employment outside the duties of his office; or
  • (c) is, in the opinion of the President, unfit to continue in office by reason of infirmity of mind or body.

The 100-MP petition is the distinguishing feature — and it is the strongest tenure protection in the entire compendium. The CIC and the CVC can be referred to the Supreme Court by the President acting alone; the Lokpal cannot be touched without one hundred Members of Parliament first signing a petition. Write it as a deliberate design choice: the body that can investigate the Prime Minister was given a removal threshold the Prime Minister cannot meet alone. Compare the impeachment-style protection of judges (Art. 124(4)) and of the CAG (Art. 148(1)) — the Lokpal was consciously placed in that family.

Also note what is absent from the Lokpal's Track 2 list: there is no "moral turpitude conviction" ground and no "prejudicial financial interest" ground, both of which appear for the CIC and the CVC (§4.1.5, §4.3.3). Shorter list = harder to remove. Consistent with the point above.

4.2.7 Salary, and the post-office bar ¶

  • Salary, allowances and other conditions of service — (i) the Chairperson shall be the same as those of the Chief Justice of India; (ii) other Members shall be the same as those of a Judge of the Supreme Court.
  • On ceasing to hold office, the Chairperson and every Member shall be ineligible for —

- (i)reappointment as the Chairperson or a Member of the Lokpal;

- (ii)any diplomatic assignment, appointment as administrator of a Union territory and such other assignment or appointment which is required by law to be made by the President by warrant under his hand and seal;

- (iii)further employment to any other office of profit under the Government of India or the Government of a State;

- (iv)contesting any election of President or Vice-President or Member of either House of Parliament or Member of either House of a State Legislature or Municipality or Panchayat within a period of five years from the date of relinquishing the post.

This is the most complete "post-retirement insulation" clause in Indian public law — and it is your best evidence in any answer on post-retirement appointments. It closes four exit routes: the body itself, diplomatic/UT postings, any office of profit, and elective politics for five years. The argument to make: the integrity of an oversight office is decided less by how its holder is appointed than by what he may become afterwards. The Lokpal Act understood this; most other statutes did not. Contrast the standing controversy over judges and regulators taking post-retirement government appointments [ADDED], and note that the CIC and CVC bar only reappointment and (for the CVC) further government office — neither bars contesting elections.

  • Financial autonomy:"The administrative expenses of the Lokpal, including all salaries, allowances and pensions payable to or in respect of the Chairperson, Members or Secretary or other officers or staff of the Lokpal, shall be charged upon the Consolidated Fund of India." "Charged upon the Consolidated Fund" = not subject to the annual vote of Parliament, the same protection given to the CAG, the Supreme Court and the ECI. [ADDED] ▲ But note the limit of that protection — being charged protects the expenditure from being voted down; it does not compel the government to propose an adequate sum. The budget collapse from ₹101.29 crore to ₹18.01 crore (§13.4) happened despite this clause. That contrast — constitutional-grade financial protection, ninth-grade actual funding — is a first-class answer point.

4.2.8 The two wings ¶

WingHeadStatutory purpose (verbatim)
Inquiry WingDirector of Inquiry"for the purpose of conducting preliminary inquiry into any offence alleged to have been committed by a public servant punishable under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988"
Prosecution WingDirector of Prosecution"for the purpose of prosecution of public servants in relation to any complaint by the Lokpal under this Act"

This is the Lokpal's decisive structural advantage over the CVC — and says so explicitly (§4.4): "The Lokpal act provides for its own independent investigative wing, while the CVC depends on the CBI and other vigilance officers to conduct investigations."

▲ But hold the qualification, or the point is wrong. The Inquiry Wing conducts a preliminary inquiry; the full investigation still travels to the CBI/DSPE under §3.7.4. So the Lokpal owns the front end (inquiry) and the back end (prosecution) — and rents the middle (investigation). That is exactly why "Lack of Independence" survives as the standing critique (§14, issue 22): an ombudsman that can open a file and can argue a case, but cannot itself build one, remains dependent on the agency whose independence is most contested.

4.3 THE CENTRAL VIGILANCE COMMISSION — the institution ¶

(Statutory origin — 1964, Santhanam Committee, CVC Act 2003 — at §3.9.)

4.3.1 Appointment ¶

  • The Central Vigilance Commissioner and the Vigilance Commissioners shall be appointed by the President by warrant under his hand and seal, on the recommendation of a Committee consisting of —

- (a) the Prime Minister — Chairperson;

- (b) the Minister of Home Affairs — Member;

- (c) the Leader of the Opposition in the House of the People — Member.

The 2:1 executive majority critique applies here in its purest form — two Cabinet colleagues and one opponent. ✓ Upgraded: carries a slide titled "P J Thomas Case – CVC", so the case name is now sourced — though the slide is heading-only with no body text, so everything below it remains [ADDED]. This is the committee whose working the Supreme Court examined in Centre for PIL v. Union of India (the P.J. Thomas case, 2011) (§12.1), holding that "institutional integrity" — not merely eligibility — is a mandatory consideration, and that the LoP's dissent cannot simply be recorded and overridden. Cite Thomas whenever you critique any of the three selection committees; it is the judicial authority for the proposition that majority voting is not a substitute for consensus in integrity appointments.

[ADDED] Composition of the body itself: the Act provides for a Central Vigilance Commissioner and not more than two Vigilance Commissioners. does not state this — verify before writing the number.

4.3.2 Tenure ¶

  • Central Vigilance Commissioner — four years from the date on which he enters upon his office, or till he attains the age of sixty-five years, whichever is earlier.
  • On ceasing to hold the office, the Central Vigilance Commissioner shall be ineligible for reappointment in the Commission.
  • Vigilance Commissioner — four years or sixty-five years, whichever is earlier.

The three-body tenure line to memorise:CIC — as prescribed by the Centre, max 65 · CVC — 4 years or 65 · Lokpal — 5 years or 70. Note the direction of travel: the higher the office's reach, the longer and more statutorily fixed the tenure. The CIC alone had its term removed from the statute (2019) — which is why it is the weakest of the three on paper.

4.3.3 Removal — the same two-track template¶

Track 1:"Central Vigilance Commissioner or any Vigilance Commissioner shall be removed from his office only by order of the President on the ground of proved misbehaviour or incapacity after the Supreme Court, on a reference made to it by the President, has, on inquiry, reported that the Central Vigilance Commissioner or any Vigilance Commissioner, as the case may be, ought on such ground be removed."Track 2 — direct presidential order. Grounds:

  • (a) is adjudged an insolvent; or
  • (b) has been convicted of an offence which, in the opinion of the Central Government, involves moral turpitude; or
  • (c)engages during his term of office in any paid employment outside the duties of his office; or
  • (d) is, in the opinion of the President, unfit to continue in office by reason of infirmity of mind or body; or
  • (e) has acquired such financial or other interest as is likely to affect prejudicially his functions as a Central Vigilance Commissioner or a Vigilance Commissioner.

Precision point worth a mark. Compare CIC ground (b) — "convicted of an offence which, in the opinion of the President, involves moral turpitude" (§4.1.5) — with CVC ground (b) — "in the opinion of the Central Government." Formally, "the President" acts on aid and advice anyway; but the CVC Act drops even the constitutional fiction and names the executive directly. If you notice this in an answer, you are reading statutes the way examiners want them read.

The template recurs a third time. Track 1 (proved misbehaviour or incapacity → SC reference → report → removal) is now identical across the CIC, the CVC and the Lokpal — save that the Lokpal additionally requires the 100-MP petition (§4.2.6). Learn it once, deploy it three times.

4.3.4 Role and powers ¶

FunctionContent (liftable)
Supervision and monitoringCVC supervises and monitors vigilance activities in central government organizations, public sector undertakings, and autonomous bodies.
Advisory roleIt advises the central government on matters related to corruption and recommends action against corrupt officials.
Complaint handlingIt receives complaints about corruption from individuals, government departments, and conducts preliminary inquiries.
Lokpal referralsThe Commission also conducts preliminary inquiry into the complaints referred by Lokpal in respect of Gr. A, B, C & D officials.
Superintendence over the CBI The Commission further exercises superintendence over the functioning of the Delhi Special Police Establishment (CBI) insofar as it relates to the investigation of offences under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988.

Appointment powers over the investigating agencies (the least-known, most-usable fact in the CVC section)

  • Enforcement Directorate: appointment of officers to posts of the level of Deputy Director and above (including the Director) is recommended by a committee under the chairpersonship of the Central Vigilance Commissioner, with the Vigilance Commissioner and other officers of the Government of India as members.
  • CBI: appointment of officers to posts of the level of SP and above in the CBI (except Director, CBI) is recommended by a committee under the chairpersonship of the Central Vigilance Commissioner, with the Vigilance Commissioner and other officers of the Government of India as members.

This converts the CVC from an "advisory body" into something sharper, and most candidates miss it. The CVC does not merely advise on corruption — it chairs the committee that staffs the ED and the CBI. The parenthesis is the point: "(except Director, CBI)". ✓ Now sourced: the CBI Director is appointed by a separate committee of the PM (chairperson), the LoP in the Lok Sabha, and the CJI or a Supreme Court judge nominated by him, under the DSPE Act 1946 as amended by the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013. So the CVC staffs the agency but does not choose its head — precisely the arrangement that leaves the CBI's independence contested. And completes the other half too: the ED Director's committee is set out in full at §4.6.3 — CVC as chairperson, the Vigilance Commissioners, and the Home, Personnel and Revenue Secretaries. Put the two beside each other (§4.4.4): the CBI's head is chosen by a committee containing the Leader of the Opposition and the Chief Justice; the ED's head is chosen by a committee containing five serving officials of the Union Government and no one else.

4.3.5 Impact ¶

  • Systemic reforms: the CVC has played a role in creating transparency and accountability within the government. It has introduced reforms such as Integrity Pacts in public procurement and other anti-corruption measures.
  • Deterring corruption: while the CVC has played a significant role in deterring corruption in public sector organizations, its effectiveness has been limited due to a lack of independent investigative powers and reliance on government departments for enforcement.
  • Awareness and training: the CVC has promoted vigilance awareness through campaigns, training programs, and awareness weeks in public institutions.

The Integrity Pact is the one concrete deliverable to name. [ADDED] It is a written agreement between the procuring entity and all bidders not to offer or accept bribes, monitored by Independent External Monitors, adapted from a Transparency International instrument. Vigilance Awareness Week is observed around 31 October (Sardar Patel's birth anniversary). Verify both before quoting. Use the Integrity Pact whenever a question asks for "preventive vigilance" rather than punitive action — it shows you can distinguish the two.

4.3.6 Challenges ¶

  • Lack of powers: despite being a key body in tackling corruption, the CVC lacks independent investigative powers and often relies on the CBI or departmental vigilance mechanisms.
  • Overlapping jurisdictions: the presence of multiple anti-corruption bodies like the Lokpal, CVC, and CBI sometimes creates overlaps, leading to jurisdictional conflicts.
  • Impact on high-level corruption: the CVC's focus is more on mid-level and lower officials, with limited impact on high-level political and bureaucratic corruption, which is now primarily under the Lokpal's purview.

Notice that critique of the CVC and its critique of the Lokpal converge on the same sentence: neither can investigate on its own. The CVC relies on the CBI; the Lokpal relies on the CBI (§3.7.4, §4.2.8). So the binding constraint in India's anti-corruption architecture is not the number of watchdogs — it is that they share one pair of teeth. Write that and you have the conclusion to any "multiplicity of anti-corruption bodies" question.

4.4 THE TURF-MAP — CVC vs LOKPAL vs UPSC vs CBI vs the CAG ¶

4.4.1 CVC vs Lokpal (liftable verbatim)¶

  • Jurisdiction overlap: while both bodies deal with anti-corruption, the Lokpal is more powerful and independent, with jurisdiction over complaints against public servants, including the Prime Minister, MPs, and Group A officials. The CVC, on the other hand, deals with vigilance within central government departments and public sector undertakings, except the political authorities.
  • Investigative power: the Lokpal act provides for its own independent investigative wing, while the CVC depends on the CBI and other vigilance officers to conduct investigations.
  • Conflict of powers: some see a potential overlap or conflict in jurisdiction and roles between Lokpal and CVC. For instance, if both the CVC and Lokpal receive complaints regarding the same official, it might lead to duplication or confusion.

The clean distinction to carry into the hall: the CVC is vigilance within the executive; the Lokpal is an ombudsman over the state, politicians included. The three-word discriminator is "except the political authorities."

4.4.2 CVC vs UPSC (liftable verbatim)¶

  • Role of UPSC in disciplinary cases: the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) advises the government on disciplinary matters, especially related to Group A officers. However, when the CVC advises disciplinary action in corruption cases, the UPSC might also be involved in reviewing the same case from a recruitment and promotion perspective.
  • Conflict in advisory roles: the advice given by the CVC on vigilance matters and the UPSC on disciplinary matters could sometimes conflict, particularly regarding how the integrity of an officer should be judged.

This is an unusual comparison and therefore a scoring one — most candidates never connect Art. 320(3)(c) (the UPSC's constitutional consultation role in disciplinary matters) [ADDED] with the CVC's statutory vigilance advice. The structural point: one body judges the officer's integrity, another judges his career — and neither decision binds the government, which owns both files. Advisory bodies multiplying around a discretionary decision is not accountability; it is diffusion of responsibility.

How to use this table in an answer. Any question of the form "Examine the effectiveness of India's anti-corruption/transparency institutions" is answered by reading down three columns, not by describing three bodies in sequence. The pattern that emerges is the argument: strong appointment design, weak investigative autonomy, and terms of service that the executive can adjust. The concluding line writes itself: India has built oversight bodies with the architecture of independence and the plumbing of dependence.

4.4.4 THE AGENCY TIER — CBI vs ED *(new, from; **every underlying slide re-run in →)*¶

§4.4.3 compared the three oversight bodies. This compares the two agencies they depend on — and the contrast between the two appointment committees is the sharpest single argument in the module.

The comparison to write, and it takes one sentence. India's older agency, which needs a State's permission to enter it, has a Director chosen by a committee containing the Leader of the Opposition and the Chief Justice. Its newer agency, which needs no one's permission and can attach property before trial, has a Director chosen by five serving officials of the Union Government. The agency with the fewest checks on its power has the fewest checks on its appointment.

The second-order point that lifts a good answer to a very good one: the CBI's constraints are federal (State consent) and its safeguards are appointment-side (a balanced committee); the ED's constraints are judicial (bail jurisprudence — §12.5) and its safeguards are procedural only. So when the courts relax Sec. 45, they are not being lenient on economic crime — they are supplying the only check the ED's design contains. That reframes the entire "judiciary is soft on corruption" complaint.

▲ Balance it, or it reads as advocacy. The CBI's balanced committee has not prevented the "caged parrot" criticism, and the ED's official committee is at least chaired by the CVC, a body with a two-track removal protection of its own (§4.3.3). Appointment design is necessary and not sufficient — which is, in the end, the thesis of this entire compendium.

§4.4.3 compared the three oversight bodies; §4.4.4 compared the two agencies. This adds the one constitutional office — and it inverts the pattern both of them established.

The sentence this table exists to produce — and it is the strongest single observation added.The office with the strongest protection after appointment has the weakest scrutiny at appointment.Every statutory body in this compendium is appointed by a committee containing at least the Leader of the Opposition; the one constitutional body is appointed by the executive alone. Then state the design logic behind it, because it is not an oversight: the framers protected the CAG at the exit, not at the entry — the theory being that an officer who cannot be removed, cannot be paid less, and can hold no further office has nothing left to gain from the government that chose him.

The counter, and the answer needs it.Irremovability is a defence against pressure, not against selection. An appointment process with no external voice does not need to influence the officer afterwards; it has already exercised its influence. Compare §4.5.4's opposite pathology — the CBI Director has the best committee and the weakest post-appointment protection (an annually extendable tenure). India has built one office it cannot remove but did not scrutinise, and one it scrutinised but can renew annually. Neither has both halves.That is the thesis sentence for any "appointment to constitutional and statutory posts" question.

Third-order point, if you have room. The CIC row is the warning: the 2019 amendment moved its tenure and salary from statute to executive rule (§4.1.4). The CAG is immune from that technique only because Art. 148 puts the freeze in the Constitution.Protection written in a statute can be amended by the majority that the officer audits; protection written in the Constitution cannot — which is why the source's own closing question about amending the CAG provisions (§4.7.7) matters more than it looks.

Three readings of this table, each worth a paragraph.

(1) The independence test that actually discriminates is the money row. Every body in this compendium has an impressive removal clause. Only four have expenditure charged on the Consolidated Fund — CAG, Lokpal, UPSC, and the CIC's parent statute does not — and the NHRC, the one body assessed against an international standard requiring "adequate resources", receives grants at the government's discretion. Sort the compendium's nine bodies by the money provision and you get the true ranking of their independence; sort them by the removal provision and you get a ranking that flatters almost all of them.

(2) Protection and power move in opposite directions. The best-protected offices — CAG, UPSC — produce findings and advice that bind nobody. The least-protected — CBI, ED — can arrest, attach and prosecute. India protects the offices that cannot coerce and leaves exposed the offices that can. That single sentence, with §4.4.4, §4.4.5 and this table behind it, is the sharpest institutional-design argument in the compendium.

(3) The NHRC is the only body here that is graded from outside. Domestic accountability of accountability institutions is otherwise entirely internal — the PAC for the CAG, Parliament for the Lokpal, nobody for the UPSC. The NHRC's downgrade is therefore not just a fact about the NHRC; it is the only external audit of an Indian oversight body that exists at all.

4.5 THE CENTRAL BUREAU OF INVESTIGATION — the institution ¶

(Statutory origin — SPE 1941, DSPE Act 1946, the 1963 resolution — at §3.10.1. Consent architecture at §3.10.2. Superintendence at §3.10.3.)

4.5.1 What it is (verbatim)¶

  • Dept. of Personnel, Ministry of Personnel, Pension & Public Grievances.
  • It is the premier investigating police agency in India.
  • It is also the nodal police agency in India, which coordinates investigation on behalf of Interpol Member countries.

The placement is the first analytical point, and it is free marks. The CBI sits in the Department of Personnel and Training — the ministry held by the Prime Minister [ADDED]. The agency that investigates the Union Government is administratively housed inside it, in the department headed by its head. State that neutrally and let it work; it is also the reason the Parliamentary Standing Committee wants a new law with "safeguards to ensure objectivity and impartiality" (§3.10.5).

The Interpol line is the cheapest mark in the module — one clause, rarely written, and it converts a domestic answer into one with an international-cooperation dimension. Pair it with UNCAC (§3.7.1) and the PMLA as "part of a global response" (§12.5.3): all three of India's anti-corruption instruments are anchored in international obligation.

4.5.2 Jurisdiction and its hard limit ¶

  • Extends to all Union Territories; to a State only with the consent of that State Government (§3.10.2).
  • ▲ "CBI cannot take suo motu cognizance of a case in a state — whether in a matter of corruption involving government officials of the Centre and PSU staff, or an incident of violent crime."
  • Entry survives withdrawal of consent if the case was not registered in that state (the Chhattisgarh avenue), and by entrustment from the Supreme Court or a High Court (§3.10.4).

Set this against the Lokpal and the contradiction at the heart of the architecture becomes visible. The Lokpal's jurisdiction reaches the Prime Minister (§3.7.2) — but the Lokpal has no investigators of its own beyond a preliminary Inquiry Wing (§4.2.8), so it refers to the CBI. And the CBI cannot enter a State on its own motion. An ombudsman with nationwide jurisdiction over the Union executive works through an agency that needs a State's permission to knock on a door. The jurisdictional reach of the institution and the operational reach of its instrument do not match.

4.5.3 What it investigates ¶

  • Originally bribery and corruption by Central Government servants; extended over time to PSU employees, and after the 1969 bank nationalisation to Public Sector Banks and their employees (§3.10.1).
  • Now also murder, kidnapping, terrorist crime, high-profile conventional crimes, economic offences, banking frauds and crimes with international linkages (§3.10.4).

4.5.4 The Director — appointment and tenure (verbatim)¶

  • "The CBI director is appointed according to provisions under the Delhi Special Police Establishment Act (1946) and amendments therein brought by the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013."
  • "The appointment is made by the Centre on recommendation by a three-member Committee."
  • The committee:1. Prime Minister as the chairperson, 2. the leader of the opposition (LoP) in the Lok Sabha and 3. the Chief Justice of India, or a Supreme Court judge nominated by him.
  • "Vineet Narain versus Union of India case had issued a specific order that the CBI director shall have a minimum tenure of two years."
  • "5 Years." ▲ [ADDED — interpretation] The bare figure refers to the DSPE (Amendment) Act, 2021, which permits the two-year term to be extended by one year at a time up to a total of five years, mirroring the ED provision at §4.6.4. Verify before writing it as a rule — gives only the two words.

Three separate marks live in this one slide; do not blur them.

(i) The Lokpal Act amended the DSPE Act. The statute creating the ombudsman rewrote the statute governing its investigator — which is the cleanest available proof that the 2013 Act understood its own dependence on the CBI and tried to fix the appointment end of it. Use this whenever you argue that the Lokpal's problem is implementation, not design (§13.4.7).

(ii) The committee has no executive majority.PM + LoP + CJI is 1:1:1 — compare the CVC's 2:1 (§4.3.1) and the CIC's 2:1 (§4.1.2). This is the strongest appointment design in the entire compendium, and it exists for a police agency, not for any of the three oversight bodies. Say so — it is a genuinely surprising observation and examiners reward surprise that survives scrutiny.

(iii) The tenure floor is judicial in origin, not legislative.Two years came from Vineet Narain (1997), not from Parliament. Now line the three up: Vineet Narain gave the CBI Director tenure and the CVC statutory status (2003, §3.9); Common Cause (2017) forced the Lokpal's appointment (§13.4.4); Sita Soren (2024) narrowed the Art. 105(2) bar (§3.7.3). Every load-bearing feature of India's anti-corruption architecture that actually functions was installed by the Supreme Court. That is the thesis sentence for any "role of the judiciary in governance" question.

▲ Then supply the counter-weight, or it becomes hagiography. A fixed tenure protects the incumbent from removal but does not make him independent of the government that selected him; and extension powers — one year at a time, up to five — hand the executive an annual instrument of influence over a sitting Director (§4.6.4 makes the same point for the ED). A tenure that can be extended in the gift of the executive is a term of office converted into a series of annual auditions.

4.5.5 The critique, in the CBI's own file ¶

  • DSPE Act has "many limitations" → the Standing Committee wants a new law defining status, functions and powers, with safeguards for objectivity and impartiality (§3.10.5).
  • 1,709 vacancies of 7,295 sanctioned; over-dependence on deputationists (§13.5.1).
  • Annual report not accessible to the general public; no centralised case-management database (§3.10.5).
  • Superintendence split three ways (§3.10.3); no suo motu cognizance in States (§4.5.2).

The concluding line for any CBI question: the CBI is asked to be the enforcement arm of three accountability institutions — the Lokpal, the CVC and the courts — while itself possessing no statute of its own, no autonomous entry into two-thirds of the country, a quarter of its posts vacant, and an annual report the public may not read. India did not build a weak anti-corruption architecture; it built a strong one and rested it on a 1946 wartime police order.

4.6 THE DIRECTORATE OF ENFORCEMENT — the institution ¶

(The PMLA itself — Sec. 45, the criticism, the "proceeds of crime" question — is at §3.11. The judicial arc is at §12.5. The conviction data is at §13.5.2.)

4.6.1 Origin and mandate (verbatim)¶

  • 1956, when an 'Enforcement Unit' (was established).
  • 1957, this Unit was renamed as 'Enforcement Directorate'.
  • Investigation of offence of money laundering and violations of foreign exchange laws.
  • Cryptos.

▲ [ONE-WORD SLIDE ENTRY] "Cryptos" appears as a bare bullet. [ADDED] It signals the ED's expanding remit over virtual digital assets — crypto exchanges and wallets have been investigated under PMLA and FEMA, and virtual asset service providers were brought under PMLA reporting obligations by notification in March 2023. Verify before quoting the date, but the direction is safely stated: the ED's jurisdiction now extends to asset classes that did not exist when the Act was passed.

The mandate line is worth parsing, because most candidates conflate the two halves. The ED enforces two different kinds of law: money laundering (PMLA 2002 — criminal, with arrest, attachment and prosecution) and foreign exchange (FEMA 1999 — civil, with penalties). FEMA replaced FERA in 1999 precisely to decriminalise exchange-control violations [ADDED]. So the same agency was decriminalised in one wing in 1999 and handed a bail regime borrowed from terrorism law in the other in 2002. Noting that reversal in a single sentence is a differentiating point.

4.6.2 What it can do ¶

  • Provisionally attach property alleged to be proceeds of crime; arrest; prosecute before Special Courts; and rely on Sec. 45's twin conditions to resist bail (§3.11.2).
  • ▲ Arrest without a First Information Report (§3.11.4) — the ED proceeds on an ECIR [ADDED].
  • Burden of proof: the onus is on the accused to prove that the property is not the proceeds of crime (§3.11.4).

4.6.3 The Director — appointment (verbatim)¶

"The Central Government shall appoint a Director of Enforcement in the Directorate of Enforcement in the Ministry of Finance on the recommendation of the Committee consisting of —

  • (i) the Central Vigilance Commissioner — Chairperson;
  • (ii)Vigilance Commissioners — Members;
  • (iii)Secretary to the Government of India in-charge of the Ministry of Home Affairs in the Central Government — Member;
  • (iv)Secretary to the Government of India in-charge of the Ministry of Personnel in the Central Government — Member;
  • (v)Secretary to the Government of India in-charge of the Department of Revenue, Ministry of Finance in the Central Government — Member."

Count the composition before you comment on it: five categories, and every single one is a serving official of the Union Government. No Leader of the Opposition, no judicial member, no outside eminent person. Compare, in one breath, the three appointment designs you now hold:CBI Director — PM + LoP + CJI (§4.5.4) · CVC — PM + Home Minister + LoP (§4.3.1) · ED Director — CVC + VCs + three Secretaries. The progression is not from strong to weak; it is from plural to internal. The ED's committee does not have an executive majority — it is entirely executive.

⚖️ The defence, stated fairly: the committee is chaired by the CVC, a statutory officer with two-track removal protection (§4.3.3) and a fixed four-year term (§4.3.2) — so it is not the political executive selecting directly, and the design mirrors the CVC-chaired committee for ED and CBI officers generally (§4.3.4). The rejoinder: the CVC is itself appointed by a committee with a 2:1 executive majority (§4.3.1). Insulation that is borrowed one link up the chain gets thinner at every link.

4.6.4 The Director — tenure, and the 2021 amendment (verbatim)¶

  • "Director, ED shall continue to hold office for a period of not less than two years."
  • "Provided that the period can be extended in public interest, on the recommendation of the Committee and for the reasons to be recorded in writing, be extended up to one year at a time:"
  • "Provided further that no such extension shall be granted after the completion of a period of five years in total including the period mentioned in the initial appointment."

This is the best "read the provisos, not the rule" exercise in the compendium — and it is a two-sided provision, which is what makes it examinable.

The rule looks protective: a statutory floor of two years means a Director cannot be removed at will — the same logic as Vineet Narain for the CBI (§4.5.4). Security of tenure is a genuine independence safeguard, and you must concede it.

The first proviso then reverses the direction of the protection. An extension "in public interest", granted "up to one year at a time", means the incumbent's continuance is decided annually, by a committee of the very executive he investigates. A floor protects the office; an annually renewable ceiling captures the officer. Note the asymmetry: the floor is available to everyone, the extension is available to one man.

The second proviso is the concession that proves the point — a hard outer limit of five years including the original term. [ADDED] It was inserted after the Supreme Court, in Common Cause v. Union of India (2021), upheld a retrospective extension while directing that no further extension be granted; the ceiling has since been litigated again. Verify the case and the sequel before citing, but the structure is sourced and safe: Parliament answered a judicial limit on extensions by legislating the power to extend, and capping it.

The transferable principle — write this, and it works for the CBI, the ED, the CVC and the CIC alike: the independence of an office is set less by the length of the term than by who decides what happens at the end of it. Fix the term, and you protect the office; make the term extendable, and you acquire the officer. Reform → §15, #36.

4.7 THE COMPTROLLER AND AUDITOR-GENERAL — the institution ¶

(The Articles are at §3.12; the DPC Act 1971 at §3.13; the case law at §12.6; the audit findings at §13.6. This section carries the institutional* argument — and §4.7.6 is the most examinable thing in the whole deck.)*

4.7.1 The office in one box ¶

The one-line characterisation to open any CAG answer: the CAG is a constitutionally protected officer exercising statutorily granted powers, whose entire executive force is the obligation of somebody else to lay his report on a table. Protection at the top, delegation in the middle, dependence at the point of effect — that is the shape of the institution, and every criticism and defence in §4.7.5–§4.7.7 is a consequence of it.

▲ The question never asks, and you should. [ADDED] The office is called Comptroller and Auditor-General — but in India the CAG exercises no comptrol: he has no power over the issue of money from the Consolidated Fund, only over its audit afterwards. (In the United Kingdom, from which the title is borrowed, the Comptroller and Auditor General does authorise issues from the Consolidated Fund.) India took the name and kept only half the office — audit is entirely post facto.Verify the UK detail before writing it, but the Indian half is safe and it is the sharpest structural point available on this topic. → reform #42.

4.7.2 What he audits — the mandate assembled in one place ¶
