11.3 EVALUATIONS OF THE RTI ACT — the assessment literature ¶

How to use this section: every RTI question is a "successes but…" question. §13.2 gives the successes; §11.3 gives the seven independent authorities that certify both the success and the failure. Cite two of them and you outrank a candidate who cites none.

11.3.1 Second Administrative Reforms Commission (2006) ¶

The Second ARC (2006), in its report "Right to Information: Master Key to Good Governance", hailed the RTI Act as a powerful tool for promoting good governance. The Commission noted that the RTI Act had empowered citizens to hold the government accountable, leading to more informed decision-making. However, the report highlighted challenges:

  • Inadequate awareness among the public.
  • Lack of infrastructure and human resources in public authorities to handle RTI requests efficiently.
  • Delays in response due to administrative bottlenecks.

(This is Report 1 of the 15 listed in §11.1 — and the same June 2006 report that recommended repealing the OSA, §3.4.6.)

11.3.2 Transparency International Report (2019)¶

According to Transparency International, the RTI Act significantly improved transparency and reduced corruption. However, it also flagged inefficiencies:

  • Backlog of cases at Information Commissions, resulting in delayed appeals.
  • Non-compliance by public authorities, which either deny information or fail to disclose it in a timely manner.
  • Instances of misuse by vested interests, which overburdens the system with frivolous applications.

11.3.3 Commonwealth Human Rights Initiative (CHRI) ¶

The CHRI has been actively involved in evaluating implementation. Concerns raised:

  • Weakness of Information Commissions — many suffer from lack of adequate staff, poor budget allocation and unfilled positions, undermining the Act's efficiency in handling complaints and appeals.
  • Dilution of the Act — the recent amendments, especially in 2019, which reduced the tenure and salary protections of Information Commissioners, have been viewed as a potential threat to the independence of these bodies. (Ties directly to §4.1.4.)
  • Access issues for marginalised groups due to digital divides and lack of awareness.

11.3.4 Views of activists ¶

  • Aruna Roy, a key activist in the RTI movement, has repeatedly pointed out the growing resistance from public authorities in releasing sensitive information. She notes that while the RTI Act has been a game changer, recent trends like attempts to curb its scope have eroded its effectiveness.
  • Anjali Bhardwaj has argued that the RTI Act's success largely depends on strengthening the Information Commissions and protecting whistleblowers. She has highlighted that many RTI activists have faced harassment, and in some cases, violence or death, showing the need for better safeguards.

The Bhardwaj link is the highest-value connection in this module: RTI and whistleblower protection are one problem, not two. An RTI applicant who exposes wrongdoing becomes a de facto whistleblower — but the WBPA 2014 is not in force (§3.6.3). The right to ask exists; the protection for asking does not. Use this as the conclusion to any RTI or whistleblowing answer.

11.3.5 Reports from civil society organisations¶

Organisations like Satark Nagrik Sangathan (SNS), which have been actively tracking RTI implementation, have revealed that the Act has been immensely successful in revealing scams and ensuring transparency. However, they stress:

  • Lack of proactive disclosures by public authorities.
  • Non-implementation of Section 4 (suo motu disclosure), which is key to reducing the number of RTI applications and improving governance.
  • Long pendency of cases, with some Information Commissions taking years to decide cases.

11.3.6 Academic assessment¶

Shiv Visvanathan notes that while the RTI Act has improved citizen–state interactions, its success has been uneven across states due to varying levels of institutional readiness. In some states the Act has brought greater accountability to public services, while in others it remains underutilised due to bureaucratic apathy.

"Uneven across states due to varying institutional readiness" is the phrase to lift — it converts a vague "implementation is poor" into a federalism-aware observation, and it is directly evidenced by the state-wise data in §13.3.

11.3.7 The misuse debate — settled with data ¶

Shailesh Gandhi, former Central Information Commissioner: "Right to information is misused, but those who do so make up less than 5% of total applicants."His four categories of RTI applicant:

  1. Those who file applications with the hope of exposing corruption or arbitrariness and to improve and correct governance.
  2. Those who do so to correct a wrong that they perceive has been done to them — basic intention is to get justice for themselves.
  3. Those who use the Act to blackmail people — largely targets illegal buildings, mining, or some other activity that runs foul of the law.
  4. Those who use it to harass public officials to get undue favours.

The evidence: a detailed study by the RTI Assessment and Analysis Group (RaaG), and a small study by Shailesh Gandhi, show that such applications (categories 3 and 4) are actually less than 5% of the total number. Most applicants are unaware of appeal procedures, or do not have the time and inclination to pursue appeals.Where the applications actually come from (RaaG Foundation):

  • About 50% of RTI applications are made because departments do not discharge their duty under Section 4 of the RTI Act, which mandates disclosure of most of the information suo moto as per law.
  • Another 25% seek information about the delay in ration cards, the progress of their application for various services, or complaints of illegal activities for which the government departments should have replied.
  • There is no condemnation of the officers who do not do their duty without extracting bribes. This was an unfortunate admonishing of the citizen without any evidence or basis.

This is the killer counter-argument, and it inverts the question. If 75% of applications exist only because the state failed to do what the law already required — proactive disclosure (50%) plus routine service replies (25%) — then RTI "overload" is a symptom of administrative failure, not of citizen misuse. Deploy against the judiciary's "75% of staff, 75% of time" fear (§12.3).

**The "ridiculous RTI applications" exhibit* — the anecdotes usually offered as proof of misuse:

  1. A resident of Andhra — how many times the Governor goes to the temple and what is the dinner menu at his residence.
  2. Why symbols used in EVMs are black and white and not colourful.
  3. Where are the question papers of AMU printed and where are they checked.
  4. A duplicate DU marksheet costs ₹500. RTI costs ₹10.
  5. Someone asked "Kya ache din aye hain?"
  6. "Time is money. But how much?" — Punjab University is asked.
  7. A man in TN asked the SIC to let him know about a suitable life partner working at any Govt Deptt.

How to use the list — carefully. It is rhetorically vivid but statistically marginal (<5%, per RaaG and Gandhi). Item 4 is not misuse at all — it is a citizen rationally choosing the cheaper of two lawful routes, and it indicts fee structures, not the applicant. Present the list, then demolish it with the 5% and 75% figures. Never present it as evidence that RTI is abused.

11.4 THE CIVIL-SERVICES REFORM LITERATURE ¶

Body / reportYearWhat it said (as stated in )
Constitution Review Commission (National Commission to Review the Working of the Constitution)2002domain specialization instead of generalized competence
Second Administrative Reforms Commission2008 (and 2005 on the vacancies slide — see the conflict note at §4.10.4)domain specialization; "many positions in the government remain vacant, and lateral entry could fill these positions more efficiently"; and separately the capacity-building slate — mandatory induction and periodic training as a condition for promotion, higher academic qualifications and publication, eminent experts in training institutes, and a National Institute of Good Governance
NITI Aayog, Three-Year Action Agenda2017domain specialization; lateral entry to "fill gaps in knowledge and skills, especially in rapidly changing sectors like IT and finance"
2nd ARC — diagnosis—"Civil Service in India is more concerned with the internal process than with results" · over-centralisation · resists change
The five-point reform slate ▲ [unattributed research note]—anti-transfer legislation · data-driven placement · institutionalised compulsory retirement on performance review · greater latitude for local State-cadre officers · more research on bureaucratic efficiency (§4.10.5)

The examinable pattern: three official bodies across fifteen years said the same thing — specialise — and the argument in the country is still about lateral entry, which is only one of several ways to specialise. Domain specialisation can be achieved by mid-career specialisation within the service (the abolished ICS practice the source itself records), by sectoral cadres, by long tenures in one ministry, or by recruiting outsiders — and only the last of these is contested. Making that distinction is the single best way to lift a lateral-entry answer out of the standard for-and-against.

11.5 THE PARIS PRINCIPLES AND GANHRI — the international assessment framework ¶

  • Adopted at the first international workshop on national institutions, Paris, 1991; endorsed by the UN General Assembly, 1993 (§3.14.1, and note the internal date conflict flagged there).
  • The six criteria:broad mandate based on universal human rights norms · autonomy from government · independence guaranteed by statute or Constitution · pluralism, including membership that broadly reflects society · adequate resources · adequate powers of investigation.
  • GANHRI unites 120 NHRIs; the Sub-Committee for Accreditation (SCA) consists of sixteen 'A' status NHRIs, four each from the Americas, Europe, Africa and the Asia-Pacific; review every five years, or on a change of function affecting compliance; conducted with OHCHR, UNDP, international and regional organisations and civil society.

Why this belongs in §11 and not only in §4.8: it is the only external, periodic, published evaluation framework for an Indian institution anywhere in this compendium. Everything else in §11 is a domestic committee evaluating a domestic body. Use GANHRI whenever a question asks how India's institutions compare internationally, or how institutional performance can be measured at all. And note the transferable idea for a reform answer: a periodic, published, criteria-based external review is precisely what the Lokpal, the CVC and the Information Commissions do not have (§15, reform #59).

11.6 THE DARPG EVALUATION OF CITIZENS' CHARTERS (2002–03) — the assessment literature for the Charter ¶

This is the Charter module's equivalent of §11.3 (the RTI evaluations) — and it matters disproportionately, because it is the only evaluative evidence about Citizen's Charters anywhere in ten decks. ▲ Note what it is not: it is not the 2nd ARC.never cites the 2nd ARC's 12th Report and never mentions Sevottam — so reform #4's anchor in §15 remains [ADDED], exactly as it has been.

11.6.1 What was commissioned (verbatim)¶

  • "During the Year 2002-03, DARPG engaged a professional agency to develop a standardised model for internal and external evaluation of Citizens' Charters in a more effective, quantifiable and objective manner."
  • "This agency also carried out evaluation of implementation of Charters in 5 Central Government Organisations and 15 Departments/Organisations of States of Andhra Pradesh, Maharashtra and Uttar Pradesh."
  • "This Agency was also required to suggest methods for increasing awareness, both within the organisation and among the users, and to suggest possible methods for orientation of management and the staff in the task of formulating and deploying Charters."

The sample to quote precisely: 5 Central Government Organisations + 15 Departments/Organisations across three States (Andhra Pradesh, Maharashtra, Uttar Pradesh) — twenty units in all. ▲ The agency is never named and the study is never titled — so attribute it as "a DARPG-commissioned evaluation of 2002–03", never to a named report.

▲ Note the vintage before you use it: this is a 2002–03 study, cited in a 2026 lecture, with nothing in between. That gap is itself a finding for §14 issue 88 — the instrument has not been systematically evaluated in over two decades.

11.6.2 MAJOR FINDINGS (verbatim — four, and every one is liftable)¶

  1. "In majority of cases Charters were not formulated through a consultative process." → the negation of element 6, stakeholder involvement (§5.8.2)
  2. "By and large service providers are not familiar with the philosophy, goals and main features of the Charter." → the awareness failure is inside the organisation, not only outside it
  3. "Adequate publicity to the Charters had not been given in any of the Departments evaluated. In most Departments, the Charters are only in the initial or middle stage of implementation." → note the absolute: "in any of the Departments evaluated" — not "most", not "many"
  4. "No funds have been specifically earmarked for awareness generation of Citizens' Charter or for orientation of staff on various components of the Charter." → the resource failure that explains findings 2 and 3

Finding 2 is the one to build on, because it inverts the usual narrative.The standard criticism of the Citizen's Charter is that citizens do not know their rights under it. The DARPG evaluation found that the officials did not know the instrument either. §5.8.3's factor 1 says exactly this — "this lack of awareness extends to both service recipients and the officials responsible for its implementation" — and finding 2 is its evidence. An instrument unknown to both sides of the counter is not under-enforced; it is unstaffed.

Findings 1 and 4 together produce the cleanest causal sentence in the module:a Charter drafted without consulting the citizen and publicised without a budget is a document that was never intended to be used — and that is a considerably stronger claim than "poor implementation."

11.6.3 KEY RECOMMENDATIONS (verbatim — six; these are the sourced backbone of §15 reforms #81–#90)¶

  1. "Need for citizens and staff to be consulted at every stage of formulation of the Charter." (note: citizens and* staff, and at every stage, not merely at the start)*
  2. "Orientation of staff about the salient features and goals/ objectives of the Charter; vision and mission statement of the department; and skills such as team building, problem solving, handling of grievances and communication skills."
  3. "Need for creation of database on consumer grievances and redress." → the only recommendation in the six that would generate outcome data — see §14 issue 88
  4. "Need for wider publicity of the Charter through print media, posters, banners, leaflets, handbills, brochures, local newspapers etc. and also through electronic media."
  5. "Earmarking of specific budgets for awareness generation and orientation of staff."
  6. "Replication of best practices in this field." → and supplies the best practices to replicate: Madhya Pradesh and Karnataka (§3.20)

The recommendation to lead with is #3, and almost nobody writes it.A database on grievances and redress is the only one of the six that would tell anyone whether the Charter works. Recommendations 1, 2, 4 and 5 improve the input*; #6 copies someone else's; only #3 measures the *output — and §13.11 records that, twenty-odd years later, no such figure appears anywhere in this source.

▲ The recommendation that is missing, and its absence is the most examinable thing about this list.Not one of the six recommends legal backing — even though the source's own factor 3 (§5.8.3) names the absence of statutory backing as the reason citizens have "no legal recourse." A 2002–03 evaluation prescribed consultation, orientation, publicity and budgets for an instrument whose defining defect was that it was not law — and the cure eventually came, in 2010, from a State legislature that was not asked (§3.20.3). Use that sentence as the pivot from "identify the factors" to "suggest measures" in the 2024 answer.

11.6.4 How the DARPG findings map onto the six hindering factors (the cross-walk to write, not to read out)¶

§5.8.3 factorDARPG evidence (§11.6.2)
1. Lack of AwarenessFindings 2, 3 — providers unfamiliar; no adequate publicity in any department evaluated
2. Poor ImplementationFinding 3 — "only in the initial or middle stage of implementation"
3. Absence of Legal Backing▲ Not tested by the study, and not addressed by any of its six recommendations
4. No Effective Grievance RedressalRecommendation 3 implies it (no grievance database existed)
5. Bureaucratic ResistanceFindings 1, 2 — no consultation of staff; philosophy unknown to providers
6. Inadequate TrainingFindings 2, 4; recommendations 2, 5

The table's punchline is its one empty cell.Five of the six hindering factors have sourced evidence behind them; the root cause has none — because the only evaluation ever commissioned was designed to assess implementation, not legal form. That is a genuinely sophisticated point about how governments evaluate their own instruments, and it belongs in a GS-IV or Essay answer as much as in GS-II.

11.7 NITI AAYOG'S NATIONAL STRATEGY FOR ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE — #AIforAll (2018) ¶

11.7.1 What it is¶

  • Named in the source as "NITI Aayog – AI for All Strategy (2018)" and, in the evidence annexe, as "NITI Aayog's National Strategy for AI (AIforAll)".
  • ▲ It is a strategy paper by a policy think-tank — not a statute, not a scheme and not a mission (§3.21.1). Its authority is persuasive; every deployment in §4.13 was made by some other body.

11.7.2 The five core sectors (verbatim — a guaranteed one-marker)¶

"Identified 5 core 'AI for social good' sectors: healthcare, agriculture, education, smart cities & infrastructure, and smart mobility & transportation."

  1. Healthcare · 2. Agriculture · 3. Education · 4. Smart cities & infrastructure · 5. Smart mobility & transportation

Double-stated within the source. Slide 4 gives the same list in compressed form — "Focus sectors: Health, Agriculture, Education, Smart Mobility, Smart Cities" — so the five sectors are the one item in this module confirmed twice by the source itself. Prefer the slide-16 wording when quoting; it is the fuller form and names infrastructure and transportation.

Note the framing phrase and use it: "AI for social good". ▲ All five sectors are developmental. Internal security is not among them — yet §4.13.8 records that policing, facial recognition and prison surveillance are among the largest AI deployments in the country. The strategy's sectors and the state's actual deployments have diverged, and the source contains the proof of both halves. That contrast is the most sophisticated point available in this module and it is entirely sourced.

11.7.3 The three proof-of-concept pilots (verbatim)¶

"Ran proof-of-concept pilots in agriculture (crop yield prediction), healthcare, and education (school dropout prediction) to demonstrate governance use cases."

PilotWhat it became at scale
Agriculture — crop yield predictionYES-TECH under PMFBY, and KDSS yield estimates (§4.13.2–§4.13.3)
Healthcare (no application named)▲ The source names no health pilot; ATMAN and the screening programmes are separately sourced (§4.13.5)
Education — school dropout predictionAndhra Pradesh–Microsoft, then Gujarat's statewide EWS (2025) (§4.13.6)

This is the most useful thing in §11.7 and almost nobody can write it: two of NITI Aayog's three 2018 proof-of-concept pilots are now running at national and statewide scale, and the source documents both. Crop-yield prediction became the basis on which insurance claims are settled in Madhya Pradesh; dropout prediction became a risk score attached to 1+ crore Gujarati schoolchildren. A "proof of concept" became an operational determination without any intervening statute (§3.21.1). ▲ That single sentence answers a "policy to implementation" question, an "AI challenges" question and an "accountability" question at once.

Where this sits against the compendium's other evaluative literature.§11.1–§11.2 (the 2nd ARC), §11.3 (the RTI evaluations), §11.5 (Paris Principles/GANHRI) and §11.6 (the DARPG evaluation) are all assessments of something already built. ▲ §11.7 is the opposite — a prospectus, written before deployment, and never revisited. There is no evaluation of AI in governance anywhere in eleven decks — which makes this the sixth consecutive module with the compendium's signature defect. ▲ Reuse the standing sentence, which now covers a sixth module: Indian programme reporting counts what was promised or built, and not whom it served.

That sentence alone is worth writing.

12.2 RTI & THE JUDICIARY — the Subhash Chandra Agarwal line ¶

12.2.1 How it began — the 2009 CIC orders¶

  • 2009: The Central Information Commission (CIC) ordered the Supreme Court to disclose information regarding judges' personal assets.
  • 2009: The CIC ordered the Supreme Court of India to disclose information regarding the Collegium's decision making.

12.2.2 The three questions before the Court¶

  1. Would disclosing the information requested by Subhash Chandra Agarwal interfere with the independence of the judiciary? Is it therefore NOT in the public interest to disclose this information?
  2. Would disclosing the information requested erode (i) the credibility of the Collegium's decision and/or (ii) curtail the future "free and frank expression" of Collegium members, when appointing judges to the Supreme Court?
  3. Does Section 8(i)(j) of the RTI Act exempt the CPIO from providing the requested information? Section 8(i)(j) exempts the disclosure of "personal information" that has "no relationship to any public activity or interest".

12.2.3 The 2019 five-judge ruling ¶

  • The Office of the Chief Justice of India (CJI) is a 'public authority' under the Right to Information (RTI) Act.
  • On the CIC order pertaining to personal assets, the Court upheld the Delhi High Court judgment and directed the CPIO to disclose the relevant information to SC Agarwal.The procedure the Court laid down:
  • Assets of judges and official communication during the process of elevation of judges to the Supreme Court are treated as confidential third-party information. In such cases the PIO should follow the procedure:
  • A notice should first be issued to the third party — the judge concerned — about the RTI request for information. The view of the third party should be considered before the PIO takes a call.
  • "Personal information, which if disclosed, could lead to an unwarranted invasion of privacy right… what should be disclosed would depend on authentic enquiry relating to the public interest," the Supreme Court observed.

The takeaway line: the CJI's office is inside RTI, but entry is procedural, not automatic — disclosure turns on a case-by-case public interest enquiry with the affected judge heard first. Transparency won the jurisdictional question; judicial independence won the calibration.

12.3 DILUTION OF RTI BY THE JUDICIARY ¶

  • The law provides for no appeals against the decisions of the Commission. However, these decisions are being challenged in High Courts through writ petitions by many public authorities to deny information to citizens. In most of these cases, a stay is obtained ex-parte.

Why this is devastating in practice: the applicant wins at the Commission, then the public authority — using public money — obtains an ex-parte stay the applicant never got to contest. The information is not denied; it is deferred indefinitely. A right delayed past the point of usefulness is a right defeated. (Structural source: §4.1.6.)

  • The judicial caution: *"Indiscriminate and impractical demands or directions under RTI Act for disclosure of all and sundry information (unrelated to transparency and accountability in the functioning of public authorities and eradication of corruption) would be counter-productive as it will adversely affect the efficiency of the administration and result in the executive getting bogged down with the non-productive work of collecting and furnishing information. The Act should not be allowed to be misused or abused, to become a tool to obstruct the national development and integration, or to destroy the peace, tranquility and harmony among its citizens. Nor should it be converted into a tool of oppression or intimidation of honest officials striving to do their duty. The nation does not want a scenario where 75% of the staff of public authorities spends 75% of their time** in collecting and furnishing information to applicants instead of discharging their regular duties."*

[ADDED] This passage is from CBSE v. Aditya Bandopadhyay (2011); quotes it without attribution — verify before citing the case by name.

The rebuttal, straight from own data (§11.3.7): the "75%" fear is hypothetical; the RaaG findings are empirical. 50% of applications exist only because Sec. 4 proactive disclosure was not done, and another 25% because routine service replies were not given. So 75% of the burden is self-inflicted by the administration — the cure is compliance, not curtailment. And per Shailesh Gandhi and RaaG, genuine misuse is under 5%. Note the pleasing symmetry: the judgment fears 75% of staff time; the data shows 75% of applications are the state's own fault.

Balanced position for a Mains answer: the Court's concern about RTI as a tool of oppression or intimidation of honest officials is legitimate and should be conceded — but the remedy is Sec. 4 compliance and better records management, not a narrowing of the citizen's right. Concede, then redirect. That is how a 15-marker gets full marks.

12.4 THE LOKPAL AND THE JUDICIARY — the accountability gap ¶

slide, in full: Lokpal in Judiciary — C.S. Karnan · Shanti Bhushan affidavit in the Supreme Court (2010) · Justice Ruma Pal's 7 sins.

▲ [SLIDE IS BULLETS ONLY] gives these three as bare names with no explanation. The expansion below is [ADDED] — verify before quoting any detail; the names are sourced, the content is mine.

Reference[ADDED] What it isWhy the lecturer put it here
Justice C.S. KarnanSitting judge of the Calcutta High Court who levelled corruption allegations against sitting and retired judges; a seven-judge bench of the Supreme Court convicted him of contempt in 2017 and sentenced him to six months' imprisonment — the first sitting High Court judge to be jailedShows that the system's only working response to intra-judicial allegations was contempt — the allegation was never independently investigated. Punishing the allegation is not the same as testing it.
Shanti Bhushan affidavit (2010)The former Union Law Minister filed an affidavit in the Supreme Court naming former Chief Justices of India he alleged were corrupt, and invited contempt proceedings against himself so that the allegations would have to be examined in open courtA deliberate test of whether the judiciary can be publicly questioned. The case was not decided on the merits — which is precisely the gap an ombudsman would fill
Justice Ruma Pal's "seven sins"In a lecture on judicial independence, the retired Supreme Court judge listed the judiciary's besetting failures — commonly rendered as turning a blind eye to a colleague's injudicious conduct · hypocrisy · secrecy · plagiarism and prolixity · self-arrogance · professional arrogance · nepotism The most quotable internal indictment available. "Turning a blind eye to the injudicious conduct of a colleague" and "secrecy" are the two to lift — they are the institutional sins, not personal ones, and they are exactly what an external ombudsman is designed to correct

The structural point — and this is the whole reason the slide exists. Look back at the jurisdiction clause (§3.7.2): the Lokpal covers the Prime Minister, Ministers, MPs and Groups A–D officers of the Central Government. The judiciary is not in that list. So India's anti-corruption ombudsman does not reach the branch that adjudicates corruption.

Argue it both ways.

Against inclusion: subjecting judges to an executive-appointed body would breach the separation of powers and chill judicial independence — the very concern the Court weighed in Subhash Chandra Agarwal (2019) (§12.2.3) when it let RTI in through the door but kept a third-party notice procedure on the threshold.

For inclusion: the existing alternatives are weak by design — [ADDED] impeachment (Arts. 124(4), 217) has never once succeeded in India; the in-house procedure is non-statutory and confidential; the Judicial Standards and Accountability Bill, 2010 lapsed; and K. Veeraswami (1991) requires the CJI's prior sanction even to register an FIR against a judge. Verify each before citing.

The line that ties §12.4 to §12.2: the judiciary has been brought inside the transparency statute (RTI) but left outside the integrity statute (Lokpal) — it may be asked what it holds, but not investigated for how it behaves.

Cross-link to §12.3. The same judiciary that stays CIC orders ex-parte is the branch outside the Lokpal's reach. Used carefully — and without rhetoric — that pairing makes a genuinely original paragraph on who watches the watchmen.

12.5 THE PMLA BAIL LINE — struck down, re-enacted, upheld, then softened ¶

Why this is the most teachable sequence in the whole compendium. It is a complete, four-stage institutional dialogue — Court strikes down → Parliament re-enacts → Court upholds → Court softens in application — running from 2017 to 2024, entirely within one section of one Act. Learn it as a spine, not as five cases. It answers questions on judicial review, separation of powers, Money Bills, personal liberty, and the misuse of investigative agencies — five syllabus areas from one slide-run.

12.5.1 Stage 1 — struck down: Nikesh Tarachand Shah v. Union of India (2017) ¶

Verbatim: "A two-judge Bench struck down the bail provision as unconstitutional on the ground that the onerous conditions were not a reasonable classification."

Unpack "reasonable classification" — it is the doctrinal core and assumes it. [ADDED] Art. 14 permits classification only where the differentia is intelligible and bears a rational nexus to the object. The Court's objection was that Sec. 45 attached the twin conditions to the punishment prescribed for the scheduled (predicate) offence, not to the money-laundering offence itself — so whether an accused got the harsher bail regime depended on an accident of which schedule his predicate offence sat in, producing arbitrary and discriminatory outcomes. Verify the reasoning before elaborating it; gives you only the one sentence — but the sentence contains the phrase that matters.

12.5.2 Stage 2 — re-enacted: the Finance Act, 2018 ▲ ¶

▲ [HEADING-ONLY SLIDE] gives "Amendment via Finance Act, 2018" as a title with no body text at all. [ADDED] The amendment substituted the words in Sec. 45(1)(b), replacing the reference to "punishable for a term of imprisonment of more than three years under Part A of the Schedule" so that the twin conditions attach to offences under the PMLA itself, thereby curing the classification defect Nikesh Tarachand Shah had identified — and, in effect, restoring the twin conditions. ▲ Verify the exact language before quoting it. The fact of legislative reversal is sourced by the slide's placement between the 2017 and 2022 cases; the mechanism is mine.

Two high-value points, and the second is the one almost nobody writes.

(i) This is legislative reversal of a judgment — the second clean example in this module. The first was Sec. 6A DSPE → struck down in Subramanian Swamy (2014) → restored as Sec. 17A PCA (2018) (§3.8, §12.1). Both reversals happened in 2018, and both restored a protection the Court had removed. Name the pattern: Parliament curing a defect of form rather than accepting a finding of substance. That single observation covers any "judicial review vs parliamentary sovereignty" question.

(ii) It was done through a Finance Act. A Finance Act is a Money Bill — passed with the Rajya Sabha having only recommendatory power (Art. 109) [ADDED]. So a bail provision affecting personal liberty was re-enacted through a money-bill route. This is exactly the "Money Bill question?" that flags on the Vijay Madanlal slide (§12.5.3) — the two slides are one argument, and the source leaves you to join them. Join them.

12.5.3 Stage 3 — upheld: Vijay Madanlal Choudhary v. Union of India (2022) (verbatim)¶

  • Seriousness of the offence of money-laundering, including about it posing serious threat to the sovereignty and integrity of the country.
  • PMLA — part of a global response to money laundering and terror financing.
  • Maximum Punishment of 7 years & Terrorism.
  • Money Bill question?

Read four bullets as two for and two against — the lecturer has laid out both sides and left them unlabelled.

The two that uphold: gravity (threat to sovereignty and integrity) and international obligation (part of a global response to money laundering and terror financing — the FATF anchor, §3.11.1). Together they justify borrowing the NDPS/UAPA bail architecture (§3.11.3).

The two that undercut:"Maximum Punishment of 7 years & Terrorism" is a proportionality objection — if the offence is comparable to terrorism, why is the sentence seven years? And "Money Bill question?" is a procedural objection — the amendments upheld here were made through a Finance Act (§12.5.2), and whether that was constitutionally permissible was expressly left open. [ADDED] The Money Bill issue was referred to a larger bench and a review petition was admitted in 2022; the question remains open.Verify the current status before writing it as settled — and note that this is live litigation, which makes it a strong current-affairs line (§13.5.4).

The examiner-facing formulation: the PMLA's severity has been upheld on the ground that money laundering threatens national sovereignty, while the punishment Parliament chose for it is seven years — and the provisions creating that severity were enacted by a route that bypassed the Council of States. The substantive justification and the procedural history point in opposite directions, and the Court has resolved the first while leaving the second open.

12.5.4 Stage 4 — softened in application: the August 2024 liberty line (verbatim — the best quotation in )¶

"Liberty of the individual is always the rule and deprivation is the exception. Deprivation can only be by the procedure established by law, which has to be a valid and reasonable procedure. Section 45 of the PMLA, by imposing twin conditions, does not rewrite this principle to mean that deprivation is the norm and liberty is the exception."

And the operative test: "Section 45 could be relaxed if an accused had been in custody for a considerable time and there was no likelihood of conclusion of trial within a short span."

This is the Bhosale quotation of the PMLA section — the one line to carry into the hall, and it should be deployed once. It works because it does not attack the statute; it re-subordinates the statute to a constitutional principle. Note the precise construction: the Court does not read down Sec. 45 — it holds that Sec. 45 "does not rewrite" the rule/exception relationship. A statute may make bail harder without making liberty the exception. That distinction is the whole holding, and stating it precisely is worth more than the quotation itself.

The second sentence is the practical doctrine and the one that decides cases: prolonged incarceration + no realistic prospect of an early trial = the twin conditions relax. This converts the argument from constitutionality to delay — and delay is a fact the state cannot dispute. Pair it with §13.5.2's conviction data: if 5,297 cases have produced 40 convictions, then "no likelihood of conclusion of trial within a short span" is not a plea in an individual case — it is a description of the system.That is the single strongest analytical sentence available from.

▲ Attribution caution: identifies this only as "Aug, 2024 – Bail to an aide of Jharkhand CM" and names no case. [ADDED] It is reported as Prem Prakash v. Union of India. Safest practice: quote the line and attribute it to "the Supreme Court, August 2024, in a PMLA bail matter" rather than risk a wrong case name.

12.5.5 The proviso applied — K. Kavitha (2024) (verbatim)¶

"BRS leader K. Kavitha's bail judgment saw the top court clarify that a woman should not be denied the benefit of the proviso to Section 45(1), which relaxes the twin conditions, merely because she was educated or sophisticated or an MP or an MLA."

This is a small holding with a large use, and it belongs to two syllabus areas at once.

As criminal law: the proviso to Sec. 45(1) (§3.11.2) says a woman "may be released on bail, if the Special Court so directs" — a discretion, not an entitlement. The clarification is that the discretion may not be refused on the ground of the woman's education, sophistication or public office.

As gender jurisprudence — and this is the harder, better point: the proviso is protective classification of the kind that assumes vulnerability. The High Court had, in effect, reasoned that an educated, powerful woman does not need the protection. The Supreme Court's answer is that a statutory category may not be narrowed by the court's assessment of who deserves to be inside it. Argue both sides: for — the rule of law requires the statute to mean what it says; against — a protection premised on vulnerability applied to the powerful is protection detached from its rationale. Note that the same objection would abolish the proviso, which is Parliament's to do, not the court's. That reconciliation is what earns the mark.

Cross-link: this is the only place in the entire compendium where a gender dimension is sourced rather than supplied — use it in any GS-I/GS-II question on women and the criminal justice system, and note that the beneficiary being a serving legislator is what makes it examinable rather than sentimental.

12.5.6 The one-page spine — learn these five lines and you own the section¶

StageYearWhat happenedThe transferable point
1. Struck down2017Nikesh Tarachand Shah — twin conditions unconstitutional; onerous conditions were not a reasonable classificationArt. 14 limits how a legislature may sort accused persons into harsher regimes
2. Re-enacted2018Finance Act 2018 ▲ (heading-only — mechanism [ADDED]) — defect of classification cured, twin conditions restoredLegislative reversal of a judgment — the twin of Sec. 17A PCA, same year (§3.8)
3. Upheld2022Vijay Madanlal Choudhary — gravity + global response to money laundering and terror financing; but "7 years" and "Money Bill question?" left standingSeverity justified by gravity and international obligation; procedure left open

The closing sentence for any PMLA question: Parliament has twice legislated the PMLA's severity and the Court has upheld it; what the Court has done instead is insist that severity operate inside the ordinary constitutional rule that liberty is the rule and deprivation the exception. With 5,297 cases and 40 convictions (§13.5.2), the practical question is no longer whether the twin conditions are constitutional, but whether a statute this hard to get out of can be justified by a record this thin.

12.6 THE CAG AND THE COURTS — expansion upheld, direction refused ¶

12.6.1 Arvind Gupta v. Union of India (2013) — the mandate expanded (verbatim)¶

  • "The Supreme Court upheld that the CAG's function to carry out Performance Audit."

One sentence, and it is load-bearing for the whole of §4.7.6.Performance audit has no textual foundation in the duty clause of the DPC Act (§3.13.2), which speaks only of legality, application and conforming authority. So the authority for the CAG's most contested function is judicial, not statutory — and that is why the "for" case at §4.7.6(iii) rests on "Supreme Court judgments have upheld the CAG's right to conduct performance audits."

Add it to the pattern the compendium has been building since §4.5.4.Vineet Narain gave the CBI Director tenure and the CVC its statute; Common Cause (2017) forced the Lokpal's appointment; Subramanian Swamy struck down Sec. 6A DSPE; Sita Soren narrowed the Art. 105(2) bar; and Arvind Gupta underwrites the CAG's performance-audit mandate. Every load-bearing feature of India's accountability architecture that actually functions was installed or confirmed by the Supreme Court.That sentence now covers five institutions and is the strongest available thesis for a "role of the judiciary in governance" question.

▲ Caution. gives no facts, no bench, no reported citation and no reasoning — one line on an otherwise empty slide. Cite it for the proposition, not for the holding: write "the Supreme Court has upheld the CAG's performance-audit function" and, if you name the case, name it without elaborating what was argued. Verify before writing anything more. See.

12.6.2 Reghu Nath Kelkar v. Union of India, Bombay HC (2009) — a PIL, and the courts step back (verbatim)¶

  • "In this case decided by the High Court of Bombay, an allegation was made about the failure of the CAG to conduct a comprehensive audit."
  • "The Court considered scope of Section 23 of the CAG (DPC) Act."
  • "The Court observed that the time, scope and extent of audit are all matter which fall within the jurisdiction of the CAG and is not a matter on which Court ought to tread."

Read the two cases together — this is the synthesis, and it is the single most useful thing in §12.6. In 2013 the Supreme Court was asked whether the CAG may audit more than the text provides, and said yes. In 2009 the Bombay High Court was asked to make the CAG audit more thoroughly, and said no. The courts have expanded the CAG's mandate and simultaneously refused to police it — they have made him larger and left him unsupervised.

The doctrinal name for what Kelkar is doing is worth using: it treats audit judgement — what to audit, when, how deeply — as a matter within the CAG's own discretion, in the same way the Court treats the prosecutor's discretion or the executive's policy choice. Independence is a two-way street: an office insulated from executive direction is also, necessarily, insulated from judicial direction.

And that closes a circle with §4.7.6. The critics' objection is that the CAG may stray into policy. Kelkar shows there is no external forum that will pull him back — the check on the CAG is internal (audit standards and self-restraint) and political (the PAC's reception of his reports), not judicial. Write that, and you have supplied the strongest version of the critics' case while explaining exactly why it does not follow that performance audit is unlawful.

Note the procedural point in passing — the case is a PIL, so the vehicle by which citizens tried to compel a deeper audit is the same vehicle by which they compelled the Lokpal's appointment (§13.4.4). One succeeded, one did not — and the difference is that the Court will order an institution to exist, but not to exercise its judgement differently.

✓ A small but genuine gain for your citations: this slide gives you "Sec. 23 of the CAG (DPC) Act" — only the second numbered statutory provision anywhere in five decks (after Sec. 45, PMLA). Gap 24's rule stands for everything else.

12.7 THE NHRC AND THE COURTS — recommendations urged, never made binding ¶

12.7.1 Paramjit Kaur v. State of Punjab (1998) — the enforcement gap named (verbatim)¶

  • "In Paramjit Kaur v. State of Punjab (1998), the Supreme Court highlighted that the NHRC's recommendations should carry more weight, urging authorities to treat them seriously. However, the Court did not mandate making NHRC's recommendations binding."

Cite it for exactly one proposition and stop: the Court urged; it did not compel. ▲ The source gives no facts, no bench and no citation — and [ADDED — context, verify before using] the case arose from the Punjab mass-cremations matter, in which the Supreme Court referred the inquiry to the NHRC, which is itself a notable fact: the Court has treated the NHRC as an instrument it can task, while declining to make the NHRC's own output binding. An institution good enough to receive a Supreme Court reference but not good enough to have its recommendations enforced — state the paradox; it is the whole of §4.8.6(ii).

12.7.2 The Manipur extra-judicial killings (2017) — "a toothless tiger", from the inside and from the Bench (verbatim)¶

  • "In June 2016, the then Chairperson of the NHRC and former Chief Justice of India, HL Dattu, described NHRC as 'a toothless tiger.'"
  • "In 2017, the Supreme Court of India seemed to support Justice Dattu's remarks while dealing with the alleged extra-judicial killings of 1,528 persons in Manipur by police and armed forces."
  • "Considering that such a high powered body has brought out its difficulties through affidavits and written submissions filed in this Court, we have no doubt that it has been most unfortunately reduced to a toothless tiger. We are of the clear opinion that any request made by the NHRC in this regard must be expeditiously and favourably respected and considered by the Union of India otherwise it would become impossible for the NHRC to function effectively and would also invite avoidable criticism regarding respect for human rights in our country," the SC had observed.

This is the strongest evidential sequence in, and its force lies entirely in who is speaking.The criticism is made by the Commission's own Chairperson — a former Chief Justice of India — and then adopted by the Supreme Court on the basis of the Commission's own affidavits. It cannot be dismissed as an activist claim or an opposition talking point: the institution testified against its own capacity and the Court believed it.Use it exactly once in an answer, at the pivot, in the same way §16.1b uses Justice Bhosale on the Lokpal.

Note the remedy the Court chose and what it reveals: having found the body toothless, the Court did not order compliance — it directed that NHRC requests "must be expeditiously and favourably respected and considered by the Union of India." Even the Supreme Court's cure for unenforceability was an exhortation to consider — which is the judicial half of §14 issue 43's diagnosis, authority without consequence, now in its third institution (Lokpal, CAG, NHRC).

▲ The 1,528 figure is the alleged number of extra-judicial killings before the Court, not a finding of fact.Write "alleged", as the source does.

12.8 T.S.R. Subramaniam v. Union of India (2013) — the civil-service tenure case ¶

  • "Bench asked the Parliament to create a Civil Services Act that would establish a CSB (Civil Service Body) and provide direction and advice to the political administration about transfers and postings, disciplinary actions, etc."
  • "The Supreme Court also ruled that civil servants must only abide by written orders/instructions from superiors."

The written-orders rule is the most practically consequential judicial direction in this entire compendium, and almost nobody quotes it. It attacks the exact mechanism by which the civil service is politicised: the oral instruction, which transfers the benefit to the politician and the record-risk to the officer. Requiring the order to be written does not forbid the instruction; it forbids the deniability — the same logic as Sec. 17A PCA's written prior approval (§3.8) and the CBI's "reasons recorded in writing" requirements. Say that and you have shown a pattern across three institutions.

Pair it with reform slate #1 (§4.10.5): "despite judicial prodding, most states have stalled." The Court ordered a Civil Services Board and fixed tenure in 2013; the Union re-constitutes a CSB annually by executive order (§4.10.6) and the States have largely not legislated at all. That gap — between a 2013 direction and a 2024 executive order — is your evidence that the problem is political will, not legal uncertainty.

▲ [ADDED — the source omits it and it is the most-quoted part of the judgment] The Court also directed a minimum tenure for civil servants to insulate them from frequent transfers.Verify the specifics before writing a number.

12.9 THE INDIAN COMPARATIVE CASES — socialism and secularism as constitutional commitments ¶

12.9.1 Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) (verbatim)¶

"The Supreme Court of India ruled that the basic structure of the Constitution, which includes socialism, cannot be altered. This decision safeguarded India's democratic socialism."

Note what does with the most famous case in Indian constitutional law: it cites it for socialism. Every other course cites it for the amending power under Art. 368. Both readings are usable and the second is the safer one [ADDED]: the basic-structure doctrine holds that Parliament's amending power cannot be used to destroy the Constitution's essential features — and later benches have listed secularism, democracy, the rule of law, judicial review and federalism among them.

▲ A precision worth keeping. The source says the basic structure "includes socialism". [ADDED] "Socialist" was inserted into the Preamble three years after Kesavananda, by the 42nd Amendment (1976) — so the proposition is more accurately stated as later decisions treating the Preamble's commitments, including socialism, as part of the basic structure. Write "the Court's basic-structure doctrine, later read to protect the Preamble's socialist and secular commitments" and you are correct on both the doctrine and the chronology.

12.9.2 Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980) (verbatim)¶

"The court held that India's socialist character must balance both socio-economic development and protection of individual rights."

This is the case that decides the shape of Indian socialism, and the source states its conclusion without its mechanism. [ADDED — verify] Minerva Mills struck down clauses of the 42nd Amendment that had made Directive Principles override Fundamental Rights and had put amendments beyond judicial review, holding that the harmony and balance between Part III and Part IV is itself part of the basic structure. Socialism in India is therefore constitutionally bounded: the state may pursue socio-economic transformation, but not by extinguishing the rights of those it transforms.

Use this case whenever an answer needs to explain why India is not China. Both states pursue development through state direction; only one of them has a court that will strike the direction down for what it costs an individual.

12.9.3 D.S. Nakara v. Union of India (1983) (verbatim)¶

"Indicates the incorporation of the philosophy of 'socialism'; which aims at elimination of inequality in income and status and standards of life."

The value of this line is its definition, not its holding."Elimination of inequality in income and status and standards of life" is the closest thing in the sourced material to a judicial definition of Indian socialism — and it is a three-part definition (income · status · standard of living), which is more than most candidates can supply. Lift it when you need to show that "socialist" in the Preamble has been given operative content by courts rather than left as rhetoric.

[ADDED — the facts, in one line; verify] Nakara concerned a pension scheme applied only to those retiring after a cut-off date, which the Court held to be arbitrary classification — i.e. the socialism point was made in a case about pensions, which is exactly how constitutional philosophy usually arrives.

12.9.4 ▲ S. R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994) — a heading with no content [ADDED — reconstruction; verify before writing]¶

gives one bullet: the case name and the year. What the case is cited for, and why it belongs in a secularism answer:

  • Secularism is part of the basic structure of the Constitution — the doctrinal bridge between Kesavananda and the Preamble's word.
  • A State government that acts on sectarian or anti-secular lines may be dismissed under Art. 356, and the proclamation itself is justiciable — the Court may review it and, if it is invalid, restore the government.
  • It is therefore the case in which secularism acquired teeth against a government, as distinct from against a statute.

This matters for the 2024 PYQ specifically.In the USA, the Establishment Clause restrains a legislature; in India, Bommai restrains an entire State government and can dissolve it.No comparable federal remedy exists in the American system [ADDED]. ▲ But present Bommai as your own knowledge — the source contributes only the name.

12.9.5 ▲ The Essential Religious Practices doctrine — a two-word bullet [ADDED — reconstruction; verify]¶

  • The doctrine: the protection of Art. 25 and Art. 26 extends to what is essential or integral to a religion; practices found non-essential may be regulated or abolished by the state. Originating in the Shirur Mutt line of cases (1954).
  • The critique, and it is the examinable half:the doctrine requires a secular court to decide a theological question — which is precisely the intervention that mutual exclusion (§5.5.1) forbids and principled distance (§5.5.2) permits.
  • The obvious modern illustration [ADDED — verify]: the Sabarimala litigation (2018 and the subsequent reference), where the doctrine decided whether an exclusionary practice was protected religion or reformable custom.

Why the two heading-only bullets belong together, and this is the best point available on Indian secularism:Bommai tells you the state must be secular; the ERP doctrine tells you the courts will decide what religion is. Indian secularism is therefore not a wall between two domains but a boundary drawn, case by case, by the state itself — which is the strength of the model and the whole of the objection to it.

12.10 THE COMPARATIVE CASE BANK — the USA and the UK ¶

12.10.1 Engel v. Vitale (1962) (verbatim, and the source's fullest case treatment)¶

  • Issue:"Whether the recitation of a state-written prayer in public schools violated the Establishment Clause."
  • Ruling:"In a 6-1 decision, the Court ruled that school-sponsored prayer in public schools is unconstitutional."
  • Significance:"This ruling was one of the most significant steps in reinforcing secularism in public education. The decision emphasized that government should not be in the business of composing or endorsing religious practices in public institutions, including schools. It set a precedent that religious activities in public schools must be voluntary and not initiated by the state."

"Government should not be in the business of composing or endorsing religious practices" is the cleanest statement of the separationist principle in the source. Set it directly against Art. 28 (§3.17.4), which reaches the same result by a different route — no religious instruction in wholly state-funded institutions — and you have a genuine India–US comparison rather than two descriptions.

12.10.2 Santa Fe Independent School District v. Doe (2000) (verbatim)¶

  • Issue:"Whether student-led prayer before high school football games violated the Establishment Clause."
  • Ruling:"The Court ruled 6-3 that even student-led, student-initiated prayers at public school events are unconstitutional if they are perceived as endorsed by the school."
  • Significance:"This ruling clarified that public schools cannot allow religious practices to be intertwined with school-sponsored activities, even if led by students, as it creates the appearance of school endorsement of religion."

The pair Engel → Santa Fe is a doctrine hardening over 38 years: first the state may not write the prayer, then it may not host one. The operative test in the second is perception — "if they are perceived as endorsed by the school" — which is a far more demanding standard than intent, and it is the standard India has never adopted.

▲ [ADDED — verify] The source's American school-prayer line stops in 2000. Kennedy v. Bremerton School District (2022) upheld a coach's post-game prayer and expressly moved Establishment Clause analysis away from the Lemon endorsement test towards "historical practices and understandings". If that is right, the trend the source presents as settled has partly reversed — which is exactly the kind of qualification a 2026 answer should carry, and it pairs with Dobbs (§12.10.5) as evidence of the same shift.

12.10.3 Masterpiece Cakeshop v. Colorado Civil Rights Commission (2018) (verbatim)¶

  • Issue:"Whether a baker could refuse to make a wedding cake for a same-sex couple based on religious objections."
  • Ruling:"The Court ruled 7-2 in favor of the baker, finding that the Colorado Civil Rights Commission had shown hostility to the baker's religious beliefs, violating the Free Exercise Clause."

▲ Read the holding narrowly, because the source's summary invites the opposite reading. [ADDED — verify] The Court decided the case on the Commission's conduct — its hostility in the proceedings — and expressly did not resolve whether a religious objection generally permits refusal of service. Write it as "the Court found against the Commission's process, not for a general religious exemption" and you have both the source's fact and the correct proposition.

Why the case is in a secularism module at all:it is the point at which the Free Exercise Clause collides with an anti-discrimination statute — i.e. the American version of the question India answers with Art. 25(2)(b): may a religious claim be overridden in the name of equality? India's constitution answers yes and says so in the text; the American answer is litigated case by case and is currently moving the other way.

12.10.4 ▲ Trans World Airlines, Inc. v. Hardison (1977) — a title with no content [ADDED — reconstruction; verify before using]¶

gives the case name on an otherwise blank slide. [ADDED] It is the leading American authority on religious accommodation in employment under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act, holding that an employer need not bear more than a de minimis cost to accommodate an employee's religious observance — a standard widely criticised as making the duty nearly empty, and revisited in Groff v. DeJoy (2023), which recast it as substantial increased cost.

If it is used at all, use it for the workplace limb of the comparison — religion in employment, alongside religion in schools (Engel, Santa Fe) and religion in commerce (Masterpiece Cakeshop). ▲ But the source supplies nothing, so do not present any holding as sourced, and consult the recording.

12.10.5 ***Dobbs*, Roe and the limits of a secular constitution (verbatim — the source's most careful passage)¶

  • "The overturning of Roe v. Wade did not explicitly invoke religious doctrine in the legal opinion, but it did reflect a conservative judicial philosophy that many critics argue aligns with certain religious and moral perspectives. The majority decision in Dobbs stated that the U.S. Constitution does not confer a right to abortion, leaving the matter to the states to regulate or ban. This decision relies on a strict interpretation of the Constitution, arguing that abortion rights were not 'deeply rooted in the nation's history and traditions.'"
  • "While the decision itself does not directly cite religious arguments, many of the groups and individuals pushing for the reversal of Roe v. Wade are motivated by religious beliefs, particularly within conservative Christian circles. Critics of the Dobbs decision argue that it represents a growing influence of religious conservatism in shaping public policy, particularly regarding reproductive rights."
  • "The U.S. remains a secular state by constitutional design, but the Dobbs ruling highlights the complexity of how secularism interacts with a pluralistic society where religious beliefs can strongly influence political and legal movements. As states regain control over abortion laws, the country now reflects a patchwork of laws, with some states imposing strict religiously-influenced restrictions, while others maintain more secular approaches to reproductive rights."

This is the most analytically disciplined passage in the whole deck and it should be copied as a method, not just a fact. It separates three things most answers merge: (a) what the judgment says (no religious doctrine, strict interpretation), (b) who campaigned for it (religiously motivated groups), and (c) what critics infer (growing religious influence on policy). Keeping (a), (b) and (c) apart is what makes a politically charged paragraph markable.

The transferable finding — and it is the best conclusion available for any comparative secularism answer:a formally secular constitution does not produce a secular polity; it only decides where religion has to do its work.In the USA it moves to legislatures and appointments; in France to the enforcement of dress codes; in India to electoral mobilisation and personal law. ▲ Write about Dobbs as a case study in institutional design, never as a position on abortion.

12.10.6 The 2019 prorogation case (UK) (verbatim)¶

"The 2019 prorogation case saw the Supreme Court rule that Prime Minister Boris Johnson's prorogation of Parliament was unlawful. Critics argue that this was an overreach of judicial authority into what was traditionally seen as a political matter."

[ADDED — verify] Reported as R (Miller) v The Prime Minister; Cherry v Advocate General for Scotland (24 September 2019), decided unanimously by eleven justices, holding the advice to prorogue unlawful, void and of no effect because it frustrated Parliament's ability to perform its constitutional functions without reasonable justification.

Why the source puts this under parliamentary sovereignty rather than under judicial review, and the point is subtle enough to be worth a mark:the Court did not strike down a statute — it protected Parliament's ability to pass one.Dicey's sovereign was defended, not defeated. In a system where Parliament is sovereign, the only thing a court can lawfully protect is Parliament itself — which is precisely why the same judges could not have struck down the legislation Parliament went on to pass.

The comparison to make with India: the accusation levelled at the UK Supreme Court in 2019 — judicial overreach into a political matter — is word for word the accusation levelled at the Indian Supreme Court over the basic-structure doctrine (1973) and over the collegium [ADDED]. Two constitutions at opposite ends of the sovereignty spectrum have produced the same complaint about their courts, which suggests the complaint is about judicial power as such, not about how the constitution is written.That is a first-class closing line for the 2023 PYQ.

Read the American column top to bottom and you have a trend, which is what an examiner wants and a list is not: 1962 and 2000 restrain religion in public institutions; 2018 and 2022 restrain the state's power to restrain religion. American secularism has not weakened — its centre of gravity has moved from the Establishment Clause to the Free Exercise Clause.That single sentence is worth more than all six case summaries.
