13.2 RTI SUCCESS STORIES — the case bank ¶

Why memorise these: GS-II answers die of abstraction. One named village plus one named outcome beats a paragraph of theory. Each of these cost the citizen a ₹10 application.

CaseWhat happenedOutcome
The Absconding Teacher (Panchampur village, district Banda, Uttar Pradesh)Soon after the Act came into force, parents used it to track their local school teacher, who rarely made an appearance in the classroom. After learning from RTI activists that they could seek attendance and leave records of the government school teacher, 15 villagers filed an application asking about his whereabouts, and also questioned the responsibility of the Primary Education Department in such a situationImmediate action: a new school teacher was appointed to the village school, and an enquiry was ordered against the absconder
The Seven Ponds (Kushmal village, Orissa, 2010)K.S. Sagaria smelt a rat when the paperwork showed that seven ponds had been constructed for below-poverty-line families, but no one in the village could spot them. He filed an RTI application, which revealed that the ponds were never dug, and that the "labourers" who worked to "construct" the ponds included dead peopleFollowing complaints, the administration suspended the officials involved in the scam, and the project was renewed — this time the villagers vowed to keep a check on its progress
School Uniforms (Gulrahai Primary School, Allahabad, December 2006)Students did not receive their school uniforms; nine parents filed an RTI application questioning the administration about the missing uniformsSchool dresses delivered in the first week of January 2007
School Uniforms — second instance (Chitrakoot, Uttar Pradesh)Parents of a government schoolProcured school uniforms by filing an RTI application
Corruption exposés CWG (Commonwealth Games) and Adarsh Housing Society scamsThe national-scale proof that RTI reaches beyond village grievances

The analytical point to draw (worth more than the anecdotes themselves): notice what these cases have in common — teacher attendance, pond construction records, uniform procurement. Every one is information that Sec. 4 required the state to publish suo motu anyway. RTI here is not an extraordinary right being exercised; it is an ordinary duty being enforced. This connects §13.2 → §11.3.7 (RaaG's 50%) → §3.3.2 (Sec. 4) into a single argument.

Also note the escalation ladder: dead men digging ponds (Kushmal) is fabricated muster rolls — exactly the record type that the DPDP Act 2023 may now shield as "personal data" (§3.5.2). Use Kushmal to show concretely what is lost when 8(1)(j) hardens.

13.3 RTI RESPONSIVENESS — state performance ¶

  • Tamil Nadu has been the worst performing on RTI responsiveness, furnishing only 14% of the information sought.
  • Maharashtra was second-worst, sharing 23% of the information asked for.
  • Only 10 Information Commissions provided full information in response to the RTI applications filed as part of this assessment. These included Andhra Pradesh, Haryana, Jharkhand and the northeastern States of Sikkim, Nagaland and Tripura.

▲ [SOURCE UNNAMED] presents these figures without naming the assessing organisation or the year. [ADDED] The methodology described — filing RTI applications with the Information Commissions themselves to test their own responsiveness — is the signature of the Satark Nagrik Sangathan (SNS) / CHRI "Report Card on the Performance of Information Commissions in India" series (§11.3.3, §11.3.5). Attribute as "civil society assessments (SNS/CHRI)" rather than to a specific report, and confirm the year before quoting the 14% / 23% figures in an answer.

The irony is the answer-worthy part: the bodies created to enforce disclosure were themselves the least forthcoming when asked to disclose. This is Visvanathan's "uneven across states due to varying institutional readiness" (§11.3.6) rendered as data — and note that the best performers include small northeastern states, which cuts against any assumption that capacity tracks state size or wealth.

13.4 THE LOKPAL — THE PERFORMANCE DATA ¶

Why this is the most valuable half-page in. Every candidate can describe the Lokpal's composition. Almost none can say how many complaints it received, how many it registered, or what its budget did. These figures convert a descriptive answer into an evaluative one.

13.4.1 The complaint data ¶

  • Anti-corruption ombudsman Lokpal received 5,680 complaints during 2021-22, of which over 5,100 were yet to be registered, according to an RTI reply.

Do the arithmetic in the answer — it is the single most damning line available.5,680 received, 5,100+ not even registered → roughly 90% of complaints had not crossed the registration stage. The processing failure precedes the investigation failure. And note the delicious source: the fact is known only because of an RTI reply — the transparency statute (§3.3) auditing the integrity statute. Use that observation; examiners notice it.

13.4.2 The budget data ¶

  • The Lokpal was allocated ₹101.29 crore for 2019-20, which was later revised to ₹18.01 crore.
  • In 2020-21, the original allocation was ₹74.7 crore, which was revised to ₹29.67 crore.
  • In 2021-22, the Lokpal was allocated ₹39.67 crore.
  • Recent budget: the anti-corruption ombudsman Lokpal has been allocated ₹33.32 crore for 2024-25. The provision is for establishment and construction-related charged expenditure for the Lokpal.

Read the revisions, not the allocations — that is where the argument is.

2019-20: ₹101.29 cr → ₹18.01 cr — a cut of roughly 82%.2020-21: ₹74.7 cr → ₹29.67 cr — roughly 60%. A revised estimate falling that far below the budget estimate means the money was not spent, which means the institution was not working at the scale it was funded for. It is evidence of under-utilisation, not merely under-funding — and that is the more sophisticated reading.

Then note the trend line:₹101.29 cr (2019-20) → ₹33.32 cr (2024-25). The budget of India's apex anti-corruption ombudsman is roughly a third of what it was at inception, and records that even that provision is largely for "establishment and construction-related" expenditure — buildings and salaries, not investigations.

▲ Now recall §4.2.7: these expenses are "charged upon the Consolidated Fund of India" — the same protection the CAG enjoys. Being charged protects money from being voted down; it does not oblige the government to offer any. That contrast — constitutional-grade financial protection sitting on top of a two-thirds real-terms cut — is the best single illustration in this compendium of the gap between institutional form and institutional life.

13.4.3 Delay in appointment ¶

▲ [HEADING-ONLY SLIDE] gives "Delay in Appointment" as a title with no body text. Content below is [ADDED] — verify before quoting dates.

[ADDED] The Act received assent on 1 January 2014 and came into force on 16 January 2014. The first Lokpal — Justice Pinaki Chandra Ghose — was appointed only in March 2019, a gap of more than five years. The government's stated obstacle was the absence of a formally recognised Leader of the Opposition in the 16th Lok Sabha — the position the Supreme Court rejected (§12.1, and the Analysis slide at §13.4.4). The Chairperson's post then lay vacant again between the first Chairperson's demise of office and the appointment of Justice A.M. Khanwilkar in 2024. ▲ Verify the 2024 appointment and any position later than that before writing it.

The argument, not the dates: an institution can be defeated without repealing it — simply by not staffing it. This is the same technique as the Information Commission vacancies (§14, issue 14) and the Karnataka ACB substitution (§3.7.8). Name it: "institutional attrition" — dilution by delay, vacancy and duplication rather than by amendment. That phrase, used once, will carry an entire answer.

13.4.4 Analysis — how the appointment logjam broke ¶

  • A PIL; then a contempt case.
  • The Supreme Court directed that the appointments should be made even without a formally recognized Leader of Opposition (LoP) in the Lok Sabha.

[ADDED] The PIL is generally reported as Common Cause v. Union of India (2017), followed by contempt proceedings that produced the 2019 appointments. Verify the case name before citing it — names no case. The statutory basis for the Court's view is the clause providing that no appointment shall be invalid merely by reason of any vacancy in the Selection Committee [ADDED].

Why it earns marks: it is a clean, recent example of judicial enforcement of a legislative mandate against executive inaction — the same species of order as Vineet Narain (1997) on the CVC (§3.9). Pair the two and you can argue that India's two principal anti-corruption bodies were both brought to life by the Supreme Court rather than by the government that legislated them.

13.4.5 The output problem — high-profile cases and convictions ¶

"Any high profile case?", with the four items it lists:

  • PPP Contracts
  • 'Handing Over Airports and Ports to Private Companies'
  • Defence Purchases
  • "Complaint against Sebi chief falls short of persuading us to probe: Lokpal"And verdict:
  • Lack of Independence: the Lokpal still relies heavily on the CBI for investigations, which raises concerns about the autonomy of its investigations since the CBI itself has been subject to political interference.
  • Low Conviction Rate:despite having sweeping powers, the Lokpal has not secured any significant convictions, casting doubt on its effectiveness.
  • Limited Public Engagement:one of the goals of the Lokpal Act was to encourage public engagement in anti-corruption efforts. While the institution is empowered to receive complaints from citizens, there has been a lack of widespread awareness about the complaint process and the institution's functioning. Many citizens remain unaware of how to file complaints with the Lokpal, and there is little public communication from the Lokpal regarding its activities or successes.

▲ [ADDED] The SEBI headline refers to the Lokpal's 2024 disposal of complaints against the then SEBI Chairperson, Madhabi Puri Buch, arising from the Hindenburg allegations. Verify the name, the year and the outcome before using it — gives only the headline.

The pattern across the first three items is the point:PPP concessions, airport and port privatisation, and defence procurement are exactly the domains where discretion is largest and documentation weakest — and defence and space fall inside the PM-exclusion heads of §3.7.3. The Lokpal's thinnest case-record lies precisely where its jurisdiction is most fenced.

On "Limited Public Engagement", note the mirror-image of RTI. RTI is criticised for too many applications (§12.3's "75% of staff, 75% of time"); the Lokpal is criticised for too few, and for not registering the ones it gets. A right citizens over-use has become a burden; an institution citizens under-use has become an ornament. The difference is not citizen behaviour — it is whether the institution made itself usable.

13.4.6 The insider's indictment — Justice Dilip B. Bhosale¶

  • A major indictment about the functioning of the Lokpal came from one of its own.
  • Justice Dilip B. Bhosale, former chief justice of the Allahabad High Court, who was one of the four judicial members appointed in March 2019, resigned on 6 January 2020, just nine months after taking oath, citing personal reasons and lack of enough work.
  • In his words: "I felt I was wasting my time. I was sitting absolutely idle. I used to get around 15-20 cases in a month. As chief justice of Allahabad High Court, I was used to working 14-15 hours a day, handling some 50-100 cases a month. I am told not much has changed since I left. If the Lokpal continues to function in this manner, it will fail to meet its objective. It will not deliver."

This is the best quotation in the entire module for an anti-corruption answer, and it should be used exactly once, at the pivot of the essay or the 15-marker. It is first-hand, from a judicial member, on the record, and self-damaging to the institution he served.

The figures inside the quote are the argument: 15–20 cases a month at the Lokpal against 50–100 a month as a High Court Chief Justice. Set that beside 5,680 complaints received and 5,100+ unregistered (§13.4.1) and the contradiction is complete: the complaints existed; they simply never reached the members.The bottleneck is administrative, not judicial — which is a fixable problem, and therefore a reform recommendation rather than a lament (§15).

Close with his last five words — "It will not deliver." Attribute it precisely (Justice Dilip B. Bhosale, judicial member of the Lokpal, on resigning in January 2020) and it lands with authority.

13.4.7 own conclusion (liftable verbatim — a ready-made closing paragraph)¶

  • The Lokpal Act, 2013 was a monumental step in India's anti-corruption framework, driven by popular demand and civil society movements. However, its impact has been limited due to delays in implementation, structural limitations, and political inertia. While the law has created an institution capable of addressing corruption at the highest levels, significant reforms are needed to ensure that the Lokpal can function as an independent, autonomous, and effective body.
  • Key areas requiring attention include empowering the Lokpal with an independent investigative mechanism, extending its jurisdiction, ensuring timely appointments, and providing comprehensive whistleblower protection.If these reforms are undertaken, the Lokpal could become a more potent instrument in India's fight against corruption.

Memorise the three-noun diagnosis — "delays in implementation, structural limitations, and political inertia" — and the four-part prescription — independent investigation · wider jurisdiction · timely appointments · whistleblower protection. That is a complete conclusion in two sentences, and the fourth prescription stitches the Lokpal answer back to §3.6 (WBPA), closing the module's loop.

▲ [HEADING-ONLY SLIDE] also carries a title slide reading "Lokpal was 'not meant to succeed'" with no body text. It appears to introduce this conclusion. [ADDED] The phrase is associated with commentary arguing that the Act's design defects — CBI dependence, the seven-year bar, the PM carve-out and executive control of appointments and budget — were foreseeable rather than accidental. Use it as a provocation to be tested and then qualified, never as an assertion: "It has been argued that the Lokpal was never meant to succeed; the evidence supports the weaker claim that it was never equipped to."

13.5 THE INVESTIGATING AGENCIES — THE PERFORMANCE DATA ¶

What §13.4 did for the Lokpal, §13.5 does for the agencies. These four numbers — 1,709 / 7,295, 5,297 / 40, 0.75% vs 93%, and ₹10.7 lakh crore → ₹1.86 lakh crore — are what convert a description of the CBI and the ED into an evaluation of them.

13.5.1 CBI capacity (Parliamentary Standing Committee, )¶

  • A total of 1,709 posts are vacant in the CBI against its sanctioned strength of 7,295 — impacts the effectiveness and efficiency of the agency.
  • CBI should reduce its dependence on deputationists and strive to recruit permanent staff in the ranks of inspector of police and deputy superintendent of police.
  • ▲ Annual report of CBI is also not accessible to the general public.
  • CBI should maintain a case management system which would be a centralised database containing details of cases registered with it and the progress made in their disposal.

Do the arithmetic in the answer — it is the same technique that made §13.4.1 devastating.1,709 of 7,295 is a vacancy rate of roughly 23% — very nearly one post in four. Then state the consequence rather than the number: the agency that investigates for the Lokpal, for the CVC, and on the entrustment of the Supreme Court and the High Courts is running a quarter short — while its mandate has expanded from departmental bribery to murder, kidnapping, terrorism, banking fraud and transnational crime (§3.10.4).

The deputationist point is an independence argument, not a staffing one, and this is where marks are won. An officer on deputation returns to a parent State cadre or service whose government may be a party to his investigation; his career is decided elsewhere. Permanent recruitment at inspector and DySP level is therefore the cheapest available independence reform — it makes the investigator's future independent of the investigated. Cross-link to §4.5.4: tenure protection at the top is worthless if the officers who build the case are on loan.

▲ The inaccessible annual report is the sharpest irony in the module and it belongs in a transparency answer, not only an anti-corruption one. The CBI is exempt from the RTI Act under Sec. 24(2) / the Second Schedule [ADDED] — the same device that removed CERT-In in 2023 (§3.4.7). The Lokpal's failure is known because of an RTI reply (§13.4.1); the CBI's cannot be, because the agency is outside the Act. The one is measurable and therefore reformable; the other is not.

13.5.2 PMLA conviction data — and internal contradictionWhat the source states, on two different slides:¶

  • (criticism slide, §3.11.4) "Low Conviction Rate: Despite numerous investigations, the low conviction rate has raised concerns about the overuse of the Act to harass individuals, particularly political opponents or business figures (0.75%)."
  • (data slide) "Conviction rate under PMLA is 93 pc: Govt — August, 2024."
  • (same data slide) "A total of 5,297 cases have been registered under the PMLA from 2014 to 2024, while only 40 cases have seen convictions and 3 acquitted, the data shows."
  • (headline slide) "Supreme Court highlights low conviction rate under PMLA, questions ED on quality of prosecution — Justice Ujjal Bhuyan observed that in over 5,000 cases being investigated by Enforcement Directorate, there were only 40 convictions so far."

▲ [CONFLICT — internal to: the source asserts a conviction rate of 0.75% on one slide and reports 93% on another.] Do not treat this as an error to be resolved by picking one. It is the single most valuable thing in the source, because both figures are arithmetically correct and they use different denominators.

The 93% figure = convictions ÷ decided cases = 40 ÷ (40 + 3) = 93%. Of the cases that have reached a verdict, almost all ended in conviction.

The 0.75% figure = convictions ÷ registered cases = 40 ÷ 5,297 = 0.755%. Of the cases begun, almost none have reached a verdict at all.

So the two numbers are not in dispute about the facts — they are in dispute about what should count as the denominator, and that is a question about what the Act is for.If the PMLA's purpose is to secure convictions, the relevant denominator is cases decided, and 93% is a strong record of prosecutorial quality.If its consequences — attachment of property, arrest without an FIR, and bail under the twin conditions — begin at registration, then the relevant denominator is cases registered, and 0.75% is the rate at which those consequences are ever tested at trial.

The sentence to write:Only 43 of 5,297 cases have been decided in ten years. The conviction rate is either 93% or 0.75% depending on whether you count the cases that ended or the cases that started — and the gap between those two numbers is the number of people who have borne the Act's consequences without a verdict either way.

This connects directly to §12.5.4. The Court's test — relax Sec. 45 where custody is long and there is "no likelihood of conclusion of trial within a short span" — is, on this data, not an exceptional finding but the ordinary condition. The bail jurisprudence is the system correcting for its own trial delay.

⚖️ State the government's side fairly or the point loses force. [ADDED] Money-laundering trials are document-heavy, often await the predicate-offence trial, and involve cross-border evidence-gathering — so low disposal partly reflects complexity rather than weak prosecution, and the 93% figure genuinely does show that when cases are completed they are usually well-founded. The rejoinder is not that the defence is wrong, but that it is an argument for fixing trial capacity — not for a bail regime premised on guilt that the trial will take a decade to test.

▲ Handle the "0.75%" carefully in an exam. gives it inside a criticism slide without a source, and the underlying 5,297 / 40 / 3 figures are attributed to Government data of August 2024. Safest practice: quote the raw numbers — "5,297 cases registered 2014–2024, 40 convictions, 3 acquittals" — and let the examiner do the division. Raw numbers you can defend; a percentage you cannot source, you cannot.

13.5.3 The coal scam — the CAG's two estimates ¶

  • The alleged scam was spotlighted by a report by the Comptroller and Auditor General of India in 2012 that appeared to show inefficient and possibly illegal allocation of coal blocks between 2004 and 2009. The report said the blocks were allocated by the government without a process of competitive bidding, leading to a presumptive loss to the exchequer.
  • The CAG initially estimated the quantum of presumptive loss to the exchequer at a staggering ₹10.7 lakh crore, but toned this amount down to ₹1.86 lakh crore in the final report.

This slide is doing double duty and most candidates will use only half of it.

Half one — the governance failure: allocation of a finite natural resource without competitive bidding, which is the holding of Common Cause (2014) (§12.1) and the factual spine of the CBI's largest case-load of the period.

Half two — and this is the better half — the audit point. The estimate moved from ₹10.7 lakh crore to ₹1.86 lakh crore between draft and final report: a revision of over 80%. "Presumptive loss" is a counterfactual, not a discovered fact — it depends entirely on the assumed alternative price. The number that entered public debate was the draft one; the number the CAG stood behind was a fifth of it.

The mature line, and it will separate you from the field: the coal case demonstrates both that transparency institutions work — a CAG report forced a policy reversal, a Supreme Court judgment and a criminal investigation — and that accountability by headline figure carries its own risks, since the number that shaped public understanding was revised by 80% before the report was final. Institutional accountability requires defending the process even when the initial number does not survive it. This is a GS-IV probity point as much as a GS-II one.

Cross-link to §13.4.5: list of the Lokpal cases the public expected — PPP contracts, airports and ports, defence purchases — is the same category of decision as coal allocation: discretionary allocation of public assets. The one such case that produced real consequences was driven by the CAG and the courts, not by the anti-corruption ombudsman created for exactly that purpose.

13.5.4 What to refresh before the exam ▲ ¶

[ADDED] figures are August 2024 vintage at the latest. Before the exam, refresh: (i) PMLA cases registered / convictions / attachment values; (ii) the status of the Vijay Madanlal review and the Money Bill reference (§12.5.3) — live litigation; (iii) the number of States that have withdrawn general consent (§3.10.2); (iv)CBI sanctioned strength and vacancies; (v) the current CBI Director and ED Director and any extension granted. The arguments in §13.5 survive a change in the numbers; the numbers themselves will not.

13.6 THE CAG — THE AUDIT RECORD ¶

What §13.4 did for the Lokpal and §13.5 for the agencies, §13.6 does for the auditor — with one difference that is worth stating. The Lokpal and the agencies are measured by their own output (complaints registered, convictions secured). The CAG can only be measured by what his findings caused in other institutions (§4.7.5). So read the three cases below not as audit results but as three different fates of an audit report: one that named a loss, one that named a structural failure, and three that produced national consequences.

13.6.1 The Indian Olympic Association and Reliance Industries — audit reaching outside government (verbatim)¶

  • "The Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) report regarding the Indian Olympic Association (IOA) and Reliance Industries Limited (RIL) sponsorship revolves around a flawed agreement that resulted in a ₹24 crore loss to the IOA. The main issue was the failure to adjust the sponsorship amount when additional rights were granted to RIL for more sporting events without an increase in payment."

The important thing here is not the number — it is who was being audited.The IOA is not a government department. This is the substantially-financed provision (§3.13.3) doing its work: public audit following public money out of government and into a sports federation. ▲ [ADDED — the source never states the statutory basis; do not assert Sec. 14 as sourced]

The audit finding itself is a clean value-for-money proposition and it is the best short illustration of performance audit you have.The rights granted went up; the payment did not. Nothing here is a policy question — nobody is asking whether the IOA should have had a sponsor. The question is whether the consideration matched what was given away, which is exactly the "implementation, not merit" line at §4.7.6(ii).Use this case whenever you need to show, rather than assert, that the policy/implementation distinction is workable.

▲ Handle "loss" figures carefully — the compendium has already taught you why.₹24 crore is a computed loss on a contractual comparison, not cash traced out of a till; the coal-block estimate moved by more than 80% between draft and final report (§13.5.3). Quote the finding and the mechanism (rights expanded without repricing); treat the figure as the auditor's estimate, which is what it is.

13.6.2 The urban-local-bodies audit, 2015–2020 (Uttar Pradesh) — the best-value slide in the source for cross-topic use (verbatim)¶

  • "The Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) has found that the urban local bodies (ULBs) in Uttar Pradesh lack powers and resources, with 68.72 per cent of their total funds coming from government grants and only 16.16 per cent generated from their own revenue."
  • "Out of 15 functions fully and one function partially stated to have been devolved, ULBs were solely responsible for only one function; had no role in one function; had limited role in eleven functions; were mere implementing agencies in two functions; and in respect of one function, they had a dual role with Government Departments. This defeated the purpose of the 74th Constitutional Amendment Act."
  • "Only one function — construction, operation, and maintenance of crematoriums and burial grounds — was fully under the control of ULBs."

Learn the last line verbatim. It is the single most quotable sentence in and it will earn a mark in three different papers. Of sixteen functions said to have been devolved to urban local government in India's largest State, the only one actually devolved was the management of crematoriums and burial grounds. State it flatly and let it work. Do not editorialise — the fact is the argument.

The two numbers are the structural half, and they are the ones to write first.68.72% of ULB funds are government grants; 16.16% is own revenue. A body that raises a sixth of its money and controls one of its sixteen functions is not a tier of government; it is a delivery channel.This is the "3F deficit" — funds, functions, functionaries — with a sourced figure attached to two of the three Fs, which is exactly what §17's 2017 PYQ on local self-government has never had.

The SCA's three standing concerns, verbatim — "The concerns of the Sub-Commitee for Accreditation (SCA) have carried over through the years:"

  1. "the composition of the human rights body lacks diversity,"
  2. "it has an opaque appointment process, fails to cooperate with civil society, involves police personnel in investigations creating 'conflict(s) of interest,'"
  3. "and is unable to respond to escalating human rights violations."The closing assessment, verbatim:"Experts and human rights bodies such as Amnesty International have expressed fears that the NHRC has been reduced to an ornamental body, imperilling the fate of Indian democracy."

Learn this table as a pattern, not as dates: deferred 2016 → restored 2017 → withheld 2023 → deferred again 2024. The 2016 and 2023 reason-lists are nearly identical — political appointments, no gender balance, no pluralism, then opacity, police in investigations, no minority or female representation. The same defects were identified, formally accepted as cured in 2017, and found again in 2023. That is the finding: not that the NHRC failed a review, but that it passed one without changing.

▲ Two cautions before you write this.(a) The claim of "an 'A rating' since 1999" sits awkwardly with deferrals in 2016, 2023 and 2024 — a deferral postpones the review rather than downgrading the rating, so the 'A' formally persists while the assessment is pending. Write "accreditation deferred", not "downgraded to B", unless you have checked the current status.(b) This is the compendium's most perishable data.The status may have changed since the source was made — check the current GANHRI position before the exam.

The consequence, restated for the answer: deferral leaves the NHRC unable to speak with full status at the UN Human Rights Council — B-status NHRIs "can participate in GANHRI meetings, but cannot vote nor hold governance positions" (§4.8.7).

The three-sentence reading of §13.10.2, and it is the answer to the 2021 PYQ in miniature:

The divide is no longer primarily about geography — rural India has more users than urban India and uses the internet almost as intensively (94 minutes against 101). It is now about activity and gender: roughly half of rural India is still not an active user at all, and 8 percentage points of the active population are missing on the female side. ▲ So an e-governance platform that assumes a personal smartphone reaches a population that is disproportionately male and disproportionately non-rural — which is why the CSC and the offline route are inclusion policy, not legacy infrastructure.
