Four inferences, and they should shape the last month of your preparation.

  1. The module is worth roughly two to three questions a year, and in 2024 it was four. This is not a peripheral module.
  2. The civil services and oversight bodies lines are asked every year in some form; the comparative line clusters in 2018–2024; the Citizen's Charter recurs on a five-to-six-year cycle (2013, 2018, 2024) — ▲ and it has just been asked, which lowers its probability for the next paper and raises the value of preparing it once, properly.**
  3. The marks pattern changed: 12.5-markers (200 words) through 2016; 10/15 (150/250 words) from 2017. Practise pre-2017 questions at the modern limits.
  4. Of the 27, this compendium answers 24 from sourced material. ▲ The three it cannot are the 2021 Right to Equality question, the 2018 India–USA basic-tenets question and the 2022 NCBC question — all three are [ADDED] skeletons above, and all three should be your next self-study block.

17H ▲ AI IN GOVERNANCE — NO PYQ, AND HOW TO PREPARE AN UN-EXAMINED TOPIC¶

▲ carries no PYQ.It is the first deck since to reproduce none, and the sourced bank therefore stands unchanged at TWENTY-SEVEN questions. ▲ [CORRECTED AT AUDIT — do not add these numbers together] The 27 sourced by SUBSUME the earlier nine, they do not add to them. §17G's year-by-year table sums to 27, and it contains all six of e-governance questions (2024 Interactive Service Model, 2023 inadequacies, 2021 digital literacy, 2020 4IR, 2019 ICT projects, 2018 use value) and all three of /8's comparative questions (2024 secularism, 2023 parliamentary sovereignty, 2019 France). That is why records as tripling the total from nine to twenty-seven rather than raising it to thirty-six.** The correct figure to carry is 27 sourced questions, of which this compendium answers 24 (§17G, inference 4).

▲ There is no past question on AI in governance anywhere in this compendium — not in the sourced tables, and not in the older [ADDED] from-memory bank either. Treat that as information, not as a reason to skip the topic.

How to prepare a topic with no PYQ — and this is the whole of §17H's value.

  1. Prepare it as a limb, not a topic.AI has no question of its own; it is the strongest available content for questions that already exist. Specifically: the e-governance "successes, limitations and potential" line (§17's six sourced questions) and the citizen's charter / service delivery line (§17C's three). An e-governance answer that ends at UMANG and CSC is a 2019 answer; one that ends at KDSS, YES-TECH and the monsoon pilot is a 2026 answer, and the difference is visible in the first line of the conclusion.
  2. The structure to reuse is already sourced.§5.9.2's five-domain scope map is exactly what a "scope and applications" question wants; §14's issues 91–100 are exactly what a "limitations" question wants; §15's reforms 91–100 are the "way forward". The source is badly organised but it is organised along the examiner's own axes.
  3. Where AI wins marks in a question that never mentions it. In §17B's constitutional-bodies questions — six of eight ask about a body's effectiveness, and "the CAG cannot audit an algorithm" is a live, current and almost unwritten point (§15, reform 94). In §17's civil-services questions, all five of which are reform questions — capacity to interrogate an algorithmic output is the newest form of the neutrality-and-competence argument (§15, reform 95). And in any transparency question — the RTI Act reaches a record and it is untested whether it reaches a model (§2.7.3, §15, reform 98).
  4. ▲ What not to do. Do not build a whole answer on AI where the question is about something else — ▲ the topic is un-examined, which means the examiner's mark scheme will not have a line for it. Use it for the illustration, the contemporary example and the conclusion — the three places where an unexpected but accurate reference is always rewarded.

One prediction, offered as this compendium offered before confirmed it.The syllabus line most likely to absorb this topic is line 1 — e-governance… successes, limitations and potential — and the most likely form is the one every Charter and e-governance question in §17 has already taken: a two-part limitations-plus-measures question. Build one 250-word answer from §5.9.2 (scope) + §14's issues 96–100 (limitations) + §15's reforms 91, 94 and 97 (measures), and you hold that question in whatever form it arrives.

Scope of this compendium — the ten modules covered expand
18. RAPID REVISION BOX (10 on governance + 10 on transparency/RTI + 10 on the anti-corruption architecture + 10 on the investigating agencies + 10 on the CAG and public audit + 10 on the NHRC and human rights + 10 on the civil services + 10 on the comparative constitutional scheme + 10 on e-governance + 10 on the citizen's charter)
  1. Governance = mechanisms, structures, processes and institutions through which a society is directed, controlled and regulated — at all levels, and not confined to the state.
  2. UNDP: exercise of economic, political and administrative authority at all levels; citizens articulate interests, exercise rights, meet obligations, mediate differences. World Bank: the manner in which power is exercised in managing a country's economic and social resources for development.
  3. Fukuyama: capacity to make and enforce rules and deliver services, regardless of whether the government is democratic → governance ≠ democracy. Bevir & Rhodes: processes, institutions and networks. Locke: legitimacy = consent of the governed + protection of life, liberty, property.
  4. Seven aspects: Transparency · Accountability · Rule of Law · Participation · Effectiveness & Efficiency · Equity & Inclusiveness · Consensus-Oriented. (Add Responsiveness for the UNESCAP eight.)
  5. Governance triangle:government + civil society + private sector, delivering decisions that are transparent, inclusive, accountable, responsive.
  6. Non-state actors: corporations (Korten — corporations as political entities), civil society (Kaldor), individuals (Castells — whistleblowers to influencers).
  7. Power lens:Foucault (power is everywhere, diffuse) · Gramsci (cultural hegemony — rule by consent, not only force) · Scott (negotiation, resistance, informal governance filling state vacuums).
  8. Technology's double edge:Tapscott (blockchain — accountability built into the code) vs Zuboff (whoever controls the data exerts influence) vs Tufekci (control of the narrative beats control of institutions).
  9. India's three challenges through the new lens:fragmented power structures (Nandy — multiple overlapping structures vying for legitimacy) · culture–law conflict (Menon) · digital governance vs inclusion (Aadhaar; Khera).
  10. Good vs bad: Good = accountability (Scandinavia), rule of law (Singapore), transparency (Germany/Sweden), participation (Norway), efficiency (Singapore), inclusiveness (New Zealand). Bad = corruption (Nigeria), no accountability (North Korea), weak rule of law, exclusion (Venezuela), inefficiency (Zimbabwe). India: CPI 2025 — 91/182, score 39; WJP Rule of Law 2025 — 86/143, score 0.49.— TRANSPARENCY & RTI (from ) —
  1. Transparency = openness, clarity and accessibility of government processes, actions and decision-making → informed citizens → accountability and trust → ↓corruption, ↑civic engagement, ↑public services. Stiglitz: information is a public good; transparency cures information asymmetry. Bentham: the more strictly we are watched, the better we behave. Locke: meaningful consent needs access to information. Sen: transparency prevents famines, forces answerability. International anchor: UDHR Art. 19 — seek, receive and impart information.
  2. RTI Act 2005 — the numbers: request in writing/electronic, English/Hindi/official language, to CPIO/SPIO (or APIO); no reasons required; transfer to correct authority within 5 days; decision in 30 days, or 48 hours where life or liberty is concerned; failure = deemed refusal; penalty ₹250/day, capped at ₹25,000, plus disciplinary action for persistent default; burden of proving diligence is on the CPIO.
  3. Sec. 4 — constant endeavour to disclose suo motu, including by internet, "so that the public have minimum resort to the use of this Act." RaaG: ~50% of applications exist only because Sec. 4 is flouted; +25% are routine service queries → 75% of the load is administrative failure, not citizen misuse.
  4. Sec. 8(1) exemptions (a)–(j): sovereignty/security/foreign relations · contempt of court · breach of privilege · commercial confidence* · fiduciary* · foreign government confidence · endangerment of life/source · impeding investigation · Cabinet papers (but decisions, reasons and material must be published once the matter is over) · personal information*. \*= public-interest override applies. Proviso: information that cannot be denied to Parliament shall not be denied to any person — ▲ now shrunk by DPDP 2023 to Sec. 8(1)(j) alone.
  5. CIC:Chief IC + up to 10 ICs; appointed by the President on a committee of PM (Chair) + LoP in Lok Sabha + a Union Cabinet Minister nominated by the PM; eminence in public life — law, science & technology, social service, management, journalism, mass media, administration; no MP/MLA, office of profit, political party, business or profession; term as prescribed by the Centre, max 65 years, no reappointment; an IC may become CIC, aggregate not more than 5 years; removal by President on SC inquiry for proved misbehaviour or incapacity, plus five direct grounds (insolvency · moral turpitude conviction · outside paid employment · infirmity of mind or body · prejudicial financial interest).
  6. RTI works — the case bank:Panchampur (Banda, UP) — 15 villagers, absconding teacher → new teacher appointed + enquiry ordered. Kushmal (Orissa, 2010) — K.S. Sagaria, seven ponds never dug, "labourers" included dead people → officials suspended. Gulrahai Primary School, Allahabad (Dec 2006) — nine parents → uniforms delivered January 2007; also Chitrakoot. National scale: CWG and Adarsh.
  7. The evaluations:2nd ARC (2006) RTI: Master Key to Good Governance — inadequate awareness, lack of infrastructure, delays. TI (2019) — backlog, non-compliance, alleged misuse. CHRI — weak Commissions, 2019 amendment diluted tenure/salary protection, digital divide. Aruna Roy — resistance from public authorities. Anjali Bhardwaj — strengthen Commissions, protect whistleblowers (harassment, violence, death). SNS — no proactive disclosure, Sec. 4 unimplemented, long pendency. Visvanathan — success uneven across states, bureaucratic apathy. Shailesh Gandhi + RaaG — misuse is under 5%.State data: Tamil Nadu worst at 14%, Maharashtra 23%; only 10 ICs gave full information (AP, Haryana, Jharkhand, Sikkim, Nagaland, Tripura).
  8. RTI & judiciary:2009 — CIC ordered the SC to disclose judges' assets and Collegium decision-making. 2019 five-judge ruling — the Office of the CJI is a "public authority" under RTI; Delhi HC upheld; CPIO directed to disclose to SC Agarwal. Assets and elevation communications = confidential third-party information → notice to the judge concerned first; disclosure turns on "authentic enquiry relating to the public interest."Deshpande (2012–13) — memos, show-cause notices, censure orders, assets, income returns, gifts of a public servant are personal information exempt under 8(1)(j); "matters between the employee and the employer." Dilution: no appeal against Commission orders, so authorities file writs, and stays are obtained ex-parte.
  9. RTI vs OSA 1923: RTI = post-liberalisation, democratic accountability, information is a public good; OSA = colonial, protects the state's security apparatus, built for the British Empire in India. Sec. 22 → RTI overrides OSA, except where the public interest in confidentiality clearly outweighs disclosure secrecy is the exception, not the rule. OSA never defines "official secrets" → over-classification; and has no public-interest test. Penalty for spying — 3 years and 14 years; "prohibited place"; offences by companies bind persons in charge. Parrikar v. Goa SIC (2014) — balance public interest against security. Law Commission 43rd (1971) — codify "official secrets". 2nd ARC (June 2006) — repeal OSA, substitute a chapter in the National Security Act. Live cases: Rafale, investigative journalism, defence-purchase corruption.
  10. The 2023 squeeze:CERT-In exempted via Sec. 24(2), Second Schedule serial 27 — defensible on national security, cyber-cooperation, data privacy and anti-panic grounds; but costs oversight of spending and collaborations, risks withholding breach information (Aadhaar-scale databases, power grid, election integrity), and starves researchers and journalists of data. DPDP Act 2023 — Parliament-parity proviso narrowed to 8(1)(j) alone; Sec. 35 bars suits against the Centre/Board for good-faith acts. WBPA 2014 — Competent Authority, written complaints, confidentiality of identity, protection from victimisation, 2 years + fine for false complaints, preliminary inquiry first; not applicable to SPG and Army; ▲ no anonymous complaints, investigator sits inside the accused's hierarchy, no incentives, weak implementation, and ▲ never brought into force.

— THE ANTI-CORRUPTION ARCHITECTURE (from ) —

  1. Why the Lokpal exists — four lines: the Constitution established a Democratic Republic to ensure justice for all; India ratified the UN Convention Against Corruption; the Government's commitment to clean and responsive governance has to be reflected in effective bodies to contain and punish corruption; and it was necessary to enact a law for more effective implementation of the said Convention and to provide for prompt and fair investigation and prosecution in cases of corruption. [ADDED] First ARC (1966–70) proposed it; Act assented 1 Jan 2014, in force 16 Jan 2014, first Lokpal March 2019.
  2. Lokpal — composition:Chairperson (is/has been CJI, or is/has been a Judge of the Supreme Court, or an eminent person) + Members not exceeding eight, of whom 50% Judicial Members; not less than 50% of Members from SC/ST/OBC/Minorities and women.Judicial Member = is/has been SC Judge or Chief Justice of a High Court; other Member = impeccable integrity and outstanding ability, ≥25 years' expertise in anti-corruption policy, public administration, vigilance, finance including insurance and banking, law and management.Disqualified: legislator or member of a local body · moral-turpitude conviction · under 45 years · removed/dismissed from Union or State service · office of profit, profession or business.
  3. Lokpal — appointment, tenure, removal, salary : appointed by the President on a Selection Committee of PM (Chairperson) + Speaker of the House of the People + LoP in the House of the People + CJI or an SC Judge nominated by him + one eminent jurist nominated by the President. Term 5 years or 70, whichever earlier; may resign in writing to the President. Removal for misbehaviour by the President after a Supreme Court inquiry on a reference made on a petition signed by at least 100 MPs ; plus three direct grounds — insolvency · outside paid employment · infirmity of mind or body. Salary: Chairperson = CJI; Members = SC Judge. A Member may become Chairperson if total tenure does not exceed five years.
  4. Lokpal — post-office bar & finance : on ceasing to hold office, ineligible for — reappointment · any diplomatic assignment, administrator of a UT, or any appointment required by law to be made by the President by warrant under his hand and seal · any other office of profit under the Union or a State · contesting any election of President, Vice-President, MP, MLA, Municipality or Panchayat for five years from relinquishing the post.Administrative expenses, salaries, allowances and pensions are charged upon the Consolidated Fund of India.
  5. Lokpal — jurisdiction and its fences : covers the Prime Minister, Ministers, members of Parliament, Groups A, B, C and D officers and officials of the Central Government, plus bodies receiving foreign donation under FCRA 2010 in excess of ₹10 lakh a year.Fences: PM excluded on international relations, external and internal security, public order, atomic energy and space, and inquiry needs a full bench with ≥⅔ approval; Art. 105(2) bars anything said or voted in Parliament; no complaint after seven years from the alleged offence.
  6. Lokpal — machinery:Inquiry Wing under a Director of Inquiry (preliminary inquiry into PCA 1988 offences) · Prosecution Wing under a Director of Prosecution · superintendence over, and power to direct, the Delhi Special Police Establishment in respect of matters referred by the Lokpal · Special Courts constituted by the Central Government as recommended by the Lokpal, to complete each trial within one year · every public servant declares assets and liabilities of self, spouse and dependent children — the 2016 Amendment moved disclosure from 'website' to the 'manner prescribed by the Central Government'.
  7. Lokpal — the performance record :5,680 complaints in 2021-22, of which over 5,100 were yet to be registered (RTI reply). Budget ₹101.29 cr (2019-20) revised to ₹18.01 cr; ₹74.7 cr (2020-21) revised to ₹29.67 cr; ₹39.67 cr (2021-22); ₹33.32 cr (2024-25) for establishment and construction-related charged expenditure.No significant convictions.Justice Dilip B. Bhosale, one of four judicial members appointed in March 2019, resigned on 6 January 2020 citing lack of enough work — "I was sitting absolutely idle… 15-20 cases a month… It will not deliver." A PIL, then a contempt case; the Supreme Court directed appointments even without a formally recognised LoP.
  8. Lokayukta — Karnataka :Justice N. Santosh Hegde (2006–2011) investigated the illegal mining scam involving former CM B.S. Yediyurappa, leading to the Chief Minister's resignation; the institution was effective in initiating action against corrupt officials. ▲ Its powers were diluted — the Anti-Corruption Bureau (ACB) created in Karnataka in 2016 took away many of its functions, significantly reducing its effectiveness. Institutions are diluted by duplication, not repeal.
  9. CVC :apex body promoting integrity, transparency and accountability in public administration; established 1964 on the Santhanam Committee's recommendation; statutory under the Central Vigilance Commission Act, 2003 (following Vineet Narain, 1997). Appointed by the President by warrant under his hand and seal on a committee of PM (Chairperson) + Minister of Home Affairs + LoP in the House of the People. Term 4 years or 65, whichever earlier; CVC ineligible for reappointment in the Commission. Removal for proved misbehaviour or incapacity by the President after SC inquiry, plus five grounds — insolvency · moral-turpitude conviction (in the opinion of the Central Government) · outside paid employment · infirmity · prejudicial financial interest.Role: supervision and monitoring of vigilance in central organisations, PSUs and autonomous bodies · advisory · complaint handling and preliminary inquiry · preliminary inquiry into Lokpal referrals (Gr. A, B, C & D) · superintendence over the DSPE (CBI) for PCA 1988 investigations · chairs the committees recommending ED appointments (Deputy Director and above, including the Director) and CBI appointments (SP and above, except Director, CBI).Impact:Integrity Pacts in public procurement, vigilance awareness. Challenges:no independent investigative power, overlapping jurisdictions, focus on mid- and lower-level officials.
  10. The turf, in one line each :Lokpal = more powerful and independent, reaches the PM, MPs and Group A, has its own investigative wing; CVC = vigilance inside central departments and PSUs, "except the political authorities", and depends on the CBI; overlap risks duplication or confusion where both receive a complaint about the same official; and the UPSC's disciplinary advice can conflict with the CVC's vigilance advice on the same officer's integrity. ▲ Sec. 17A, PCA 1988 — no police officer may enquire, inquire or investigate an offence relatable to any recommendation made or decision taken by a public servant in discharge of official functions without previous approval of the Union Government / State Government / the authority competent to remove him. Two watchdogs, one investigating agency, four exits.— THE INVESTIGATING AGENCIES (from ) —
  1. CBI — what it is :Dept. of Personnel, Ministry of Personnel, Pension & Public Grievances; premier investigating police agency in India; nodal police agency coordinating investigation on behalf of Interpol Member countries. ▲ No Act of its own.
  2. CBI — the origin sequence :Special Police Establishment created under a Deputy Inspector General of Police by the Government of India in 1941 by an executive order, to investigate bribery and corruption in transactions with which the War and Supply Department was concerned; extended to Railways at the end of 1942; Delhi Special Police Establishment Act brought into force in 1946, transferring superintendence to the Home Department and enlarging functions to all departments of the Govt. of India; jurisdiction over all Union Territories, extendable to States with the consent of the State Government concerned; renamed CBI by Home Ministry resolution dated 1.4.1963; PSU employees added in due course, and Public Sector Banks and their employees after the 1969 nationalisation. Executive order → wartime statute → resolution for the name.
  3. CBI — consent and its limits : consent is case-specific or general; general consent = "consent by default, in the absence of which the CBI would have to apply to the state government in every case, and before taking even small actions." ▲ CBI cannot take suo motu cognizance of a case in a state — corruption involving Centre officials and PSU staff, or violent crime. Avenues:if the case was not registered in that state (Chhattisgarh case), and entrustment by the Supreme Court or High Courts on petitions by aggrieved parties.
  4. CBI — superintendence, split three ways :PCA 1988 investigations → the CVC · matters referred by the Lokpal → the Lokpal · "all other matters" → the Central Government (which also holds cadre, postings and budget). Three masters, one employer.
  5. CBI Director : appointed under the DSPE Act (1946) and amendments brought by the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013; by the Centre, on a three-member Committee — PM (chairperson) · LoP in the Lok Sabha · CJI or a Supreme Court judge nominated by him. The only committee in this compendium with no executive majority. Vineet Narain v. Union of India ordered a minimum tenure of two years; "5 Years" [ADDED — the 2021 extension cap].
  6. CBI — the Standing Committee's verdict (department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Personnel, Public Grievances, Law and Justice): the DSPE Act "has many limitations" → enact a new law defining the status, functions and powers of the CBI, with safeguards to ensure objectivity and impartiality; 1,709 posts vacant of a sanctioned 7,295; reduce dependence on deputationists, recruit permanent inspectors and DySPs; ▲ annual report not accessible to the general public; maintain a centralised case-management database.
  7. ED :'Enforcement Unit' 1956, renamed 'Enforcement Directorate' 1957; Ministry of Finance; investigation of the offence of money laundering and violations of foreign exchange laws; Cryptos.Director appointed by the Central Government on a committee of — Central Vigilance Commissioner (Chairperson) · Vigilance Commissioners · Secretary, Home Affairs · Secretary, Personnel · Secretary, Department of Revenue. All serving Union officials — no LoP, no judge.2021 CVC Amendment: office for not less than two years, extendable in public interest, on the Committee's recommendation, for reasons recorded in writing, up to one year at a time, with no extension after five years in total including the initial appointment.
  8. PMLA Sec. 45 (the only section number quoted in the whole series): "Offences to be cognizable and non-bailable" — (a) every offence punishable under this Act shall be cognizable; (b) no accused of an offence punishable above three years under Part A of the Schedule shall be released on bail unless (i) the Public Prosecutor has been given an opportunity to oppose, and (ii) where he opposes, the court is satisfied there are reasonable grounds for believing that he is not guilty of such offence and that he is not likely to commit any offence while on bail — the twin conditions.Proviso: a person under sixteen, or a woman, or sick or infirm, may be released on bail if the Special Court so directs. Same device in the Drugs and Cosmetics Act 1940, the NDPS Act 1985 and the UAPA 1967.
  9. The PMLA bail spine :Nikesh Tarachand Shah (2017) — two-judge Bench struck down the bail provision as unconstitutional, the onerous conditions "not a reasonable classification" → Finance Act, 2018 re-enacted it ▲ (a Money Bill route) → Vijay Madanlal Choudhary (2022) upheld it: seriousness of money-laundering, "posing serious threat to the sovereignty and integrity of the country", "part of a global response to money laundering and terror financing" — but note the source's own two counters: maximum punishment of 7 years, and "Money Bill question?" → Aug 2024 "Liberty of the individual is always the rule and deprivation is the exception… Section 45, by imposing twin conditions, does not rewrite this principle", and Sec. 45 may be relaxed where custody has been long with "no likelihood of conclusion of trial within a short span" → K. Kavitha (2024) — a woman is not denied the proviso to Sec. 45(1) merely because she was educated or sophisticated or an MP or an MLA.
  10. PMLA — the criticism and the numbers :draconian powers (arrest without an FIR, provisional attachment, detention) · low conviction rate (0.75%) raising concerns of overuse to harass political opponents or business figures · broad definition of "proceeds of crime" — which may include property equivalent in value, even if acquired before the offence and from legitimate known sources ▲ [attribution garbled in the source — see] · allegations of arbitrary and political use · burden of proof reversed — "the onus is on the accused to prove that the property or asset is not the proceeds of crime." ▲ [CONFLICT within ]"Conviction rate under PMLA is 93 pc: Govt, August 2024" vs "0.75%" — both correct: 5,297 cases registered 2014–2024, 40 convictions, 3 acquittals → 40/43 = 93% of decided cases, 40/5,297 = 0.75% of registered cases. Justice Ujjal Bhuyan: the Supreme Court questioned the ED on quality of prosecution — over 5,000 cases, only 40 convictions. Way forward: Institutional Autonomy · Parliamentary Oversight · Transparent Appointments.— THE CAG AND PUBLIC AUDIT (from ) —
  1. Art. 148 — the five protections :"There shall be a Comptroller and Auditor-General of India who shall be appointed by the President by warrant under his hand and seal and shall only be removed from office in like manner and on like grounds as a Judge of the Supreme Court." · oath in the Third Schedule · "the salary and other conditions of service shall not be varied to his disadvantage after his appointment" · "shall not be eligible for further office" · "expenses of the office … including all salaries, allowances and pensions payable to or in respect of persons serving in that office, shall be charged upon the Consolidated Fund of India." ▲ What Art. 148 does not provide: any selection committee, any qualification, any consultation.
  2. The other Articles :Art. 149 — Duties and Powers, prescribed by or under law made by Parliament → the CAG (DPC) Act, 1971 ▲ (heading-only slide). Art. 150 — Form of Accounts of the Union and of the States, prescribed by the President on the advice of the CAG ▲ (heading-only). Art. 279 — calculation of "net proceeds", ascertained and certified by the CAG, certificate final ▲ (heading-only). Art. 151 — Union reports → President → each House of Parliament; State reports → Governor → the State Legislature.
  3. The DPC Act, 1971 :salary equal to a Judge of the Supreme Court · term 6 years or 65 years of age, whichever is earlier · resignation · the 1976 Amendment. Duty: "to audit all expenditure from the Consolidated Fund of India and of each State and of each Union territory having a Legislative Assembly and to ascertain whether the moneys shown in the accounts as having been disbursed were legally available for and applicable to the service or purpose to which they have been applied or charged and whether the expenditure conforms to the authority which governs it"; and "to audit all transactions of the Union and of the States relating to Contingency Funds and Public Accounts."
  4. The substantially-financed test — two limbs, conjunctive: a grant or loan from the Consolidated Fund of India or of any State in a financial year of not less than ₹25 lakhANDnot less than 75% of the total expenditure of that body or authority. The test is about dependence, not size — which is why the largest recipients are often the least auditable.
  5. The two cases :Arvind Gupta v. Union of India (2013) — the Supreme Court upheld the CAG's function to carry out performance audit. Reghu Nath Kelkar v. Union of India*, Bombay HC (2009), a PIL — on an allegation of failure to conduct a comprehensive audit, the Court considered Sec. 23 of the CAG (DPC) Act and held that "the time, scope and extent of audit are all matters which fall within the jurisdiction of the CAG and is not a matter on which Court ought to tread." The courts enlarged the mandate and refused to police it.*
  6. The jurisdictional debate — the four moves:(1) the shift — from financial/regularity audit to performance audit of efficiency, economy and effectiveness (Mid-Day Meal, MGNREGA, infrastructure). (2) the distinction — "policy decisions (the prerogative of the executive)" vs "implementation of policies (which the CAG is tasked with auditing)"; he "cannot question the merit or demerit of policy decisions themselves."(3) against — close scrutiny of implementation may indirectly influence policy and overstep into political decision-making and policy formulation. (4) the test — no overstepping so long as the focus is a) transparency in government expenditure · b) efficiency in policy implementation · c) prevention of misuse of public resources.
  7. The two essay lines (unattributed — use as views, not quotations):"As policy and systems are a cause and effect construct, the outcome of policy on systems is open to question. The CAG has the wherewithal to analyse both … The larger question is if the role of the CAG is only one of attesting public expenditure, or if it extends to assisting those engaged in governance." · "His role could not have been envisaged by the framers of the Constitution as one of merely an accountant to the government … Viewing the CAG's role as adversarial is self-defeating."
  8. The accountability chain :Enhancing Parliamentary Oversight — reports scrutinised by the Public Accounts Committee (PAC) and the Committee on Public Undertakings (COPU) · Promoting Public Awareness · Exposing Corruption — 2G Spectrum, Coal Block Allocation, Commonwealth Games, producing public outcry and judicial action. ▲ [ADDED] Laying does not compel examination; PAC recommendations are not binding. He can discover everything and enforce nothing — authority without consequence.
  9. The audit findings :IOA–RIL — a flawed sponsorship agreement causing a ₹24 crore loss to the Indian Olympic Association, the issue being failure to adjust the sponsorship amount when additional rights were granted to RIL for more sporting events without an increase in payment. Urban local bodies, Uttar Pradesh, 2015–2020 — 68.72% of total funds from government grants, only 16.16% from own revenue; of 15 functions fully and one partially devolved, ULBs were solely responsible for one, had no role in one, limited role in eleven, were mere implementing agencies in two, and shared one with government departments — "this defeated the purpose of the 74th Constitutional Amendment Act"; the only fully controlled function was the construction, operation and maintenance of crematoriums and burial grounds.
  10. The 1976 change and the multi-member question :"In 1976, the separation of Union government accounts from audit at the ministry level led to the creation of the civil accounts cadre. The CAG ceased to control this cadre and this was brought under the secretary (expenditure) in the ministry of finance." Multi-member CAG — for: individual bias, collective deliberation, sectoral members (defence, infrastructure, health, education), workload, resistance to political pressure; commissions of audit, and courts of audit in France and Mexico vested with quasi-judicial and punitive powers; Germany, and the UK National Audit Office with a Board structure ▲ (the source garbles these three into one sentence). Against — the source's two questions: the Constitution provided the option of a multimember Election Commission and deliberately did not for the CAG — "would it be right to obliterate that distinction by an amendment?"; and the CAG's provisions fall outside Art. 368(2), presumably because the framers did not expect them to be amended — but would any amendment affecting an office that is "CAG for the States as well as the Centre" not require consultation with the States?— HUMAN RIGHTS & THE NHRC (from ) —
  1. NHRC = statutory (PHRA 1993), est. 1993, in conformity with the Paris Principles (Paris workshop 1991, endorsed by the UNGA 1993). The Act provides for three tiers — NHRC · SHRCs · Human Rights Courts.
  2. Composition (post-2019): Chairperson — has been CJI or a Judge of the Supreme Court; one Judge of the SC; one former Chief Justice of a High Court; three members, at least one a woman; plus seven ex-officio chairpersons — NCSC, NCST, NCW, NCBC, National Commission for Minorities, NCPCR, Chief Commissioner for Persons with Disabilities.
  3. 2019 amendment: term 5 years → 3 years (or 70), for NHRC and SHRCs; and the five-year limit on reappointment removed. Shorter term + uncapped renewal = the sharpest independence critique available.
  4. Five functions: investigate (own motion or petition) · intervene in court proceedings · advise government on policy · monitor standards and safeguards · promote research and awareness · annual reports. Not one of them ends in an order.
  5. Investigation Division = on-the-spot verification of State replies, "a disincentive… against sending false or unsubstantiated reports" — the strongest defence of a recommendatory body. ▲ And the same Division draws the SCA's "police personnel… conflict(s) of interest" objection.
  6. Independence, in the source's own words: supposed to be completely independent — "even though the PHRA, 1993 does not say so"; Sec. 11 = manpower from the government; Sec. 32 = grants "as it may consider fit"; annual reports delayed two to three years.
  7. "Recommendatory powers" only — Paramjit Kaur v. State of Punjab (1998): recommendations should carry more weight, but the Court did not make them binding. Krishna Iyer: "the biggest post office in India."HL Dattu (June 2016): "a toothless tiger"; SC 2017, on 1,528 alleged extra-judicial killings in Manipur, adopted the phrase.
  8. Paris Principles — six criteria:broad mandate · autonomy from government · independence guaranteed by statute or Constitution · pluralism · adequate resources · adequate powers of investigation. Score the NHRC against them: one clearly met.
  9. GANHRI — 120 NHRIs; SCA = 16 'A'-status NHRIs, four per region (Americas, Europe, Africa, Asia-Pacific); review every five years, with OHCHR, UNDP and civil society. Timeline: first accredited 1999 · 'A' 2006 · retained 2011 · deferred 2016 · 'A' restored 2017 · withheld 2023 · deferred again May 2024.
  10. The cost of losing it: the NHRC "cannot represent India or vote at the UN Human Rights Council"; 'B' status = participate, but no vote and no governance positions.Amnesty and others fear it is "reduced to an ornamental body."— THE CIVIL SERVICES (from ) —
  1. Art. 310 — every member of a defence service, a Union civil service, an all-India service or a civil post under the Union holds office during the pleasure of the President; State services, during the pleasure of the Governor.
  2. Art. 311 — (1) no dismissal or removal by an authority subordinate to that which appointed; (2) no dismissal, removal or reduction in rank except after an inquiry with notice of charges and a reasonable opportunity of being heard. Three exceptions:conviction on a criminal charge · not reasonably practicable (reasons in writing) · security of the State (President/Governor satisfied) — and the practicability decision is final.
  3. Art. 312 — Rajya Sabha resolution by two-thirds of members present and voting, in the national interest, lets Parliament create all-India services (including an all-India judicial service); IAS and IPS are deemed created under it; AIJS shall not include any post inferior to a district judge.
  4. Constituent Assembly, both sides: Patel — "maintaining the structure of the administration", a service with "independence to speak out its mind"; Ambedkar — prevents provincialization; against — KT Shah (loyalty to the Centre, not the states) and T. T. Krishnamachari (less responsive to the needs of the states). Nehru on the ICS: "neither Indian, nor Civil, nor a Service."
  5. Rationale of AIS: national integration · co-operative federalism · repository of talent · President's Rule · independence — plus administrative uniformity in law enforcement, revenue collection and service delivery.
  6. Art. 315–320 (UPSC): appointment by President/Governor; half the members must have ten years' government service; 6 years or 65 (Union) / 62 (State/Joint); no reappointment; removal only on misbehaviour after a Supreme Court reference and report, plus insolvency, paid employment, infirmity, and contract-interest = deemed misbehaviour; conditions not variable to disadvantage; UPSC Chairman ineligible for any further government employment; expenses charged on the Consolidated Fund.

Lateral entry — against:63% of Mains candidates 2017–21 were engineers; 2017 batch — 118 of 264 (44.69%), 19 of 20 toppers; the "domain" argument is "misleading sophistry"; the civil servant is a synthesiser; 10 years in the field; the dam (land acquisition, R&R, forest diversion, EIA/SIA, financial closure, PPPs); public administration is itself the hardest domain; patronage — "birds of passage… in one generation there shall be no permanent civil service left."
  10. Reform:TSR Subramaniam (2013) — Civil Services Act, a CSB, and civil servants to obey only written orders; the CSB as re-constituted 30.01.2024 is chaired ex-officio by the Cabinet Secretary; Mission Karmayogi (2020) — iGOT, 46 lakh employees, ₹510.86 crore (2020-21 to 2024-25), $50 million multilateral, "rule-based → role-based", Yogah Karmasu Kaushalam; onboarding 3.13 lakh (Jan 2023) → ~44.3 lakh on the dashboard. ▲ All input measures; no outcome measure.— THE COMPARATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL SCHEME (from ) —
  1. The Preamble:"WE, THE PEOPLE OF INDIA… SOVEREIGN SOCIALIST SECULAR DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC… JUSTICE, social, economic and political; LIBERTY of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship; EQUALITY of status and of opportunity; FRATERNITY assuring the dignity of the individual and the unity and integrity of the Nation… this twenty-sixth day of November, 1949." ▲ [ADDED] "Socialist", "secular" and "integrity" were inserted by the 42nd Amendment, 1976; Berubari (1960) said the Preamble was not part of the Constitution, Kesavananda (1973) held that it is.
  2. Indian socialism:"rooted in democratic principles… blends state intervention with the protection of individual rights and a market economy"; inclusive and non-totalitarian. Ambedkar — equality, Dalit empowerment and land reforms, but "within democratic and constitutional limits"; Nehru — a mixed economy with the state holding infrastructure and energy. Instruments: MGNREGA, health insurance, UBI.
  3. The three socialism cases:Kesavananda (1973) — basic structure, which includes socialism, cannot be altered; Minerva Mills* (1980) — socialism must balance socio-economic development and individual rights; D.S. Nakara* (1983) — socialism aims at "elimination of inequality in income and status and standards of life."
  4. The other socialisms:China — Marxism–Leninism → Deng's "socialism with Chinese characteristics", post-1978 market socialism, SOEs in banking, energy, telecom, BRI, the Jack Ma / Ed-Tech crackdown. Russia — Lenin and Stalin, central planning to 1991; Yeltsin and Putin → oligarchic capitalism with universal healthcare, pensions and state oil and gas (Gazprom, Rosneft); ▲ the source wrongly calls Gorbachev a "post-Soviet intellectual" — he was the last Soviet leader, and perestroika/glasnost were Soviet-era policy. Cuba — Marxist-Leninist, all industry state-controlled, universal healthcare as its success; Venezuela — Chávez and Maduro, 21st-century socialism, oil nationalisation + populist spending → hyperinflation and collapse.
  5. Four secularisms in one line each:India = principled distance — the state may "intervene or abstain… whichever better promotes liberty, equality and social justice", plus positive secularism and sarva dharma sambhava. USA = separationist — First Amendment, Jefferson's wall of separation, Locke. France = laïcité — 1905 law, neutral public space, Durkheim (national unity) and Rousseau (civic religion). China = state-controlled secularism — atheist party, Marx's "opium of the people", Mao, Xinjiang "re-education camps".
  6. The four features of laïcité:strict separation of church and state · neutral public space (symbols in schools, government buildings and public offices discouraged or banned) · equal treatment of all religions · religious freedom, with strict rules on the public display of religious identity. Enforcement: 2004 conspicuous-symbols ban · 2010 full-face-covering ban upheld by the Constitutional Council on laïcité and gender equality · Charlie Hebdo, 2015.

Doe (2000, 6–3) — student-led prayer unconstitutional if perceived as school-endorsed. Masterpiece Cakeshop* (2018, 7–2) — the Commission showed hostility to religious belief, violating Free Exercise. TWA v. Hardison* (1977) ▲ heading-only. Dobbs — no constitutional right to abortion; not "deeply rooted in the nation's history and traditions"; the result is "a patchwork of laws."

Challenges, as a four-word list:UCC · terrorism · mob lynching and cow vigilantism · minority appeasement and majority religion dominance. ▲ [ADDED] The source cites no Article — supply Art. 25, 26, 27, 28, 29–30 and 44 yourself.

The four summaries, verbatim:India — democratic socialism, blending state control with capitalism and constitutionalism; China — state-controlled capitalism under the banner of socialism… political authoritarianism; Russia — from authoritarian socialism to oligarchic capitalism; Cuba and Venezuela — state-centric socialism… Cuba maintaining stability but stagnation, Venezuela severe economic challenges. — E-GOVERNANCE (from ) —

  1. The definitions:Bhatnagar — IT applied to government functioning to produce SMART governance: Simple, Moral, Accountable, Responsive, Transparent.Nilekani — "not just about technology, but about fundamentally changing the way government interacts with citizens."UN — ICT for "information and public services", improving governance through participation, efficiency and transparency.UN EGDI: India 97 of 193 (2024 survey) — ▲ [ADDED] its three components are OSI, TII and HCI.

Halachmi's five models:Broadcasting (dissemination for an informed citizenry) · Critical Flow ("routing information of critical value to the targeted audience") · Comparative Analysis (assimilating best practices for developing countries) · E-Advocacy / Mobilisation and Lobbying (virtual communities influencing global decision-making) · Interactive-Service ("individuals' direct participation… greater objectivity and transparency in decision-making"). ▲ Two taxonomies, one shared name — Halachmi ranks Interactive-Service last, the maturity ladder ranks it third (§5.7.4).
  4. Applications:G2C — Aadhaar (UIDAI, 12-digit, biometric + demographic; DBT, PDS, financial inclusion), DigiLocker, UMANG. G2B — MCA21, GST Portal. G2G — e-Office, NeGP, KHAJANE (Karnataka treasury; first in the country to computerise the entire treasury; the only project where activity is trackable from budget approval to rendering of accounts). ▲ [ADDED] the fourth channel, G2E, is missing — supply it.

The platforms in one line each:DigiLocker — MeitY, Digital India, 330.49 M users / 7.76 B documents, ▲ "limited to those with access to the internet and smartphones."UMANG — MeitY + NeGD, Mobile Governance, Central to Local. MADAD — MEA consular grievances + locate Missions abroad; an ISL Chatbot. ▲ DigiYatra — heading only.

BHOOMI, the before picture (the most examinable case study in the source): land records held by 900 village accountants, each serving 3–4 villages; the document is the RTC — Record of Rights, Tenancy and Crops, needed for crop loans, hypothecation, electricity connection, subsidies, sale of land and partition deeds; the wait was 3 to 30 days; mutation notices were "often" never issued or pasted; and an update by the Revenue Inspector"would usually take one-two years."

The data:821 Mn active users, 55% penetration (2023), growing 8% y-o-y; 574 → 821 Mn over 2019–23; rural overtook urban in 2021 and is now 442 Mn vs 378 Mn; rural 54% of all users, towns under 10 lakh 23%, top 9 cities 14%, small metros 9%; male 54% / female 46%; 98 minutes a day all-India (urban 101, rural 94), 93% using it daily; ▲ "around half of rural India are still not active." Source: IAMAI–KANTAR, Internet in India Report 2023.

The one enforceable service in nine decks — Aaple Sarkar, under the Maharashtra Right to Public Services Act: an Income Certificate in 15 days, from a Nayab Tahsildar, appealable to the Tahsildar and then the Sub Divisional Officer. Contrast it with the 3-to-30 days and one-to-two years of pre-Bhoomi Karnataka — that pairing is the whole argument for statutory service standards.

Potential, and the caution:BharatNet and digital literacy · AI and big data (CRIS's Ideal Train Profile, 2022, vacant berths in 200+ trains) · blockchain for land records and elections · UMANG integration · MyGov participation · mobile governance. ▲ The source has no limitations section at all — supply IN-CAP (Infrastructure · Capacity · Access · Process · Protection, §5.7.6) and the two structural gaps: no entitlement and no outcome measurement.— THE CITIZEN'S CHARTER (from ) —
  1. The definition, and the collision inside it: a Citizen's Charter is a "written, voluntary declaration by service providers" highlighting standards of service delivery · availability of choice for consumers · avenues for grievance redressal; also "an official document issued by public service providers… to make public services more transparent, accountable, and responsive." An official document containing a voluntary promise — and "the Charter lacks statutory backing… Citizens have no legal recourse."
  2. Origin and diffusion: launched in the UK in 1991; John Major — "sees public services through the eyes of those who use them… For too long the provider has dominated and now it is the time of the user… raise quality, increase choice, secure better value and extend accountability." Adopted by Belgium, France, Canada, Australia, Malaysia, Spain, Portugal, India.
  3. India's adoption: began at the 1996 Conference of Chief Secretaries of all States and UTs on "Effective and Responsive Administration" → "Action Plan for Effective and Responsive Government" → first sectors: Railways, Telecom and Public Distribution → later taken up by many States. ▲ Supersedes the earlier [ADDED] "1997".
  4. What makes a great Charter — the eight, in three families: drafting — Clarity · Measurable Standards; obligation — Transparency (publish performance data) · Grievance Redressal · Service Recovery and Compensation; institutionalisation — Periodic Review · Stakeholder Involvement · Training and Sensitization. Mnemonic: CMT-G · RSST. Point 7 is the one a voluntary Charter structurally cannot deliver.
  5. The six factors hindering full potential — the 2024 PYQ's own words:Lack of Awareness (extends to officials too) · Poor Implementation ("remains a formality"; standards "vague, lacking specific, measurable, and enforceable" ones) · Absence of Legal Backing ("no legal recourse") · No Effective Grievance Redressal ("slow and inaccessible") · Bureaucratic Resistance ("an additional burden"; red-tapism; no incentives) · Inadequate Training. Mnemonic A-PLG-BT. Write it as a chain: factor 3 causes 1, 2, 4 and 5.
  6. The DARPG evaluation (2002–03) — a professional agency built a standardised internal and external evaluation model and assessed 5 Central Government Organisations + 15 Departments/Organisations in Andhra Pradesh, Maharashtra and Uttar Pradesh. Findings: Charters "not formulated through a consultative process"; providers "not familiar with the philosophy, goals and main features"; "adequate publicity… had not been given in any of the Departments evaluated"; "no funds… specifically earmarked." Six recommendations: consult citizens and staff at every stage · staff orientation (incl. grievance handling, communication, team building) · a database on consumer grievances and redress · wider publicity · earmarked budgets · replication of best practices. ▲ Not one recommends legal backing.
  7. The two Acts that fixed it — memorise both sets of numbers.MADHYA PRADESH Public Services Guarantee Act, 2010 — "first-of-its-kind in the country"; 52 services; time fixed per service; fine ₹250/day up to ₹5,000; two-stage appeal, the second able to fine and order disciplinary action; "where fine is imposed on delinquent officer, the applicants are paid compensation"; UNPSA 2012, category "improving the delivery of Public Services", from 483 nominations across 73 countries. KARNATAKA — SAKALA, under the Karnataka Guarantee of Services to Citizens Act, 2011 (renamed Karnataka Sakala Services Act by the 2014 Amendment — see the [CONFLICT] at §3.20.4); over 1,000 services; compensation for delay; IT-enabled real-time tracking; Form-A display board — service · compensation fee · checklist · designated officer · competent officer · appellate authority, each with a stipulated time — and "Rs.20/- per day per service from his Salary."
  8. The worked Charters, and the one criticism to make of each.MIB — DTH 4 months, MSO 2 months, HITS 4 months, ▲ but every clock runs "from the date of receipt of security clearance from MHA", so the citizen's real wait is outside the promise. DOP — measured "from posting/booking to delivery": First Class local 2, rest of country 5–6 days; Speed Post local 1–2, rest 4–5; +1 day for Branch Offices; exclusions for holidays, curfew, bandh, strike, force majeure; standards tied to Gazette notification 486 of 23.09.2013. UPSC — mostly institutional autobiography. BWSSB (Sakala) — new residential connection 14 → 15 → 30 working days; multi-storeyed 42 → 15 → 30; UGD blockage 03 → 03 → 04 working days.
  9. The Bill that would have made it law — The Right of Citizens for Time Bound Delivery of Goods and Services and Redressal of their Grievances:"Every public authority should be mandated by law to publish a Citizens Charter"; the Charter to "detail the goods and services to be provided and their timelines"; a citizen "legally empowered to file a complaint" about (a) the citizens charter, (b) the functioning of a public authority, or (c) violation of a law, policy or scheme; plus "increased penalty in case of non-compliance" and "companies as well as citizens." ▲ [ADDED: introduced 2011, lapsed — verify]. Limb (c) is far wider than a Charter grievance.
  10. The RTI collision, and the closing thesis. The source: "the notion of 'information' and 'grievance' are interchangeable for all practical purposes" — "citizens are increasingly using the RTI Act to redress their grievances by asking the information related to the status of their request", risking "ample confusion for the citizens in exercising their rights." Because only RTI carries a 30-day clock and a ₹250-a-day penalty, citizens convert service grievances into information requests. ▲ And the source's realism caution:"departments should not promise more than they can deliver… the capabilities of the service provider must be taken into account." Close any Charter answer with: the Charter announced an obligation the state never incurred — an officer, a clock, an appeal and a price are what convert it into a right, and only a legislature can supply them.

— AI IN GOVERNANCE (from ) —

  1. The definition, and the two words that decide its scope: AI in governance is "the use of data-driven algorithms, machine learning, automation, and predictive analytics by the state to improve policy formulation, service delivery, regulation, and public administration." "By the state" — this is AI used by government, not AI regulated by government; "AI in governance" and "AI governance" are two different questions and only the first is taught (§2.7.1).
  2. The three stages:1. Computerisation – Digitising records · 2. E-Governance – Online service delivery · 3. AI Governance – Predictive, automated, intelligent administration. Split stage 3's three words: predictive = acts before the event · automated = no official acts · intelligent = weighs rather than applies a rule. ▲ This is the compendium's third taxonomy — it nests inside five-stage ladder (§5.9.1).
  3. The policy framework in one line — and its weakness in the next:NITI Aayog's National Strategy for AI (#AIforAll), 2018; five "AI for social good" sectors — healthcare, agriculture, education, smart cities & infrastructure, smart mobility & transportation; three proof-of-concept pilots — agriculture (crop yield), healthcare, education (school dropout). ▲ That is the entire framework: one body, one document, one year — and the deployments run to late 2025, so the deployment has outrun the framework by seven years (§3.21.2, §11.7).
  4. The seven "Key Sutras":Trust is the Foundation · People First · Innovation over Restraint · Fairness & Equity · Accountability · Understandable by Design · Safety, Resilience & Sustainability. Sutra 3 is the only one that takes a side — "Innovation over Restraint" is a stated preference for permissive regulation sitting in the same list as "Accountability", with no rule for resolving the conflict. ▲ Attribute the seven to no body and no year — the source gives the diagram no source.
  5. The scope map — five domains, fifteen applications, and the order nobody notices:A. Service Delivery (predictive analytics in welfare · chatbots · DBT fraud detection) · B. Health (outbreak prediction · radiology diagnostics · health-records analytics) · C. Agriculture (crop yield · soil health · weather) · D. Internal Security (predictive policing · facial recognition · drone surveillance) · E. Judicial Reforms (SUPACE · e-Courts digitization · case-backlog analytics). A–C advise; D and E decide — every constitutional objection attaches to the last two (§5.9.2).
  6. The estate, in the six numbers to memorise:7.63 crore Farmer IDs and 23.5 crore plots (AgriStack/KDSS) · 28-crore-record CCTNS across 16,000+ police stations · Trinetra: 5 lakh criminals and their associates · JARVIS: 70 prisons, 700+ cameras · Gujarat EWS: 1+ crore students screened, ~1.67 lakh flagged · 78 crore PMFBY farmer applications, 2016–17 to 2024–25. Plus: NPSS 66 crops/432 pest species · ATMAN (DRDO-TCAIR) chest X-rays · MVIS (Railways & DFCCIL) · YES-TECH and CROPIC (PMFBY) · AI traffic in Bengaluru, Kolkata, Chandigarh, Pune, Pimpri-Chinchwad** (§4.13).
  7. THE ONLY MEASURED BEHAVIOURAL OUTCOME IN ELEVEN DECKS: the 2025 Kharif monsoon-onset pilot combined NeuralGCM, ECMWF-AIFS and 125 years of IMD rainfall to send location-specific sowing SMS advisories to 3.88 crore farmers; 31–52% changed planting decisions. The first sourced figure in this compendium measuring a change in citizen behaviour rather than users registered or centres opened — and note the channel: SMS, which needs no smartphone and no internet (§13.12.2). ▲ Caveat honestly: the source records the behavioural change, not the yield or income effect.
  8. Advantages (five) and Limitations (five), which are the same list twice:Faster decision-making · Reduced corruption · Predictive governance · Cost efficiency · Targeted welfare delivery — against Algorithmic bias · Privacy concerns · Lack of accountability · Digital divide · Job displacement. Write them as one sentence, not two lists: targeting is profiling, prediction is pre-judgment, and automation is the removal of the official who could have been persuaded (§5.9.3).
  9. The constitutional slide, written as one escalating argument:Art. 14 – Risk of discrimination · Art. 19 – Free speech implications · Art. 21 – Privacy and due process. Art. 19 is what the citizen stops doing when watched; Art. 14 is who the system watches more closely; Art. 21 is the citizen's inability to answer back — chilling effect, distributional defect, procedural void. The anchor is Puttaswamy and its proportionality test — ▲ the source cites no case at all** (§3.21.4, §12.11). ▲ Art. 14 is now named in the course for the first time in eleven decks — but as a six-word heading, so is narrowed, not closed.
  10. The Way Forward (six, verbatim) and the closing thesis:Human-in-the-loop model · Ethical AI legislation · Independent AI Regulatory Authority · Algorithmic transparency audits · Capacity building of civil servants · Public consultation in AI policy. Close with the source's own line: "AI in governance represents a constitutional moment… Unchecked algorithmic governance, however, may weaken democratic oversight and civil liberties." And add the sentence the source never writes: every accountability mechanism in this syllabus — the CPIO who pays a penalty, the designated officer on Sakala's Form-A, the public servant within the Lokpal's jurisdiction — presupposes a human being who decided and can be asked why; algorithmic governance is the first mode of Indian administration that does not (§14, diagnosis 8).

Do not put any of them inside quotation marks as the speaker's words. Attribute the position instead — "as Justice Chandrachud has argued", "in Harari's formulation" — which is safe, accurate and costs nothing. ▲ Note on: the e-governance module is entirely domestic and adds nothing to this bank.Nine decks in, every comparator above still comes from, or. But the module does supply something this appendix has never had — an internal comparison bank, which is more useful for a governance answer than a foreign one:Karnataka (Bhoomi land records and KHAJANE treasury — the two worked case studies, §4.11.6), Maharashtra (Aaple Sarkar under the Right to Public Services Act — the only entitlement-backed digital service in the compendium, §3.19.4), Uttar Pradesh (eDistrict — six certificates on one platform, §4.11.7), Bengaluru/BBMP (the property-tax portal — the only urban local body anywhere in nine decks), and the five Bhoomi replications — Andhra Pradesh (Mee Bhoomi), Gujarat (E-Dhar), Bihar (Bhu-Abhilekh), Haryana (HALRIS), Himachal Pradesh (Him-Bhoomi). Use these exactly as you use the country rows: a named State with a named scheme beats "some States have digitised land records" every time. ▲ The source reports the replication and no outcome for any of the five (§4.11.6).

Note on: after one wholly India-only deck, the comparators return — and the most useful one is the UK, for the third time.The Citizen's Charter is an imported instrument (UK 1991 → seven named adopters → India 1996), which changes how you should write about it: India did not invent the Charter and did not invent its weakness — it imported a voluntary instrument from a unitary state with a strong administrative-law tradition, and then discovered that a promise without a forum does less work in India than it did in Britain. The comparison to draw, and it is available in one line: the UK's Charter sat alongside an ombudsman, judicial review of administrative action and a service-complaints culture; India's sat alone until a State legislature supplied the missing forum in 2010. [ADDED — the source lists the adopters and compares none of them,] And note the compendium's second external grader: the UNPSA 2012 to Madhya Pradesh, from 483 nominations across 73 countries — the first time an Indian statute rather than an institution is internationally assessed in these notes (contrast GANHRI and the NHRC, §13.7.2).

▲ Note on: the second wholly India-only deck in the series, and the comparison it invites is one you must supply yourself.adds no country, no foreign institution and no international instrument — it is the first India-only deck since (§13.10), and the only comparator it names at all is the World Economic Forum's "human-centric AI governance" position, which is a body rather than a state (§16.1i). ▲ This matters more here than it did for e-governance, because AI regulation is the most actively comparative policy field in the world right now and an examiner will expect at least one external reference point. What this compendium can honestly give you is the shape of the comparison rather than its content: India has chosen a strategy-led, innovation-first approach — its own stated Sutra is "Innovation over Restraint" (§3.21.3) — while the principal alternative model is legislation-led and risk-tiered. ▲ Do not name a foreign statute, year or tier from memory — the safe and sufficient formulation is: India regulates AI through policy and deploys it through departments; other jurisdictions have legislated first and deployed second, and the trade-off between the two approaches is speed against enforceability. Then bring it home with the compendium's own evidence: the UK–India Charter comparison** at Appendix B already establishes that India imports administrative instruments and then discovers they need a forum — AI is the same story arriving earlier: the capability has been imported and deployed at national scale, and the forum has not been built (§14, issue 98).
